quotes.excerpt: Or see the grand beginning, Where space did not extend? Or view the last creation, Where Gods and matter end? Methinks the Spirit whispers, “No man has found ‘pure space,’ Nor seen the outside curtains, Where nothing has a place.”
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose, and it is the load-bearing stanza for how this entry is graded. Verse 2 is where the hymn answers itself, and the answer it gives is a limit on knowledge, not a cosmology: the Spirit whispers that no man has found the bounds. That answer is addressed to the spatial question (“pure space,” “the outside curtains”) rather than to the genealogical one in verse 1, which is left standing unanswered. Recorded so the entry shows that the hymn's own reply to its own questions is agnostic.

quotes.excerpt: The works of God continue, And worlds and lives abound; Improvement and progression Have one eternal round. There is no end to matter; There is no end to space; There is no end to spirit; There is no end to race.
quotes.note: The “There is no end to…” litany, which runs on through verses 4 and 5 (virtue, might, wisdom, light, union, youth, priesthood, truth; glory, love, being, and “no death above”). Tagged MANY-WORLDS for “worlds and lives abound.” Deliberately not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: “Improvement and progression Have one eternal round” says progression is a permanent feature of the universe, not that God is progressing, and reading God into it is exactly the conflation this dataset exists to prevent. Deliberately not tagged INFINITE-CHAIN either: what the litany declares endless is matter, space, spirit, and race — never a line of Gods. The chain is the one thing the endlessness list conspicuously omits.

notes: Provenance resolved: this is not a Times and Seasons text. Phelps published it as the poem “There Is No End” in the Deseret News, 19 November 1856, p. 2 — twelve years after Joseph Smith's death and nine years into the Utah period — and it entered the hymnody later under its present title. The Deseret News attribution is taken from Michael Hubbard MacKay et al., eds., Producing Ancient Scripture, p. 440 n.134 (https://corpus.noahairmet.com/b/producing-ancient-scripture-joseph-smith-s-4e4d/440), which cites the poem to that issue and identifies it as hymn 284 in the 1985 hymnal; the 1856 newspaper page itself was not inspected for this entry, so the printing date is carried on that scholarly authority rather than on a page image. The hymn text quoted here was verified verbatim against the live churchofjesuschrist.org hymn page on 2026-08-10, where it stands as no. 284 with the text credited to “William W. Phelps, 1792–1872,” the tune KINGSFOLD arranged by Ralph Vaughan Williams, and the scripture references Abraham 3:1–4, 9 and Moses 1:3–4, 33–39. Graded current-correlated on that basis: it is a currently hosted, currently sung hymn. Caveat for a later pass: the hosted text is the 1985 hymnal, which the new Hymns—For Home and Church (2024–) is progressively superseding; whether the hymn and its number survive that rollout is not asserted here. Why this entry matters to the timeline: it is the only place in current correlated worship material where the beginning-of-the-Gods question is put to a congregation at all, and it is put as a question that is never answered. B. H. Roberts saw the opportunity and closed it — in A New Witness for God (1895) he prints the prose claim that “there has been and there now exists an endless line of Gods,” then prints this hymn in full immediately after as its hymnodic form (see roberts-endless-line-1895, quote q2, which reproduces this same quatrain in the older “D'ye think that you could ever” wording). No citesId is set on this entry, because citation edges run from the citing source to the cited one and the hymn is the earlier text; the reciprocal edge belongs on roberts-endless-line-1895 and adding it is out of scope here. The practical consequence is the one Roberts's own note anticipates: the prose statement fell out of General Authority usage, and the question survived in the hymnbook.

title: Heber C. Kimball: a Father connected with one still farther back
speaker: Heber C. Kimball
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference discourse, Bowery, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 5:18–23, at 5:19)

quotes.excerpt: We must be grafted into the true vine, and continue to partake of its fatness, and then we shall go back to our Father and God, who is connected with one who is still farther back; and this Father is connected with one still further back, and so on; and just so far as we respect our superiors and try to save our children, so shall we receive blessings from this time forth and forever, and shall become as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.
quotes.note: The chain runs in both directions inside one sentence — ancestors “still further back” and posterity “as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.” One of the cleanest explicit-chain sentences in the Journal of Discourses.

notes: Verified verbatim against the printed Journal of Discourses. Pitman shorthand report; the speaker did not review the text before publication — hence hearsay C under the v2 rebasing of Journal of Discourses material.

title: Wilford Woodruff: God Himself is increasing and progressing
speaker: Wilford Woodruff
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 6:115–121, at 6:120)

quotes.excerpt: If there was a point where man in his progression could not proceed any further, the very idea would throw a gloom over every intelligent and reflecting mind. God himself is increasing and progressing in knowledge, power, and dominion, and will do so, worlds without end. It is just so with us. We are in a probation, which is a school of experience.
quotes.note: Affirmation. The argument runs from the intolerability of a ceiling on human progress to God's ongoing progression — anthropology first, theology second. Later official denials attack the conclusion without engaging this premise. “God himself” is not further specified, hence the ambiguous referent.

notes: One of only two unambiguous affirmative divine-progression sentences located in the Journal of Discourses corpus; the other is Brigham Young's of 13 January 1867 (JD 11:282–291), see young-progressing-eternally-1867. No later pulpit affirmation was located. Watt shorthand, not reviewed by the speaker.

title: Brigham Young: exaltation "by no means lessens" the power to propagate
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Remarks in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:274–276)

witnesses.scribe: G. D. Watt (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 7:274–276. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: Who can define the divinity of man? Only those who understand the true principles of eternity—the principles that pertain to life and salvation. Man, by being exalted, does not lose the power and ability naturally given to him; but, on the contrary, by taking the road that leads to life, he gains more power, more influence and ability during every step he progresses therein. Mankind have power given them to propagate their species. An exaltation to the celestial kingdom of God by no means lessens that power. On these points the children of men are shrouded in mystery and uncertainty.
quotes.note: The claim arrives by negation, which is what keeps it a euphemism rather than an explicit forward chain: Young names the faculty ("power given them to propagate their species") and says exaltation does not diminish it, but never names an object for it — no spirit children, no worlds, no increase. Read strictly this is a claim about what the exalted man retains, not about what he produces. Worth noting how early and how physiological the vocabulary already is: three days later, in the discourses that became young-origin-caution-1859 and by-chain, the same speaker is warning against inquiring after the origin of the Gods.

quotes.excerpt: The generality of mankind are ignorant of the real relationship that exists between them and Heaven. They do not understand that God is our Father. By adoption? No; but we are his children by a legal inheritance. He gave his only begotten Son, pertaining to the flesh, to redeem the whole family of man.
quotes.note: A denial, and the tag records the question rather than the position: Young rejects adoption as the account of divine sonship and puts "legal inheritance" in its place. He does not go on to state a generative mechanism — nothing here about begetting, gestation, or a mother — so the viviparous alternative is not asserted, only the adoptive one refused. Two paragraphs earlier he draws the same distinction about Christ ("not by adoption, in the strict sense of the word, but is flesh of our flesh and bone of our bone"), which is where the anti-adoption instinct in this sermon starts.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1859/1859-10-young-eternal-life-blessings.md, whose text was read line by line against the BYU/Internet Archive page images of Journal of Discourses volume 7, pp. 274–276, in the vault's final-review pass (that pass restored the printed British spellings "honour," "vapour," "Saviour," "labour," and "for ever," which an earlier transcription had silently Americanized). Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by G. D. Watt, published without the speaker's review, hence C. Delivered at the Thursday afternoon session of the October 1859 general conference — the same conference week as the two Brigham Young discourses already in the collection, and a useful control on them: here the procreative-continuity claim is made in the plainest possible terms and no backward inference is drawn from it at all.

title: Brigham Young: instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:282–291)

quotes.excerpt: Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause of all things; but it would be as easy for an ant to number the grains of sand on the earth. It is not for man, with his limited intelligence, to grasp eternity in his comprehension. … Instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods—instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be—instead of endeavouring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess.
quotes.note: Delivered the day after the “never was a time when there were not Gods” discourse (by-chain), in the same October 1859 conference: the same speaker holds the most explicit chain language and the earliest discouragement of the question on consecutive days.

notes: This is the caution the by-chain entry's earlier placeholder pointed at — it belongs to its own sermon (“Intelligence, Etc.,” October 9, 1859), not to the October 8 discourse. The 1997 Teachings of Presidents: Brigham Young manual (ch. 4) excerpts this passage; log that manual as its own citation entry when added.

title: Richard F. Burton: “gods in an ad infinitum ascending series”
speaker: Richard F. Burton
office: English explorer and travel writer; non-Mormon visitor to Great Salt Lake City in 1860
venue: The City of the Saints, and Across the Rocky Mountains to California, ch. IX, p. 388

quotes.excerpt: This body consists of three, viz., Eloheim, Jehovah, and Michael, which is Adam. From the Christian apostles and the Apocalypse, the Mormons deduce the dogma of gods in an ad infinitum ascending series: man, however, must limit his obedience to the last heavenly Father and Son revealed by the Holy Spirit.
quotes.note: Quoted with the preceding sentence attached, because the two cannot be separated honestly. Burton's Godhead is Eloheim, Jehovah and Michael-who-is-Adam: he is describing Adam-God, and the ascending series sits inside that description — the same pairing found in Brigham Young's discourse of 8 October 1854. The second clause is a real observation about how the doctrine functioned in practice: an infinite series upward, obedience owed only to the nearest link.

quotes.excerpt: And as God is perfect man, so is perfect man God: any individual, by faith and obedience, can, as the Brahminical faith asserts, rise to the position of a deity, until, attaining the power of forming a planet, peopling, redeeming it, and sitting there enthroned in everlasting power.
quotes.note: The forward chain as an outsider heard it in 1860, complete with world-forming. The comparative gloss “as the Brahminical faith asserts” is Burton's own frame, not his informants' — he read everything through comparative religion.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the Harper (New York) printing, at printed p. 388 in chapter IX; the 1861 date is the London first edition, and the entry is dated to it while the pagination cited is the printing actually collated. The scan's OCR renders “ad infinitum” as “ad mjinitum” and “there” as “therq”; both are plainly scanner artifacts and are corrected silently. Hearsay B rather than A: the prose is Burton's own published writing, but every doctrinal statement in the chapter is his summary of what Mormon informants told him during his 1860 visit, with no Latter-day Saint source quoted for the regress claim — so as evidence of the doctrine it stands one remove from any Latter-day Saint speaker. Its evidential value is precisely that distance. It shows that in 1860 the ascending series and Adam-God were publicly legible, and legible together, to a well-read non-Mormon visitor who had no stake in either.

title: Brigham Young relays Joseph Smith: a God who had not a Father — nor a mother
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 9:286–289)

quotes.excerpt: The idea that the Lord our God is not a personage of tabernacle is entirely a mistaken notion. He was once a man. Brother Kimball quoted a saying of Joseph the Prophet, that he would not worship a God who had not a Father; and I do not know that he would if he had not a mother; the one would be as absurd as the other. If he had a Father, he was made in his likeness. And if he is our Father we are made after his image and likeness.
quotes.note: Three stacked claims in one breath: past mortality (“He was once a man”), the Father's Father (the relayed Joseph Smith saying), and the mother clause — which is Young's own hedged inference (“I do not know that he would”), not part of the reported saying.

notes: The relayed saying is an attribution chain three links deep — Joseph Smith (d. 1844) → Heber C. Kimball (earlier the same afternoon) → Young → Watt's shorthand — so while the sermon is a contemporaneous report (C), the Joseph attribution itself is an eighteen-year-old relay and should be weighed accordingly. Also excerpted in Widtsoe's Discourses of Brigham Young compilation.

title: Brigham Young: "he inherits his faculties, attributes and powers from his Father"
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Remarks in the Bowery, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 10:265–274)

witnesses.scribe: G. D. Watt (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 10:265–274. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: He has endowed us with glorious faculties, with Godlike attributes like those which are incorporated in his own nature, and he has placed us upon this earth to honor them, and to sanctify ourselves and the earth preparatory to enjoying it in its celestial state. We are not, in anything, independent of God. We inherit what we possess from Him, and he inherits his faculties, attributes and powers from his Father.
quotes.note: Backward and unhedged, and stated in passing rather than as the point of the sermon — the subject under discussion is human dependence on God, and the Father's own Father arrives as the last clause of a sentence about inheritance. Two limits worth keeping: it goes exactly one generation back and says nothing about a series, so this is C-indefinite and not an infinite chain; and it makes no mortality claim at all — the verb is "inherits," present tense, with no probation, no manhood, no becoming.

quotes.excerpt: It was said this morning that if we will do our duty God will make us rich. How? By opening gold mines? No. If he makes us rich, he will make us rich in the same way that he became rich, by faithful labor, ceaseless perseverance, and constant exertion and industry. He labored faithfully for all he possesses, and he is willing that we should inherit all things with him, if we will pursue the same course to obtain them that he pursued.
quotes.note: Attainment language with no mortality attached, so it takes FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone: God possesses what He possesses because He worked for it, and the course He pursued is the course open to us. Note what it is not — the tense is completed throughout ("became," "labored," "all he possesses"), so this is past attainment, not the ongoing divine progression Young asserts four years later in young-progressing-eternally-1867. The homiletic setting matters for weight: the claim is deployed as the punchline of a stewardship argument against gold-seeking.

quotes.excerpt: …let us not forget that all we hold of this world's goods is the Lord's, and should be used to promote the cause of righteousness and those principles which will exalt the people to thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers in the world to come, with power to control and govern the elements and every wicked influence.
quotes.note: The bare exaltation formula, recorded for completeness. It is the D&C 132 vocabulary with the one word that carries the doctrine — increase — left out, and no offspring, mechanism, or posterity anywhere near it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1863/1863-10-young-our-relationship-and-duty-to-god.md, collated word-for-word against BYU Journal of Discourses volume 10, pp. 265–274 (printed header: remarks by President Brigham Young, made in the Bowery, Great Salt Lake City, October 6, 1863; reported by G. D. Watt) in the vault's final-review pass. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This discourse deserves more weight in the backward-direction file than it usually gets. It is a general conference sermon by a Church President, and the grandfather claim is not offered as speculation or as a relay of Joseph Smith — unlike young-father-mother-1862, where the same doctrine reaches Young through Kimball through an eighteen-year-old attribution — but simply asserted in his own voice as background to an argument about tithing and riches.

title: Brigham Young: “the God that I serve is progressing eternally”
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 11:282–291)

witnesses.scribe: Edward L. Sloan, shorthand reporter, printed in Journal of Discourses 11:282–291
witnesses.note: Wayback capture of the BYU ContentDM page images. The printed header reads “Remarks by President Brigham Young, in the Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City, January 13th, 1867. Reported by Edward L. Sloan.”

quotes.excerpt: They appear to be bounded in their capacity for acquiring knowledge, as Brother Orson Pratt, has in theory, bounded the capacity of God. According to his theory, God can progress no further in knowledge and power; but the God that I serve is progressing eternally, and so are his children: they will increase to all eternity, if they are faithful.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the most explicit one from a Church President in the corpus. Two claims in one sentence, and they must be kept apart: God is progressing eternally (D), and his children will increase to all eternity (the forward promise, stated with no object — no offspring, no worlds, no mechanism). Young joins them with “and so are,” which is exactly the symmetry that later readers turn into an argument for a chain; he does not himself make a backward claim here, so nothing backward is tagged. Orson Pratt is named as the holder of the bounded view, which dates and localizes the dispute (compare pratt-seer and fp-repudiation-1865).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1867/1867-01-young-weakness-of-the-human-mind.md, printed under the heading “Weakness of the Human Mind. Extortion. Imperfection of the Human Judgment. Introduction of Machinery.” Journal of Discourses, so C: Edward L. Sloan's shorthand report, not reviewed by the speaker before publication; the vault file is still status draft. This is the sentence Eugene England uses to open “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 33, where he sets it against Hyrum Smith's 1844 “I would not serve a God that had not all wisdom and power” to frame the whole two-modes argument; England's reproduction is lowercase OCR, so the text here is taken from the sermon, not from him. Note what the surrounding paragraphs are actually about: retail prices, judging cloth, and Saints who stop learning. The doctrinal claim arrives as an analogy for members who will not study, which is a recurring feature of this material and a reason it is easy to miss when sweeping by topic.

title: Orson Pratt: "born male and female in the spirit world" — and innumerable personal gods
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 19:311–321)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 19:311–321. An 1867 discourse printed unusually late, inside a volume otherwise covering 1877–1878; reporter credited on the printed header, speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: …in the general outline there is resemblance among all the human species, and there should be in as much as their Father and God is indeed their Father, as any in this congregation are the literal fathers of their children… But when did he beget us? I answer before this world was made; not our flesh and bones, but that being called man that was created in the image and likeness of God and who dwells in his mortal tabernacle. That being is the offspring of God; we were all begotten by him before this world was made.
quotes.note: Literal, and marked as literal by the comparison Pratt chooses: God is Father of the spirits in the same sense as "any in this congregation are the literal fathers of their children." The argument is the anatomical-analogy one — offspring resemble parents throughout the animal creation, therefore we resemble God — which is the same route to viviparous spirit birth he took in 1852 and which Erastus Snow runs again in 1885. What is claimed is our origin, not the Father's; nothing backward is asserted here.

quotes.excerpt: So God created man, male and female. He did not tell us all the particulars of the creation—that we were born male and female in the spirit world, and so on, but yet there are many sayings which indicate that such was the fact. For instance, in the books of Moses and in the books of the New Testament we read that God is the Father of all our spirits, that we were begotten sons and daughters unto God.
quotes.note: The distinct second move: not merely begotten but "born," and born already sexed. Pratt is candid about the epistemic status — scripture does not say this outright ("He did not tell us all the particulars"), it is an inference from "many sayings" — which is the same hedge he attached to the mechanism in 1852. Sexed spirit birth is the premise the whole forward chain of pratt-people-worlds-1871 later rests on.

quotes.excerpt: Then, when we come to personality, we not only believe in our personal Father, in His Son Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Ghost, as personages, but we also believe that in the eternity of eternities, in the heaven of heavens there will be innumerable millions of persons who will occupy that exalted station—each one being a personal god, as much so as the God of this creation—the Father of our spirits is.
quotes.note: Theosis at maximum strength and still nothing more than theosis: the redeemed become gods as fully as the Father is one, but no offspring, no mechanism and no increase are named, so on this project's taxonomy it stays a euphemism. It is also the direct answer to the control case — pratt-infinite-gods-1855 reached "the number of Gods is infinite" by a non-genealogical route, and here the same apostle reaches innumerable gods by the genealogical one, populating the count with redeemed persons rather than with tabernacles indwelt by a single knowledge. Earlier in the same discourse he puts the destination the same way: "we may become Gods like unto our Father who begat us."

quotes.excerpt: I do not know, that, in my remarks this morning, concerning the atonement, and the personalities and glorious attributes of God, I have varied in my views from those of the rest of the authorities of the Church. If I have I hope they will correct me and tell me wherein I am wrong, for it is my desire, and ever has been, to go in accordance with the revelations of heaven, to abide in the word of God, and to have that word abide in me.
quotes.note: Untagged; carried as register evidence. Two years after the First Presidency and Twelve publicly disowned The Seer (fp-repudiation-1865), Pratt closes a doctrinal exposition from the general conference pulpit by inviting correction and volunteering that he may have left wrong impressions in earlier teaching. The doctrine is stated with confidence; the standing to state it is not.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1867/1867-10-pratt-temples-in-ancient-america-the-god-of-mankind.md, whose body was collated against the Internet Archive scan of Journal of Discourses volume 19, pp. 311–321, and cross-checked against an independent transcript in the vault's heavyweight and final-review passes; the printed header (discourse by Elder Orson Pratt, delivered in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Oct. 7, 1867, reported by David W. Evans) was verified against the page image. Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Occasion is worth recording: this was the first general conference held in the new Salt Lake Tabernacle, and Pratt used it for a full exposition of an embodied, material God — "a personage of flesh and of bones" — from which the spirit-birth and plurality claims follow.

title: Orson Pratt: exaltation defined by increase — the angels who have none
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Thursday afternoon session, New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 13:183–196)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 13:183–196; reporter credited on the printed header. Speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: There is a difference between the classes of angels called celestial, terrestrial and telestial. The celestial angels have not attained to all of the power and greatness and exaltation of kings and priests in the presence of God; they are blessed with glory, happiness, peace and joy; but they are not blessed with the privilege of increasing their posterity to all ages of eternity, neither have they thrones and kingdoms, but they are servants to those of the highest order.
quotes.note: Exaltation defined by the presence of eternal increase, and the definition delivered by subtraction: the ministering angels get glory, happiness, peace and joy, and are still not exalted, because increase is what they lack. Euphemism rather than explicit: “increasing their posterity to all ages of eternity” names the increase and its endlessness but leaves the offspring's nature and the mechanism unstated — the same register as D&C 132's “continuation of the seeds forever.”

quotes.excerpt: We might inquire, have angels not also these affections which belong to the higher class of beings, inasmuch as they are resurrected beings? Yes, but herein they have lost, through disobedience, the privilege of attaining to the higher glory and exaltation. They have affections and desires that never can be gratified, and in this respect their glory is not full.
quotes.note: Context for q1, untagged: it makes no claim about increase itself, but it shows the argument's emotional engine — the deprivation is felt, not merely structural. This is the register in which mid-twentieth-century temple-marriage preaching would later carry the whole doctrine (see eldred-smith-no-increase-1948).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1869/1869-10-pratt-celestial-marriage.md, whose opening and closing pages were collated against the BYU JoD volume 13 scan, pp. 183–196, with the printed header confirming David W. Evans as reporter. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Its use to the collection is definitional: increase is not presented as a bonus attached to exaltation but as the differentia between the exalted and everyone else, D&C 132:17 preached as doctrine rather than cited as proof text. Same speaker, same sermon title, seventeen years after the 1852 discourse, and markedly more restrained — the mechanism has dropped out of view even though the entailment has not.

title: George Q. Cannon: "a command by which Eternity is peopled"
speaker: George Q. Cannon
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 13:197–209)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: Page-anchored Internet Archive scan of Journal of Discourses volume 13, p. 197. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: He has revealed this principle and commanded His servants to take wives. What for? That they may obey His great command—a command by which Eternity is peopled, a command by which Abraham's seed shall become as the stars of heaven for multitude, and as the sand on the seashore, that cannot be counted.
quotes.note: "Eternity is peopled" is the strongest phrase in the sermon and still an unspecified one: the command being obeyed is mortal plural marriage, and what it fills is eternity, but Cannon does not say the peopling continues after death or that its objects are spirit children. Read as it stands, it is the Abrahamic multitude promise stretched to an eternal scale.

quotes.excerpt: Hence we were told by brother Pratt that there are degrees of glory, and that the faithful man may receive the power of God—the greatest He has ever bestowed upon man—namely, the power of procreation. It is a godlike power, but how it is abused!… We were told there is a glory to which alone that power will be accorded in the life to come. Still there will be millions of women saved in the kingdom of God, while men, through the abuse of this precious gift, will not be counted worthy of such a privilege.
quotes.note: Explicit because the faculty and the timing are both named: procreation, granted in the life to come, and granted only inside one degree of glory. That is the continuation-of-lives claim rather than bare theosis, and it is defined the way Pratt defined it two days earlier — by subtraction, with the unexalted losing precisely this. The attribution is a relay ("we were told by brother Pratt") of the Oct. 7 discourse recorded at pratt-celestial-marriage-1869, but Cannon adopts the doctrine in his own voice in the next breath, so the relay affects the wording rather than the commitment.

quotes.excerpt: There is a way which God has provided in a revelation given to this Church, in which He says: “Strait is the gate and narrow the way that leadeth unto the exaltation and continuation of the lives, and few there be that find it, because ye receive me not in the world, neither do ye know me.”
quotes.note: D&C 132:22 quoted from the pulpit with no gloss on its contents. Cannon cites it to establish that a way exists and that plural marriage is it; he never says what "continuation of the lives" continues, and the surrounding argument is about mortal households, not about eternal offspring.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1869/1869-10-cannon-celestial-marriage.md, collated against the BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses volume 13, pp. 197–209 (printed header: discourse by Elder George Q. Cannon, delivered in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, October 9, 1869; reported by David W. Evans), with opening and closing page images checked against the body in the vault's final-review pass. Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. The great bulk of the discourse is a defense of plural marriage on scriptural, historical and physiological grounds; the eternal-increase material is the theological floor under that defense rather than its subject, which is exactly why it is useful — it shows what could be assumed in front of a general conference audience in 1869 without argument.

title: George Q. Cannon: "the glory of God consists in the number of his posterity"
speaker: George Q. Cannon
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 14:122–129)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 14:122–129. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: There each man will have his family and kingdom. It is said that God is Lord of lords and King of kings; but how can he be King of kings unless there be kings under him to give him homage and pay respect unto him and acknowledge him as their Lord and their King?… As the prophet says concerning our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, “To the increase of his kingdom there shall be no end.” It shall go on increasing with every cycle of eternity, as long as time endures. There shall be no end to the increase of his kingdom. His glory consisted of this; and the glory of God consists in the number of his posterity; and as generation succeeds generation, until the earth is filled and glorified, other worlds will be rolled into existence, upon which the posterity of God, our heavenly Father, shall increase throughout the endless ages of eternity.
quotes.note: The strongest single sentence in the entry, and it makes two separable claims. The first is a definition of divine glory in terms of headcount — "the glory of God consists in the number of his posterity" — which turns eternal increase from a reward into the substance of godhood. The second is the supply problem and its solution: generations fill the earth, so "other worlds will be rolled into existence" to hold the overflow. Everything runs forward. The posterity increasing on those worlds is God's, and nothing is said about where God came from.

quotes.excerpt: Men and women are married to each other for time and for all eternity; not as it is in the world, “until death shall them part;” but that tie shall be as enduring as eternity itself, and there shall never be a time when it shall be dissolved; and to their increase there shall be no end, for this is the glory of God, and this is the blessing of God upon his faithful children. The godlike power has been given us here on the earth to bear and perpetuate our own species; and shall this power, which brings so much joy, peace and happiness, be confined and limited to this short life? It is folly to talk about such a thing; common sense teaches us better.
quotes.note: The D&C 132 formula ("to their increase there shall be no end") immediately cashed out as the survival of the reproductive faculty itself — Cannon names the power, locates it in mortal bodies now, and argues from common sense that a faculty this good cannot be temporary. That argument-from-analogy is the same move Whitney makes in 1907, thirty-six years later, and it is what separates this from the bare formula quotations elsewhere in the corpus.

quotes.excerpt: We look forward to the time when this earth will be redeemed from corruption and cleansed by fire; when there shall be a new heaven and a new earth, and when the Saints shall possess their native inheritance purified from sin, redeemed from corruption, with the power of Satan curtailed, and when we shall be able to increase and multiply and fill this earth, go to other earths and carry on the work of emigration through the endless ages of eternity.
quotes.note: The Genesis command read as a permanent assignment rather than a mortal one, with "emigration" as the mechanism connecting increase to plural worlds. Note the sequence — fill this earth first, then move on — which is the same arithmetic pressure Cannon returns to in 1892 with Abraham needing to leave for want of room.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1871/1871-04-cannon-the-building-of-templesthe-keys-of.md, collated against the BYU Journal of Discourses volume 14 scan, pp. 122–129 (printed header verified in the vault's final-review pass: discourse by Elder George Q. Cannon, delivered in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, April 8, 1871, reported by David W. Evans). Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Delivered four months before pratt-people-worlds-1871 and covering much of the same ground from a different starting point: Pratt argues from resurrected physiology, Cannon from the Abrahamic covenant and the logic of the title "King of kings." The two together are the high-water mark of the forward chain in the 1871 pulpit.

title: Brigham Young: "by this, and this only, have the Gods been exalted"
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 14:91–98)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 14:91–98. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: There is but one thread that can be followed that can endure forever, but one path that we can walk in that is eternal—and that path is the path of perfection, purity and holiness. By this, and this only, have the Gods been exalted, the angels live and the heavenly hosts bask in purity. We are trying to prepare for it.
quotes.note: Attainment, in the perfect tense and in the plural: the Gods "have been exalted," and by the same path now open to the Saints. No mortality is claimed, so this takes FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone rather than the pair. The referent is the honest problem — Young says "the Gods," not the Father, and the sentence would be true of any exalted being. The class plainly is not meant to exclude the Father, which is why the stance reads as an affirmation, but anyone citing this for the Father's biography is supplying a narrowing that Young did not.

quotes.excerpt: Our religion will not permit us to command or force any man or woman to obey the Gospel we have embraced. And we are under no obligation to do this, for every creature has as good a right, according to his organization, to choose for himself as the Gods.
quotes.note: Untagged, and kept for referent discipline: it shows how the plural "the Gods" functions in this discourse. Here they are a class held up as the standard of free agency, not a genealogy — the same usage that makes the exaltation sentence above readable as a general claim about deity rather than a statement about one being's past.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1871/1871-04-young-the-one-man-powerunityfree-agencypriesthood-and-government.md, collated against the BYU Journal of Discourses volume 14 scan, pp. 91–98 (printed header verified in the vault's final-review pass: discourse by President Brigham Young, delivered in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, April 8, 1871, reported by David W. Evans). Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. The discourse itself is a defense of hierarchical unity against "one-man power" complaints and of free agency against compulsion; the theogonic sentence is an aside inside the free-agency argument, delivered the same day as cannon-glory-posterity-1871 in the same building.

title: Orson Pratt: beget children, form and create worlds, send forth our spirit children
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 14:233–245)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 14:233–245; reporter credited on the printed header. Speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: Can spirits do this? No, they remain single. There are no marriages among spirits, no coupling together of the males and females among them; but when they rise from the grave, after being tabernacled in mortal bodies, they have all the functions that are necessary to people worlds. As our Father and God begat us, sons and daughters, so will we rise immortal, males and females, and beget children, and, in our turn, form and create worlds, and send forth our spirit children to inherit those worlds, the same as we were sent here, and thus will the works of God continue, and not only God himself, and His Son Jesus Christ have the power of endless lives, but all of His redeemed offspring. They grow up like the parents; that is a law of nature so far as this world is concerned. Every kind of being begets its own like, and when fully matured and grown up the offspring become like the parent. So the offspring of the Almighty, who begot us, will grow up and become literally Gods, or the sons of God.
quotes.note: The fullest forward chain located in the corpus, with every link named in one breath: resurrected sexed bodies retaining reproductive “functions,” literal begetting, spirit children, worlds created to receive them, and those children maturing into Gods. The clause that carries the most weight is the comparative one — “the same as we were sent here” — which declares our own origin identical to the process just described, making the Father a prior instance of it.

quotes.excerpt: We heard this forenoon that, when the Saints come into the possession of their everlasting inheritance and are exalted as glorified and eternal beings, to the increase of their posterity there would be no end. "No end!" What does that mean? It means that it will be eternal--that there never will be a period throughout all the future ages of eternity, but what they will be increasing and multiplying, until their seed are more numerous than the dust of the earth or the stars of heaven… They will not only people worlds, but they will create them. There is room enough to accomplish this when we consider that space is boundless.
quotes.note: Pratt glossing “no end” as a live arithmetical claim rather than a formula — the increase is genuinely unbounded and therefore requires boundless space. Double hyphens preserved from the vault transcription of the printed page.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1871/1871-08-pratt-o-the-redemption-of-the-earthpre-existencemarriage.md, a fresh ingestion collated against the BYU JoD volume 14 page scan, pp. 233–245, with both talk boundaries confirmed directly against the scan and an independent Internet Archive OCR pass of the same leaves. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by David W. Evans, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This is the best single exhibit in the dataset for conflation trap #3. The symmetry pressure toward a backward chain is at its maximum here — the process is declared identical in both directions (“As our Father and God begat us… so will we rise… the same as we were sent here”), and the reader has only to run the sentence in reverse to reach an infinite regress. Pratt does not run it in reverse. Nothing is said about where the Father came from; INFINITE-CHAIN is carried for the succession of Gods the passage states in the forward direction — exalted couples begetting children who “will grow up and become literally Gods” — not for any backward regress. What the passage does state about the Father is narrower and worth keeping distinct: that He begat us viviparously, which is a claim about our origin, not His.

title: Daniel H. Wells: "he has passed through all the ordeals and trials of a lower estate"
speaker: Daniel H. Wells
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Discourse at the Forty-Fifth Annual Conference, New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 17:343–349)

witnesses.scribe: David W. Evans (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 17:343–349. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: There is one whose guidance we need, he is wiser than we are, for he has passed through all the ordeals and trials of a lower estate, and has gained an experience far beyond the experience of men, and he is now willing to lead and guide his children here on the earth if they will only allow him to do so. But men generally think they know best themselves, they are not willing to be guided by the God of heaven, they give the preference to the paths marked out by themselves.
quotes.note: An argument from divine biography, not a doctrinal excursus: God's fitness to direct us is grounded in the fact that He has already been where we are. Two cautions. The claim is "a lower estate," not this mortality by name — it is the estate vocabulary of Abraham 3, so the reading that gets you to a mortal probation is natural but supplied. And the referent needs checking rather than assuming: Wells identifies the speaker's subject in the next breath as "the God of heaven" whose "children" we are, and the discourse elsewhere distinguishes "our Lord and his Christ," so the Father is the reading the context supports even though the sentence in isolation would fit the Son perfectly.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1875/1875-04-wells-the-saints-have-the-priesthoodthe-kingdom.md, collated against the Journal of Discourses volume 17 scan, pp. 343–349 (printed header: discourse by President Daniel H. Wells, delivered at the Forty-Fifth Annual Conference, New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Tuesday morning, April 6, 1875; reported by David W. Evans), with the body length and closing checked for truncation in the vault's heavyweight pass. Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Worth logging because of the office: this is a member of the First Presidency, in the opening session of general conference, treating the Father's prior probation as a settled premise he can lean an exhortation on. The rest of the discourse is about self-sufficiency and temple building and never returns to the subject.

title: Brigham Young: spirits begotten, born, and brought forth by celestial bodies
speaker: Brigham Young
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 18:257–264)

witnesses.scribe: George F. Gibbs (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 18:257–264. Speaker did not review. No Internet Archive page anchor exists for this range of volume 18.

quotes.excerpt: Mankind is composed of two distinct elements; the first is a spiritual organization in eternity, the second is a natural organization on this earth, formed out of the material of which this earth is composed. Man is first spiritual, then temporal. As it is written in the revelations of God to man, all things were first created spiritual, and secondly temporal. That is, spirits were begotten, born and educated in the celestial world, and were brought forth by celestial bodies.
quotes.note: Gestation and parturition, stated as exegesis rather than metaphor: begotten, then *born*, then brought forth *by bodies*. Three separate physiological terms in one sentence is what puts this past the reach of a figurative reading. The framing matters too — Young offers it as his gloss on the Moses/D&C “all things created spiritual first” passage and as “a part of my own visions upon this matter,” so it arrives as a president's interpretation, not as cited revelation.

quotes.excerpt: Those of the Latter-day Saints who will continue to follow after the revelations and commandments of God to do them, who are found to be obedient in all things, continually advancing little by little towards perfection and the knowledge of God, they, when they enter the spirit world and receive their bodies, will be able to advance faster in the things pertaining to the knowledge of the Gods, and will continue onward and upward until they become Gods, even the sons of God.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. This is plain theosis — becoming like God — from the same discourse, and the taxonomy's second trap is that theosis is not by itself a claim about generative exaltation or about anyone's ancestry. Recorded here so the pairing is visible: in one sermon Young states the viviparous mechanism and the deification promise without ever joining them into a chain.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1876/1876-10-young-philosophy-of-man-upon-the-earththe.md, collated against BYU JoD volume 18, pp. 257–264. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by George F. Gibbs, speaker unreviewed, hence C; the vault entry is still marked draft, so the two quoted sentences deserve a page-image check before they carry public weight. Chronologically this sits between Pratt's Seer systematization and the 1909 First Presidency statement, and it shows the viviparous mechanism being taught from the general conference pulpit by the President of the Church — not merely written in a periodical by an apostle. The phrase later curriculum inherits is “begotten and born,” and this is one of its pulpit sources.

title: Wilford Woodruff: "he had his endowments a long time before we were born, and also passed through his probation"
speaker: Wilford Woodruff
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse at the Annual Conference, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 19:295–300)

witnesses.scribe: George F. Gibbs (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 19:295–300. Reporter credited on the printed header; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: And I wish all Israel to understand that when we impart of our substance to build Temples that we do not do it to benefit the Lord at all, he had his endowments a long time before we were born, and also passed through his probation. We are his children, he wishes to exalt us back to his presence, and he knows very well we are obliged to walk in the same path and receive the same ordinances in order to inherit the same glory that surrounds him.
quotes.note: Both halves of the Father-status axis in one sentence, and they are load-bearing rather than decorative — the point of the remark is that temple work benefits us and not God, and the reason given is that God already did this. "Passed through his probation" is the mortality-experience claim (the same word Woodruff uses for our own estate two sentences later); "had his endowments" is the attainment claim, and it is a striking one, because it makes the Father a recipient of ordinances administered by someone. The forward tag is the third clause: same path, same ordinances, same glory — theosis stated as an equality, with no offspring or increase named. Referent is secure: "We are his children" and "exalt us back to his presence."

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1878/1878-04-woodruff-the-blessings-realized-by-the-saintsmen.md, collated against the Journal of Discourses volume 19 scan, pp. 295–300 (printed header: discourse by Elder Wilford Woodruff, delivered at the Annual Conference, Saturday morning, April 6, 1878; reported by Geo. F. Gibbs). Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This is the same speaker who twenty-one years earlier said God Himself is increasing and progressing (woodruff-progression-1857), and the two claims should not be merged: 1857 is ongoing progression, 1878 is a completed past, and only the later one touches the Father's biography. Note also the near-neighbour in the corpus — jfs-same-ordeal-1884, delivered six years later, says almost exactly this about "a similar ordeal" and is the passage regress lists usually reach for.

title: Joseph F. Smith: the exalted man is greater than the angel
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 23:169–176, at 23:173)

quotes.excerpt: The man who passes through this probation, and is faithful, being redeemed from sin by the blood of Christ, through the ordinances of the Gospel, and attains to exaltation in the kingdom of God, is not less but greater than the angels… in fact having passed from the condition of the angel to that of a God. He possesses keys of power, dominion and glory that the angel does not possess—and cannot possess without gaining them in the same way that he gained them, which will be by passing through the same ordeals and proving equally faithful.
quotes.note: Theosis, forward direction only. The comparison being drawn is between an exalted human and an angel, and the “same ordeals” are the ordeals the exalted man passed through, not ordeals attributed to God.

notes: Re-pulled and read at Journal of Discourses 23:169–176 (discourse “Man a Mortal and an Immortal Being,” Joseph F. Smith, Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday, June 18, 1882, reported by Geo. F. Gibbs) and verified verbatim. This entry exists chiefly to stop a persistent misfiling. The passage circulates in regress lists — usually cited from its Gospel Doctrine reprint rather than from the sermon — but it makes no claim about God's past, God's Father, or a chain of Gods; its subject is the rank of an exalted human relative to an angel. Under this project's taxonomy it is theosis and nothing more, and treating theosis as evidence for divine ancestry is the second conflation trap. The sentence such lists are actually reaching for — “We are precisely in the same condition… that God our Heavenly Father was when He was passing through this or a similar ordeal” — is not in this discourse at all; it belongs to a Joseph F. Smith sermon delivered twenty months later. See jfs-same-ordeal-1884. Hearsay C: Gibbs's contemporaneous report, published without the speaker's review.

title: Joseph F. Smith: “an eternal being, without beginning of days” and “precisely in the same condition,” in consecutive sentences
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Assembly Hall discourse, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon (Journal of Discourses 25:51–60, at 25:58); reprinted in Gospel Doctrine, 64

quotes.excerpt: God has a tabernacle of flesh and bone. He is an organized being just as we are, who are now in the flesh. Jesus Christ was born of His mother Mary. He had a fleshly tabernacle; He was crucified on the cross; and his body was raised from the dead. He burst the bonds of the grave and came forth to newness of life, a living soul, a living being, a man with a body, with parts and with spirit—the spirit and the body becoming a living and immortal soul. You and I have to do the same thing. We must go through the same ordeal in order to attain to the glory and exaltation which God designed we should enjoy with him in the eternal worlds. In other words, we must become like Him; peradventure to sit upon thrones, to have dominion, power, and eternal increase. God designed this in the beginning. We are the children of God. He is an eternal being, without beginning of days or end of years. He always was, He is, He always will be. We are precisely in the same condition and under the same circumstances that God our Heavenly Father was when He was passing through this or a similar ordeal.
quotes.note: Both halves, in printed order, in one paragraph. The order matters and is usually reported backwards: Smith asserts God's beginninglessness immediately BEFORE the same-condition sentence, not after it. He puts “He is an eternal being, without beginning of days or end of years. He always was, He is, He always will be” and “God our Heavenly Father… was passing through this or a similar ordeal” in consecutive breaths and shows no sign of feeling a tension between them. Quoting either half alone — which citations in both directions routinely do — manufactures a Joseph F. Smith who does not exist. Both directions of the Father-status axis are stated within this single passage — the same-ordeal claim and the beginningless-eternal-being claim sit five sentences apart; the tags record both. The Christological hinge is restored here rather than elided: the “same ordeal” takes its antecedent from Christ's death and resurrection, which complicates — though on the closing sentence it does not defeat — the past-mortality reading. The forward content is “dominion, power, and eternal increase,” the euphemism idiom, so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM replaces FORWARD-EXPLICIT.

notes: Re-pulled and verified verbatim at Journal of Discourses 25:51–60 (Joseph F. Smith, Assembly Hall, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon, February 17, 1884, reported by John Irvine); the quoted paragraph is at 25:58. Two provenance corrections worth carrying. First, this passage is frequently mis-cited to Journal of Discourses 23:173, which is a different discourse from June 1882 about angels and exalted men (see jfs-angel-to-god-1882) and contains none of this language. Second, the passage almost always travels in its Gospel Doctrine 64 reprint, and it is in that condensed reprint context that the counter-sentence gets dropped. Categorized as backward-mortality: Smith says we are in the condition God was in, which is a past-mortality claim, and he says nothing about God having a Father — so no chain tag. Hearsay C: Irvine's contemporaneous report, speaker-unreviewed.

title: George Q. Cannon: that little infant may become "the father of unnumbered millions"
speaker: George Q. Cannon
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Discourse in the Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, semi-annual conference (Journal of Discourses 25:318–328)

witnesses.scribe: John Irvine (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: Reporter credited on the printed header of Journal of Discourses 25:318–328; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: What is there more helpless, weak, puny, insignificant, it may be said, in many respects, than a human being when it is born into the world. Yet that being if nurtured properly, if trained as it should be, has before it a career of never-ending glory. That little puling infant may become, in the eternity of our God, a God, to sway power and dominion in the eternal worlds, to be the father of unnumbered millions.
quotes.note: Theosis carried one step past itself. The infant does not merely become a God; the content of that godhood is named, and it is paternity of "unnumbered millions" — an explicit posterity, which is what puts this over the line from euphemism. What is not named is the mechanism: no spirit birth, no mother, no worlds created for the offspring, and "the eternal worlds" is the D&C 132 formula phrase rather than a cosmological claim, so MANY-WORLDS is withheld. The setting is an analogy — the Church too was born helpless in 1830 — which is a reminder that the doctrine is being used illustratively, not defended.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1884/1884-10-cannon-the-fulfillment-of-ancient-and-modern.md, whose text is transcribed from the printed Journal of Discourses volume 25, pp. 318–328 (printed header: discourse by President George Q. Cannon, delivered in the Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday morning, October 5th, semi-annual conference, 1884; reported by John Irvine). Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. The rest of the discourse is about persecution keeping pace with the Church's growth and about the discipline of members guilty of adultery; the eternal-parenthood sentence stands alone, and the entry is deliberately lean because of it.

title: Franklin D. Richards: "to their increase there shall be no end"
speaker: Franklin D. Richards
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, semi-annual conference (Journal of Discourses 25:371–376)

witnesses.scribe: John Irvine (Pitman shorthand)
witnesses.note: Reporter credited on the printed header of Journal of Discourses 25:371–376; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: The Lord has given to us the privilege of being united in the holy marriage covenant for time and eternity. We look forward to inheriting the blessings of the kingdom of God with our children, and that to their increase there shall be no end. This was the Gospel that was preached to Father Abraham—that he and his children and his generation should become as the stars in the heavens for multitude, and like the sands on the seashore that cannot be counted. We look for blessing, dominion, exaltation and glory in the eternal worlds, through similar means.
quotes.note: The D&C 132 endless-increase promise applied directly to the hearers' own families, with the Abrahamic multitude as its warrant. It stays a euphemism because nothing is said about what increases or how: no spirit children, no post-mortal begetting, no worlds. The sermon's subject is the rearing of mortal children, and the increase language arrives as the eternal frame around that duty rather than as a claim about the mechanics of exaltation.

quotes.excerpt: The past few years our emigration has attained to some three or four thousand, annually, from the various countries in which missions are established, while it has increased many times that number from the great and glorious presence of God our Father, who sends the spirits to this world to dwell. Hence it becomes the great source of our supply, of our increase, and I am sure you will join with me, many of you, this morning in realizing that we have not, in many instances, given a sufficient and proper consideration for our little children that have been committed unto us…
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. Richards locates the source of mortal births in spirits sent from God's presence, and the joke lands because he is counting them as immigration statistics — but a pre-existent spirit sent to a body is not a spirit-birth mechanism and not a tripartite staging of intelligence, spirit and body. Recorded so the passage is not later mistaken for either.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1884/1884-10-richards-remarks.md, transcribed from the printed Journal of Discourses volume 25, pp. 371–376 (printed header: discourse by Apostle F. D. Richards, delivered in the Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday morning, October 5th, 1884; reported by John Irvine); the vault notes that the discourse's real printed subject is "Little Children," the file id retaining the generic "remarks" only to avoid breaking links. Contemporaneous shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Delivered in the same session as cannon-puling-infant-1884 and immediately before it — Cannon in fact refers back to Richards's remarks about children in his own discourse — which makes the pair a good snapshot of how the eternal-family doctrine was voiced when the announced topic was Sunday School and parental duty.

title: Charles W. Penrose, “The Personality of God”: eternality in intelligence, not in ancestry
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Elder and editor of the Deseret News (ordained an Apostle 1904; later Counselor in the First Presidency)
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon (Journal of Discourses 26:18–27, at 26:23–27)

quotes.excerpt: But, if God is an individual spirit and dwells in a body, the question will arise, “Is He the Eternal Father?” Yes, He is the Eternal Father. “Is it a fact that He never had a beginning?” In the elementary particles of His organism, He did not. But if He is an organized Being, there must have been a time when that being was organized. This, some one will say, would infer that God had a beginning. This spirit which pervades all things, which is the light and life of all things, by which our heavenly Father operates, by which He is omnipotent, never had a beginning and never will have an end.
quotes.note: The anti-regress move, in the one paragraph where Penrose stages the objection and answers it. He concedes that God as an organized person had a beginning, and then locates eternality not in a line of ancestors but in an impersonal spirit of intelligence. Carried as context rather than tagged, because it asserts no ancestry in either direction — that is the point of it.

quotes.excerpt: And if you see a glorified man, a man who has passed through the various grades of being, who has overcome all things, who has been raised from the dead, who has been quickened by this spirit in its fullness, there you see manifested, in its perfection, this eternal, beginningless, endless spirit of intelligence. Such a Being is our Father and our God, and we are following in His footsteps. He has attained to perfection.
quotes.note: Past-mortality asserted as plainly as anywhere in the corpus — “raised from the dead” — but with the eternality predicated of the spirit of intelligence God embodies, not of God's person or lineage.

quotes.excerpt: The person whom I worship I acknowledge as my Father. Through Him I may learn to understand the secrets and mysteries of eternity, those things that never had a beginning and will never have an end. He has ascended above all things after descending below all things. He has fought his way from the depths up to the position He now occupies. He holds it by virtue of His goodness, of His might, of His majesty, of His power… He has won that position by His own exertions, by His own faithfulness, by His own righteousness.
quotes.note: Godhood by self-conquest. This is the alternative to a genealogy, not a step in one: nothing in the discourse says God received his position from a Father, and nothing asks who stood above him.

quotes.excerpt: As the Father had taken His upward course in worlds before this, so Jesus Christ followed in his footsteps in every respect; therefore he is entitled to sit down at the right hand of God in the heavens, to sit on his throne and be one with the Father in all things.
quotes.note: “Worlds before this” places the Father's progression in prior worlds — a real backward claim, and still not a parentage claim.

quotes.excerpt: The individual, the organized person may have had a beginning, but that spirit of which and by which they organized never had a beginning… The works of that eternal spirit of intelligence, the great Eternal God, manifested to us in our Father and through Jesus Christ, never had a beginning. There never was a first world or man; there will never be a last.
quotes.note: The closest Penrose comes to a chain, and it is deliberately not one: no first world and no first man, but no succession of divine fathers either. Structurally this is Orson Pratt's abstract “Great God” — the personages come and go, the intelligence is what is eternal — rather than Brigham Young's genealogy.

notes: The whole discourse (Journal of Discourses 26:18–27) was re-pulled and read for this entry, not just the paragraph that circulates. Verified verbatim. Two things follow from reading it whole. First, Penrose is a genuine backward-mortality source: God was organized, progressed through worlds before this one, was raised from the dead, and won his position by his own exertions. Second, he asserts no divine parentage anywhere in ten pages, and he explicitly heads off the regress by relocating beginninglessness into an impersonal “eternal, beginningless, endless spirit of intelligence” — so the entry carries no INFINITE-CHAIN tag and should not be recruited as one. It belongs with Nelson, Talmage and Widtsoe in the 1884–1915 cluster, where godhood is attained by progression through law from a beginning and eternality sits in impersonal intelligence, rather than with the Kimball–Young lineage stream. Discourse header: Elder Charles W. Penrose, Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon, November 16, 1884, reported by Arthur Winter. Hearsay C: a reporter's contemporaneous account, published without the speaker's review.

title: Erastus Snow: a Mother in heaven inferred from anatomy
speaker: Erastus Snow
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Quarterly conference discourse, Tabernacle, Provo (Journal of Discourses 26:213–227)

witnesses.scribe: John Irvine (third-person indirect report)
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 26:213–227. Irvine reports in third-person indirect style (“Proceeding, he said…”) rather than as a first-person verbatim transcript, so the printed wording is a reporter's rendering of Snow's argument, not necessarily Snow's sentences.

quotes.excerpt: Now, it is not said in so many words in the Scriptures, that we have a Mother in heaven as well as a Father. It is left for us to infer this from what we see and know of all living things in the earth including man. The male and female principle is united and both necessary to the accomplishment of the object of their being, and if this be not the case with our Father in heaven after whose image we are created, then it is an anomaly in nature. But to our minds the idea of a Father suggests that of a Mother
quotes.note: The clearest statement in the corpus of how Heavenly Mother is actually reached: not by revelation and not by scripture, which Snow concedes are silent, but by an argument from nature in which her absence would be an anomaly. That candid “it is left for us to infer this” is the datum — the doctrine is presented as an inference, in a discourse by an apostle, and later usage will present it as settled.

quotes.excerpt: "In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me, I've a Mother there."
quotes.note: Eliza R. Snow's verse quoted from the pulpit as the poetic seal on the anatomical argument — see o-my-father. Punctuation and capitalization follow the Journal of Discourses printing, which differs slightly from the hymnal text. This is the earliest pulpit quotation of the hymn located in the Pulpit corpus; roughly fifty talks quote it in all, clustering 1904–1929 and again 1973–1991.

quotes.excerpt: Hence when it is said that God created our first parents in His likeness--"in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them"--it is intimated in language sufficiently plain to my understanding that the male and female principle was present with the Gods as it is with man. It needs only a common understanding of the organism of man and of all living creatures, and the functions of this organism to show the primary object of the Creator, and that is the multiplication of the species… We need only to study the anatomy and construction of the human system, and to understand its powers and capabilities, to comprehend the object and purpose of the Creator, even though the commandment had not been written to multiply and replenish the earth.
quotes.note: Marked implied. What Snow states outright is that the male and female principle exists among the Gods and that human anatomy reveals the Creator's purpose to be multiplication of the species; the sentences about multiplying and replenishing are about earthly generation. Divine viviparous reproduction is the conclusion the argument is built to support and the one his hearers would draw, but he stops at the premise, so the tag is carried as read-into rather than stated. Double hyphens preserved from the vault transcription of the printed page.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1885/1885-05-snow-e-the-creation-male-and-female-etc.md, a fresh ingestion whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 26 page scans, pp. 213–227, with the printed header confirming John Irvine as reporter. Filed as an original rather than a citation, with citesId recording the edge to o-my-father: the hymn verse is quoted, but the entry's value is the argument around it, which is Snow's own and is not in the hymn — the hymn asserts a Mother and stops, while Snow supplies a reason, and the reason is anatomical. Provenance caveat, and it is a real one: this is the weakest-fidelity text in the pulpit lane. Irvine reports in third-person indirect style rather than transcribing, so the wording is his rendering of Snow's argument. Graded C to match the Journal of Discourses convention, since the report is contemporaneous and published, but it sits at the bottom of that grade and the phrasing should never be pressed as Snow's ipsissima verba. The vault entry is also still marked draft.

title: George Q. Cannon: "if one God was born of woman, may not others be also?"
speaker: George Q. Cannon
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference discourse, "Voice of Revelation," Salt Lake City (The Deseret Weekly, April 13, 1889, pp. 516–517)

witnesses.scribe: Deseret Weekly conference reporter
witnesses.note: Utah Digital Newspapers returns HTTP 418 to automated requests, so the page-level scan could not be re-fetched programmatically; the Wayback capture is the accessible witness. Reported for The Deseret Weekly; speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: In this respect we differ from others; among this people there is knowledge concerning God. We know to a certain extent of Him and His attributes. “As man now is, God was; as God now is, man may be.” We possess the attribute He possesses, and the object of the Gospel is to lead us to what He is. This is the true theory of evolution—that we can progress to become like unto God. This is the incentive of faithfulness.
quotes.note: The Snow couplet quoted as common knowledge from the general conference pulpit by a counselor in the First Presidency, twelve years before Snow's presidency made it famous, and with the wording slightly compressed ("God was" rather than "God once was"). Referent stays ambiguous on the couplet itself per the snow-couplet reading; what Cannon adds is the gloss — the couplet as "the true theory of evolution," which reads the second half as gradual development rather than as a discrete grant.

quotes.excerpt: The Apostle John says that “we will be like Him.” It is for this purpose that God has revealed the Gospel—that His children may become like unto Him. I do not mean in a spiritual sense; that is, in the way these things are spiritualized by some men. We believe that we are the literal offspring of Deity. We have descended from that great Being who formed this earth, and from Him we have inherited the glorious aspirations to be like unto Him.
quotes.note: Marked implied. What Cannon states is literal descent and an explicit refusal of the metaphorical reading ("I do not mean in a spiritual sense"); the physiological mechanism that the viviparous tag names — begetting, gestation, birth — is not stated here, and is supplied from what "literal offspring" meant in this pulpit. The identification is worth noting on its own terms: the Being we descend from is specified as the one "who formed this earth," which is a narrower claim than "God" and rules out reading the ancestry as generic deity.

quotes.excerpt: They worship Jesus as their God, and He is. But he was once a babe, and there are many who worship his mother Mary. He was born of a woman. And if one God was born of woman, may not others be also? To say they could not is not logical.
quotes.note: The argument is a defensive one — Christian doctrine already contains a God born of a woman, so ours is not stranger than theirs — and it is put as a question, which is why the stance is a hedge rather than an affirmation. The reasoning is by generalization from the Son's case to other Gods, exactly the inference the snow-couplet entry identifies as the couplet's Christological warrant; here the generalization is made explicit and then immediately dropped, with Cannon pivoting to how spirits could be "compressed" into infants. Referent ambiguous: "others" is unspecified and may or may not reach the Father.

quotes.excerpt: We had an existence before we came into mortality… I believe that when we meet our Father, the recollection that we were with Him will come back again. We will also know our mother, and those with whom we before associated. We will know each other, father, mother, husband, wife, children.
quotes.note: A Mother in heaven mentioned in the same breath as the Father and with no argument attached — the reunion is with "our Father" and "our mother" as a matter of course. Four years before this, Erastus Snow had to reason to her from anatomy (snow-heavenly-mother-1885); here a counselor in the First Presidency simply assumes her in a passage about pre-mortal memory.

quotes.excerpt: He has promised that we shall sit upon a throne, that we shall have a crown, that we shall have a posterity as numerous as the stars in heaven, as countless as the sands by the seashore. “For,” says he, “I seal upon you the blessings of kingdoms, of thrones, of principalities, of powers, and of dominions. I seal upon you the blessings of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob; I seal upon you the promise that you shall come forth in the morning of the first resurrection, clothed with glory, clothed with immortality, clothed with eternal life.”
quotes.note: Posterity named, and named inside a list of post-resurrection blessings sealed in the temple — throne, crown, first resurrection — which is what keeps it from being read as the mortal Abrahamic promise. The sealing formula that follows is pure euphemism (kingdoms, thrones, principalities, powers, dominions); the explicit content is the clause before it.

notes: Text taken verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1889/1889-04-cannon-discourse.md, whose body was replaced during review with the actual Deseret Weekly report of Cannon's Sunday morning discourse ("Voice of Revelation") after an earlier compiler summary proved not to match the source; the vault's heavyweight pass read the full April 13, 1889 proceedings account (pp. 481–491) and the standalone full-discourse reprint (April 20, 1889, pp. 513–516).
