office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, third day afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1899, pp. 63–67; the passage is on p. 65)

quotes.excerpt: The Latter-day Saints are promised, if they are faithful, that they shall receive the fullness, as Jesus received it: and Jesus received it as the Father received it.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the whole weight sits on the last clause. Cannon extends the D&C 93 grace-for-grace chain one link past the Son and puts the Father inside it: the Father, too, received the fulness. That is attainment language without any statement of mortality, which by the Father-status precedent is FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone, not FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE. Two things Cannon does not say, and which should not be read in: from whom the Father received it, and whether He is still receiving. The clause is not glossed, defended, or returned to.

quotes.excerpt: “They are they into whose hands the Father has given all things.” Now, these are not idle words, given merely to round out a sentence; but they are full of meaning. “They are they who are Priests and Kings, who have received of His fulness, and of His glory, … Wherefore, as it is written, they are Gods, even the sons of God.”
quotes.note: Context for the claim above. Cannon reads D&C 76:54–59 aloud and adds only an insistence that the words are meant literally (“not idle words… full of meaning”) — no exposition of what “they are Gods” amounts to. Recorded here as the scriptural platform he then extends to the Father, not as a claim of his own.

quotes.excerpt: It is God's design to make us priests and kings; not to have an empty title, not to sit upon thrones without power, but to be actually and really priests and kings. The promise is that all things that He hath shall be given unto us. We will be His heirs; we will be (if I may use the term without irreverence) co-partners with Him in all this power and authority.
quotes.note: Context. Cannon presses the promised equality with God as real power and dominion rather than honorific title, and registers his own sense of how far it goes with the apology “if I may use the term without irreverence.” Theosis, not generative exaltation: no offspring, no worlds, no chain — which is exactly why it carries no category.

notes: All three excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1899a, printed pp. 63–67) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1899/1899-04-cannon-individual-responsibility.md; line-break hyphenation closed up, and the printed spelling “fullness” retained. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Not to be confused with cannon-power-of-procreation-1899, which is Cannon three days earlier (6 April 1899) in the same conference on a different subject; this is the closing-session address on individual responsibility.

title: Lorenzo Snow: the infant Jesus “knew not that He was the Son of God”
speaker: Lorenzo Snow
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, April 1901, pp. 1–4)

quotes.excerpt: When Jesus lay in the manger, a helpless infant, He knew not that He was the Son of God, and that formerly He created the earth. When the edict of Herod was issued, He knew nothing of it; He had not power to save Himself; and His father and mother had to take Him and fly into Egypt to preserve Him from the effects of that edict. Well, He grew up to manhood, and during His progress it was revealed unto Him who He was, and for what purpose He was in the world. The glory and power He possessed before He came into the world was made known unto Him.
quotes.note: Affirmation, but read the referent chip: the being who passes through ignorance and gains knowledge is the Son in mortality, not the Father. This is the conflation the axis exists to prevent — a completed mortal progression, of the same kind George Albert Smith draws out of D&C 93 five years later (gasmith-grace-for-grace-1906), and not the claim that God the Father still advances. What it does establish, in the opening address of a general conference by the Church President who coined the couplet, is that a member of the Godhead is not embarrassed by having been ignorant and powerless.

quotes.excerpt: Whatever changes may arise, whatever worlds may be made or pass away, our identity will always remain the same; and we will continue on improving, advancing and increasing in wisdom, intelligence, power and dominion, worlds without end. … Whatever may have been our past, how long we may have existed before this, or whether there ever was a time when we did not exist, there is one thing sure — our being in the future will never be annihilated, never destroyed.
quotes.note: Context, and useful for two things. First, the human side of endless progression stated without any offspring content at all — increase in wisdom, power and dominion, not in posterity — so no forward tag. Second, the backward question about our own premortal existence raised and expressly left open (“or whether there ever was a time when we did not exist”), which is agnosticism about human origins, not about the Father's, so BACKWARD-AGNOSTIC does not apply.

notes: Verified against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1901a, printed pp. 1–4) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1901/1901-04-snow-opening-address.md, whose final review collated leaves n1–n4. Line-break hyphenation closed up. One punctuation difference worth recording: the scan OCR sets a full stop after “a helpless infant” where the vault reads a comma; the reading above follows the vault, and nothing turns on it. Conference Report, so hearsay A. This is Snow's last April conference; he died 10 October 1901.

title: Charles W. Penrose: eternal lives defined twice — power and dominion, then posterity multiplied worlds without end
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Editor of the Deseret News; not yet a General Authority (ordained an Apostle in 1904)
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1901, pp. 42–44)

quotes.excerpt: If we desire to obtain the great salvation, if we desire to obtain the crown, in the presence of the Father, if we desire to have the gift of eternal lives (which means endless increase in power, dominion and glory forever), we must abide the conditions on which this glory is predicated.
quotes.note: Penrose's first definition of “eternal lives,” given parenthetically, names no posterity at all: increase in power, dominion and glory. Taken alone this is the euphemism in its purest form — the technical D&C 132 term glossed in a way a hearer could take as personal advancement. Kept because of what he does with the same term two pages later (next quote): the same speaker, the same sermon, defines it a second time and the second time it is offspring.

quotes.excerpt: There will be immortality to all the sons and daughters of God, whether they are suffering for sin or have been redeemed; whether they are in the celestial, terrestrial or telestial worlds; but only those who attain to the celestial glory, and the power and dominion and exaltation, and the gift of everlasting increase, wherein their posterity will be multiplied worlds without end, have the real gift of eternal life.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the definitional move that makes the entry: “everlasting increase” is expressly cashed out as posterity multiplied without end, and eternal life is restricted to those who have it. “Worlds without end” here is the liturgical idiom for endlessness, not a claim about plural worlds, so MANY-WORLDS is not applied to this quote (it is applied to the next, where Penrose does describe worlds being created).

quotes.excerpt: They will pattern after the works of their Eternal Father and their Elder Brother, while eternal ages roll along, and they will be in harmony and in communion with them, and will participate with them in the glorious work of the extension of the universe and dominion of God throughout the vast domains of space; and while eternal ages go and come they will increase and multiply in light, in wisdom, in intelligence, in knowledge, in power, and in glory, and the extent of their possessions and dominions in the worlds that will be created will be from everlasting to everlasting.
quotes.note: The forward chain closed on the Father's own activity: the exalted “pattern after the works of their Eternal Father,” share in extending the universe, and hold possessions and dominions in “the worlds that will be created.” Plural worlds, still under one God and with no succession of Gods implied — MANY-WORLDS, not INFINITE-CHAIN. Ten years before the measured October 1911 address recorded at penrose-endless-increase-1911, and by a man who at this date held no general Church office at all.

notes: All three excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1901a, printed pp. 42–44) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1901/1901-04-penrose-immortality-obedience-and-glory.md, whose final review collated leaves n42–n44 against the page images. Line-break hyphenation closed up; the first excerpt begins mid-sentence at “If” (lower-case “if” in print) and the initial letter has been capitalised. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Office correction: the Pulpit vault frontmatter records Penrose as “Member of the First Council of the Seventy,” which is wrong — the April 1901 Conference Report's own roll of authorities lists the First Seven Presidents of Seventies as Seymour B. Young, George Reynolds, Brigham H. Roberts, Jonathan G. Kimball, Rulon S. Wells and Joseph W. McMurrin, without Penrose. He was editor of the Deseret News and was not ordained an Apostle until 7 July 1904. That matters for how the quote is weighed: the fullest statement of generative exaltation in this conference comes from a newspaper editor speaking as an ordinary elder, not from the hierarchy.

title: John W. Taylor at Lorenzo Snow's funeral: “He will be that much further ahead of you”
speaker: John W. Taylor
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Funeral services of President Lorenzo Snow, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1901, pp. 90–94)

quotes.excerpt: On another occasion, while pondering upon some principles that had been taught him by the Prophet Joseph, he heard a voice from heaven, and that voice made known unto him the principle embodied in these words: “As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be.” … Secondly, it was made known unto him that the sons and daughters of men may attain unto that perfection which the Eternal Father possesses.
quotes.note: The bare couplet, affirmed over Snow's coffin, so FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE only — Taylor adds no attainment or progression language to the Father's side. Two provenance points. The wording is Taylor's: “as God now is, man may be,” not the usual “man may become.” And this is a relay of a sixty-one-year-old private revelation as Taylor had heard Snow recount it (“I have heard him relate”), which is why the quote carries a hearsay override of D against the entry's A; the printed report of Taylor's own words is reliable, the 1840 origin story inside it is not the same kind of evidence. Compare snow-couplet.

quotes.excerpt: I will read a little concerning the works of our Father, and then you can imagine what possibilities you may attain to by reaching the same degree of perfection. … “And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose; and by the Son I created them, which is mine Only Begotten … For behold, there are many worlds that have passed away by the word of my power. And there are many also which now stand, and numberless are they unto man, but all things are numbered unto me, for they are mine and I know them.”
quotes.note: Taylor reads Moses 1 aloud, but note the frame he puts on it: it is a catalogue of “the works of our Father” offered so the congregation can “imagine what possibilities you may attain to.” Plural worlds under one God — MANY-WORLDS — with the succession question untouched. The scripture is quoted from the Pearl of Great Price; the elisions drop the Adam clause and Moses's request for an account of this earth.

quotes.excerpt: Can you not imagine a day when it will be possible for you to be perfect as your Father in heaven is perfect? when you will have progressed to such an exalted condition that you will be able to do the works of the Father? Such will be the case, whether you can imagine it or not.
quotes.note: Marked implied: the world-making is carried by the antecedent, not by this sentence. “The works of the Father” are the works Taylor has just read out of Moses 1 — worlds without number — and he told the congregation before reading them that they were to measure their own possibilities against them. So the exalted creating worlds is Taylor's plain sense, but he never says the word “worlds” in the claim itself, and the tag should be read with that in mind.

quotes.excerpt: If all things are added unto you, ultimately you will become like our Father and God. It is true, however, that when you reach the position He occupies today, He will be that much further ahead of you, and it will still be said to you, “Be ye perfect, even as your Father in heaven is perfect.”
quotes.note: Affirmation, in the classic never-catch-up form, and unusually clean: not progression in dominions only, but the Father occupying a position that keeps moving, stated as a correction (“It is true, however”) to the equality Taylor has just promised. Preached at the funeral of the man whose couplet the same address endorses, and a decade before B. H. Roberts wrote the same claim into a Church-published quorum manual (roberts-progress-of-god-1911).

notes: All four excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1901sa, printed pp. 90–94) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1901/1901-10-taylor-principle-of-eternal-progression.md, whose final review reconstructed two badly interleaved two-column passages directly from the page images. Line-break hyphenation closed up; three scan-level letter errors visible in the raw OCR of these passages (“Josepn,” “(irst,” “Foi,” and a dropped “w” in “*hen”) are corrected to the printed readings. The address is printed inside the October 1901 Conference Report but was delivered at Snow's funeral service on 13 October, after the conference proper; hearsay A for the report, with a per-quote override of D on the relayed 1840 couplet narrative. citesId records the two texts Taylor works from: the Snow couplet and Moses 1.

title: Hyrum M. Smith: all knowledge “even as our Father in heaven possesses it”
speaker: Hyrum M. Smith
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1902, pp. 20–23)

quotes.excerpt: And Oh! how we rejoice in it, my brethren and sisters, and in the knowledge, too, that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into our hearts, what God has in store for us as we march on in that infinite progression and advancement. All things will be given to us—all power, all glory, all knowledge, even as our Father in heaven possesses it—in due time, as we are capable of receiving them.
quotes.note: Marked implied and flagged for review: Smith never raises the question of whether God progresses, so the direction is structural rather than stated. What the sentence does is fix the terminus of “infinite progression” at what the Father already possesses — all power, all glory, all knowledge — with no suggestion that the terminus itself moves. Read against Taylor at Snow's funeral six months earlier (taylor-never-catch-up-1901), where the Father is expressly “that much further ahead,” the two make the shape of the coming debate visible in the same Conference Report series. A curator may prefer to record this as context only.

quotes.excerpt: If, then, one man, in a finite condition, can become so thoroughly acquainted with a people numbering four hundred thousand, can we not understand how easy it is for God, who is infinite, to receive all knowledge concerning all the works of His hands?
quotes.note: Context, and the reason the quote above reads the way it does. Smith explains divine omniscience naturalistically, by analogy to the Church's own reporting hierarchy from President to stake president to bishop to ward teacher — knowledge that is gathered and transmitted rather than possessed timelessly. The verb is “receive.” Whether that makes God's knowledge complete-and-static or acquired-and-growing is precisely what he does not say. The printed page reads “on become,” an OCR-level defect for “can become,” corrected here per the vault's page-image collation.

notes: Both excerpts verified against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1902a, printed pp. 20–23) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1902/1902-04-smith-value-and-possession-of-truth.md, whose final review collated leaves n20–n23 against the page images. Line-break hyphenation closed up and the printed em-dash spacing (“to us— all power… possesses it —”) normalised; wording untouched. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Hyrum M. Smith, eldest son of Joseph F. Smith, had been in the Twelve less than six months; he died in 1918 at 45.

title: Nels L. Nelson: how our Father became God
speaker: Nels L. Nelson
office: Professor of English, Brigham Young University
venue: Scientific Aspects of Mormonism; or, Religion in Terms of Life (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1904), ch. XXV “Jehovah,” pp. 273–274, and ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God,” pp. 275–276

quotes.excerpt: As respects the eternal principles underlying His purposes, He never changes; these form the very warp and woof of His divine perfection; but as respects the methods or devices for bringing about these purposes, He changes as the exigency requires; and the variations possible to His invention are practically infinite… It is by reason of this very principle of mutation in God that we perceive all things to be in a state of evolution here on earth.
quotes.note: Affirmation — but a bounded one, and the boundary has to be quoted with it. Nelson's God changes in method, not in principle, and the sentences just above hold that on attaining Godhood “how could He be other than immutable? For change would then imply degeneracy.” Lifting “this very principle of mutation in God” out of that setting produces a stronger divine-progression claim than Nelson makes.

quotes.excerpt: But since by this conception He is made to belong to the same order of beings as Christ, His Son,—the same order, indeed, as man himself,—and must consequently have attained to Godhood or creative power, it becomes a pertinent question to consider how He reached such divine sovereignty.
quotes.note: The chapter's opening question, carried as context because it is routinely quoted as though it were the chapter's answer. Note the original begins “But since by this conception…” — the concessive “But” is part of the sentence and is preserved here.

quotes.excerpt: A sufficient general answer, therefore, would be that God became God because He fulfilled the law of becoming perfect as His Father in heaven was perfect; or, in the terms of science, because He fulfilled the supreme requirements of psychic evolution.
quotes.note: Explicit divine parentage — “His Father in heaven,” a phrase Nelson builds by turning Matthew 5:48 back on God himself — with no chain length stated and no interest in stating one. The gloss “psychic evolution” is the Spencerian idiom that marks this whole cluster of Utah writers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the 1904 Putnam's first edition (item scientificaspect00nelsrich), reading continuously from printed p. 273 through p. 276 so the page breaks between the three quotes are known rather than assumed: the divine-progression material closes ch. XXV at pp. 273–274, and ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God” opens at p. 275 with the question and answers it on pp. 275–276. Nelson was a BYU English professor writing for a national trade press, not for the Church; never-official. He is one of the few authors in the dataset who is both a backward-explicit source and a divine-progression source, which is precisely why his two claims should not be merged into one: the parentage is asserted, the ongoing mutability is heavily qualified, and neither entails the other.

title: Asahel H. Woodruff: “We have left our Father and Mother in heaven”
speaker: Asahel H. Woodruff
office: President of the Northern States Mission
venue: General conference, first day afternoon overflow session (Conference Report, April 1904)

quotes.excerpt: We have left our Father and Mother in heaven, become self-exiled from the associations of our primeval existence, and have come down here on earth in obedience to the will of God, for a wise purpose He has in view.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and as bare as the category gets: the Mother is half of a compound noun in a subordinate clause about why mortality feels like exile. No argument, no hymn, no scripture, no source, and no mechanism — mortality is “similar to being away from home,” and the home has two parents in it. Nothing is said about spirit birth, so no birth tag; nothing backward is claimed, so referent n/a. What makes it worth an entry is the setting: a mission president says it in passing in 1904, inside an address whose real subject is defending the Saints against the charge of immorality in the middle of the Smoot hearings, and he plainly expects no one in the Tabernacle to blink.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1904/1904-04-woodruff-missionary-work.md, rebuilt from the official printed Conference Report of the Seventy-fourth Annual Conference (Internet Archive conferencereport1904a) and Final-Reviewed against leaves n22–n24 and the BookReader page images, which corrected three shared-OCR tokens elsewhere in the body; none falls inside the quoted sentence, and the excerpt begins just after a stray apostrophe artifact in “We 'regard our condition here.” Conference Report, so A; the printed Report supplies no formal title. Disambiguation, because the surname invites the wrong link: this is Asahel H. Woodruff, president of the Northern States Mission, not Wilford Woodruff — see woodruff-progression-1857 for the President of the Church. Where it sits: the corpus already carries conference-pulpit Mother statements from George Q. Cannon in 1889 and 1896 (cannon-literal-offspring-1889, cannon-descended-from-god-1896) and from Lorenzo Snow in 1898 (snow-mother-in-the-other-life-1898), so this is not a first — it is evidence of what happened to the claim between the Presidents of the Church who argued it and the apostles who would argue it again in 1907 and 1908 (whitney-father-and-mother-1907, iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908). In 1904 it needs no argument at all, and it is a mission president rather than a member of the First Presidency who states it, which is the register datum worth having.

title: George Albert Smith: “the Savior did not receive a fulness at once”
speaker: George Albert Smith
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1906, pp. 46–51)

quotes.excerpt: We find in the same section the information that the Savior did not receive a fulness at once, but grace was given Him for grace. As He overcame He developed and progressed.
quotes.note: Affirmation of progression in a member of the Godhead, and one of the two standard scriptural proof-texts of the whole debate — D&C 93:12–14, the section Smith has been reading aloud. But the referent chip is doing real work: this is the Son's completed mortal progression, not the Father's ongoing progression. Smith draws no inference about the Father and does not connect the passage to the couplet; the sermon's subject is parental obligation. The reason to record it is that this verse is the hinge on which later writers on both sides of the question turn.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1906sa, printed pp. 46–51) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1906/1906-10-smith-fruits-and-parental-obligations.md, which carries a page-by-page heavyweight collation and a final review of leaves n51–n52. Line-break hyphenation closed up; the raw OCR of this passage carries stray commas from the column edge (“at once,,”), removed. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Deliberately a one-quote entry: after a full read the rest of the sermon is on home industry, persecution, and teaching children, with no other axis-bearing material. Smith was ordained an Apostle in 1903 and became Church President in 1945.

title: B. H. Roberts, The Seventy's Course in Theology
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: One of the seven Presidents of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: Seventy's Course in Theology (five volumes); later The Truth, The Way, The Life

quotes.excerpt: It is customary for us to say, that there are three grand estates of existence through which intelligencies pass in the course of their exaltation to resurrected, immortal, divine beings…: first, their pre-existence as spirits, sons and daughters of God, in the spirit world; second, these spirits clothed upon with mortal bodies—earth-life of men and women; third, spirits inhabiting bodies that have been resurrected, immortal beings clothed with imperishable bodies prepared for eternal advancement in the kingdoms of God. But the doctrine of the Prophet and of the scriptures he gave to the world, require us to recognize before the first estate as set forth in the above order, the existence of the self-existent intelligencies before they are begotten spirits, sons and daughters of God. So that it could be said that there are four estates in which intelligencies exist instead of three; namely; self-existent, uncreated and unbegotten intelligencies, co-eternal with God; second, intelligencies begotten of God spirits; third, spirits begotten men and women, still sons and daughters of God; fourth, resurrected beings, immortal spirits inhabiting imperishable bodies, still sons and daughters of God, and in the line of eternal progression, up to the attainment of divine attributes and powers.
quotes.note: The framework stated as an amendment, which is the thing worth seeing. Roberts is not reporting a received three-stage model; he is arguing that the customary three estates are one short and that an uncreated intelligence must be recognised *before* the spirit. Printed pp. 11–12, note 7, headed “Effect of the Doctrine of the Eternal Existence of Intelligences on Our Terminology.” Elision covers a parenthetical cross-reference to Jaques's Catechism, ch. vi. The printed text really does read “namely;” with a semicolon and omits “first,” before the opening member of the list — verified against the page image, not the OCR. Roberts then offers the concession that has made the model portable ever since: counting changes rather than statuses, “we may still say that so far as the matter has been revealed there are three estates.”

quotes.excerpt: The difference, then, between “spirits” and “intelligencies,” as here used, is this: Spirits are uncreated intelligencies inhabiting spiritual bodies; while “intelligencies,” pure and simple, are intelligent entities, but unembodied in either spirit bodies or bodies of flesh and bone. They are uncreated, self-existent entities, possessed of “self-consciousness,” and “other-consciousness”—they are conscious of the “me” and the “not me”; they possess powers of discrimination… they discern between the evil and the good; between the “good” and “the better.”
quotes.note: The definition the whole framework rests on, printed p. 11, note 6. This is the tier that is *not* begotten, and it is why the entry carries SPIRIT-BIRTH-ADOPTION alongside the begetting quotes below: on Roberts's account what is born in the pre-existence is a body, and what inhabits it was never made. Compare abraham-3 and kfd-1844, which supply the uncreatedness he is systematising.

quotes.excerpt: “This body which ye now behold is the body of my spirit”—the house, the tenement of that uncreated intelligence which had been begotten of the Father a spirit, as later that spirit-body with the intelligent, uncreated entity inhabiting it, will be begotten a man.
quotes.note: The three stages compressed into a single sentence, printed p. 10, note 6, reasoning from Ether 3:16 and Christ's spirit body outward to all men. Roberts's verb is “begotten” at both transitions, which is why this quote takes the begetting tag and q2 takes the adoption tag: the two are not in tension for him, they are the two halves of the synthesis. No physiology is described anywhere in the lesson — the gestational mechanism that later attaches to this model comes from Melvin J. Ballard, not from here (see ballard-increase and eom-premortal-life-1992).

quotes.excerpt: According to this, then, there is a “Father of Spirits.” It follows, of course, that “spirits” have a father—they are begotten… Fatherhood to spirits is manifestly a relationship established independent of man's earth-existence; and, of course, in an existence which preceded earth-life, where the uncreated intelligences are begotten spirits.
quotes.note: Printed p. 14, Lesson II, note 2, arguing from Hebrews 12:9. The closing clause is the framework's load-bearing formula — “the uncreated intelligences are begotten spirits” — an uncreated subject undergoing a real begetting. Roberts is explicit that Paul's “Father of spirits” cannot mean “Fathers of our flesh,” so the fatherhood is premortal and literal.

notes: Placeholder closed in v2 against the printed volumes. The excerpts are from The Seventy's Course in Theology, Second Year: Outline History of the Dispensations of the Gospel (Salt Lake City: Skelton Publishing Co., 1908), Part I, “Prelude to the Dispensations,” Lesson I (“Intelligencies and Spirits”) notes 3–7 and Lesson II notes 1–2, printed pp. 8–14 — read from the Gospel Scholar Archive copy of the collected Course (PDF pp. 278–284) with pp. 10, 11, 12 and 14 additionally checked against the rendered page images, since the OCR layer of this volume introduces stray commas and hyphenation at line breaks. Line-break hyphenation is closed up; one stray comma in the OCR (“spiritual, bodies”) is not in the print and has been dropped. Roberts's own footnote to Lesson I records where the material came from and settles the status question: the notes are taken from his article “Immortality of Man,” Improvement Era, April 1907 — the Era being, in the volume's own words, “the Organ of the Seventies and of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Associations” — and the Era printed it with the editorial line, “Elder Roberts submitted the following paper to the First Presidency and a number of the Twelve Apostles, none of whom found anything objectionable in it, or contrary to the revealed word of God, and therefore favor its publication.” correlationStatus is therefore changed from never-official to historical-official, matching roberts-progress-of-god-1911: rationale — the Year Books were prepared by Roberts in his office as President of the First Council of the Seventy, copyrighted “for the First Council of Seventy,” and prescribed as the study course for Seventies quorums, and this particular material had been read by the First Presidency and members of the Twelve before publication, so grading the same series two different ways cannot be defended on the evidence. That grade is about the standing of the *source*, not the canonical standing of the *claim*: the four-estate scheme was never canonised, Roberts himself presents it as a correction to customary usage, and Joseph Fielding Smith attacks it by implication in 1963 (see jfs-agq-intelligences-1963). One housekeeping note for the maintainer: the excerpts are from the 1908 Second Year volume, so the entry's 1907–1911 range still covers them, but venue could be tightened to name the Second Year specifically.

title: Orson F. Whitney: a Mother in heaven defended as philosophy
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1907)

quotes.excerpt: Why, then, should it be deemed unphilosophic for man, the child of God, — man and woman, male and female, — to become like their Father and their Mother in heaven? We are at the defiance of the world to prove this doctrine unphilosophical.
quotes.note: A Mother in heaven asserted in passing and then used as a premise, which is the tell: Whitney does not argue for her, he assumes her and dares the world to refute the package. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only. “Become like their Father and their Mother in heaven” is theosis, not generative exaltation, and carries no FORWARD tag by itself — the A-framing trap. Spacing before the question mark normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: You earthly parents expect your children to become men and women like yourselves. You know that it is only a question of time, when, if they live, your little toddling children will become men and women, and will marry and have children of their own.
quotes.note: Marked implied. The sentence is literally about mortal children. But it is the immediate warrant for the claim in q1 — the analogy is offered so that the hearer will complete it — and what completes it is offspring, not merely likeness. Whitney stops one step short of saying so, so the forward-generative reading is carried as read-into rather than stated.

quotes.excerpt: It revealed anew the sublime fact that man is verily the child of Deity, and can become, by development, like unto his Father and his God. It taught the great truth that man is divinity in embryo, and capable, by education, through human experience, and by obedience to the principles of eternal progress, of rising to the plane whereon stands the Universal Father, who desires to make His children equal with Himself, and to put into their possession all things.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. “Divinity in embryo,” “equal with Himself,” “rising to the plane whereon stands the Universal Father” — this is theosis at full nineteenth-century strength and it still asserts nothing about spirit offspring or about a chain behind the Father. Recorded so the entry shows what Whitney does and does not claim in the same breath.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1907/1907-10-whitney-defending-the-saints.md, whose Final Review collated the full body against the archive.org scan conferencereport1907sa, leaves n45–n53, word for word against the printed page. A heavyweight pass had earlier split a separate George F. Richards address out of this file and re-anchored the leaf, so the URL points at where Whitney's own remarks begin. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. No hymn quotation appears in this talk, which is why the entry carries no citesId — Whitney reaches the Mother without Eliza R. Snow, through the same argument from nature that Erastus Snow used in 1885 (see snow-heavenly-mother-1885), but stripped of the anatomy and recast as a reply to outside critics. The setting matters: the talk is an apologetic defense of the Saints “against calumny and misrepresentation,” and the Heavenly Mother claim is deployed as an asset rather than defended as an embarrassment. Read against packer-parentage-1984 and hinckley-1997, which handle the same apologetic pressure by subtraction.

title: Heber C. Iverson: the hymn credited to Joseph Smith's inspiration
speaker: Heber C. Iverson
office: Bishop of the Second Ward
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon overflow session (Conference Report, April 1908, pp. 69–72)

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: The couplet as printed in the Conference Report; Iverson quotes the first three stanzas and stops here. Spacing before the question mark, semicolon and exclamation point normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed. See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: That doctrine was ridiculed seventy years ago, when announced by this hymn, teaching what had been given by inspiration flowing first through the mind of the Prophet Joseph Smith, that we have a mother in heaven.
quotes.note: The provenance claim that the whole later tradition rests on, made explicit from the pulpit: the hymn is not Eliza R. Snow's poetic inference but a vehicle for revelation given first to Joseph Smith. Set this beside snow-heavenly-mother-1885, where an apostle says the opposite in as many words — “it is left for us to infer this” — and beside hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, where the argument has shrunk to the observation that Joseph made no correction to what Sister Snow had written. The date arithmetic is loose: “seventy years ago” from 1908 lands in 1838, while the poem was published in 1845.

quotes.excerpt: He discourses very learnedly upon the dual sequence of the term Elohim, and proves conclusively by his deduction that there is a feminine element existing with the Deity, and that we have in Deity a mother as well as a father. There are mothers of our spirits.
quotes.note: Two things worth having. First, the corroboration is outside and secular — an unnamed writer in “one of the leading magazines of this country” arguing from the plural form of Elohim — which is a Latter-day Saint apostle-era bishop reaching for a non-Mormon philologist to underwrite a Mormon doctrine. Second, and easy to miss, the plural: “There are mothers of our spirits.” Iverson slides from one Mother to many without remark, twenty years after the Manifesto and in a Church still living with plural marriage, and the plural never becomes a doctrine anyone defends.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1908/1908-04-iverson-rejoicing-and-responsibility.md, whose heavyweight pass verified the talk boundary, speaker, session and supplied title against the archive.org Conference Report scan conferencereport1908a at printed pages 69–72, and whose Final Review pass is recorded as complete. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. Filed as an original rather than a citation, with citesId preserving the edge to o-my-father: the hymn is quoted at length, but the entry's value is the three claims Iverson builds around it — that the doctrine came by inspiration through Joseph Smith, that a secular philologist independently confirms it, and that our spirits have mothers plural — none of which is in the hymn. He is a ward bishop speaking in an overflow session, so this is not authoritative teaching; it is evidence of what a well-read local leader took the hymn to have settled, which for the reception history is the more useful thing.

title: Orson F. Whitney quotes Joseph Smith: God “finding Himself in the midst of spirits and glory, because He was more intelligent”
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1908, pp. 86–93)

quotes.excerpt: When and where did the Gospel originate? I know of no better explanation than that given by the Prophet Joseph Smith, who said: “In the beginning, God, finding Himself in the midst of spirits and glory, because He was more intelligent, saw proper to institute laws whereby the rest might advance like Himself.”
quotes.note: Denial direction: the tag marks the question, and Whitney's answer is no. God does not create the situation He is in — He finds Himself in it, in the midst of spirits and glory that are already there, and His preeminence is comparative (“because He was more intelligent”) rather than absolute. That rules out uncaused, solitary deity. What it does not do is state that God attained divinity or lived a mortality, so FATHER-BECAME-GOD and FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE are deliberately not applied. Whitney gives no citation; the saying is a condensed form of the King Follett Discourse (see kfd-1844), and he offers it as the best available account of where the gospel came from.

quotes.excerpt: We learn from this, that the Gospel—now called Mormonism,—which comprises and codifies those laws that were instituted of God in the beginning, was framed before the world was created; that it is the means of man's progression, both in time and in eternity,—the ladder up which all must climb who attain to exaltation.
quotes.note: Context: Whitney's own gloss, immediately following, and the reason the quotation is in the sermon at all. He reads the saying not as speculation about God's origin but as the charter of the gospel — the laws God instituted so that the rest might advance like Himself are simply the gospel, and the whole address is built on the image of a ladder let down into a pit. The metaphysics arrives as a premise for an evangelistic point.

notes: Both excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1908a, printed pp. 86–93) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1908/1908-04-whitney-gospel-of-salvation.md, whose final review is a full-body page-image collation of leaves n86–n94. Line-break hyphenation closed up; no other change. Conference Report, so hearsay A. sourceType stays original: the value here is not the transmission of the Joseph Smith saying but an Apostle putting it at the centre of a general conference address on salvation two years after his ordination. Compare whitney-exponent-mother-mortality-1895 and whitney-father-and-mother-1907 for the same author on the other axes.

title: Ben E. Rich: man a “trinity” — everlasting intelligence, a spirit born to Father and Mother, a mortal tabernacle
speaker: Ben E. Rich
office: President of the Eastern States Mission
venue: General conference, third day morning session (Conference Report, October 1908, pp. 101–104)

quotes.excerpt: I have heard it said, often, that man is a dual being — I say, he is a trinity. Man is a representative of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost. When a human body comes into the world, there is a light from another sphere placed within it. The spirit that God places within this tabernacle was not created in this sphere, it was created yonder, in the presence of our Father and our Mother in heaven. When that spirit tabernacle was born unto them, there was a light, there was an intelligence placed within it that existed from everlasting. So that man was created in the image of God, and, like unto God, he is from' everlasting to everlasting, and is thus a representative of the Trinity in heaven.
quotes.note: A real three-stage model, not a retrojected one, which is why TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK is applied: an intelligence “that existed from everlasting,” a spirit body distinct from it and produced later, and the mortal tabernacle the spirit is placed into — Rich says so explicitly by correcting the received teaching that man is “a dual being.” The staging is what makes the birth language legible: the spirit tabernacle is “born unto them,” both Parents named, and the intelligence is then placed within it, so what is begotten is the spirit body and not the person's ultimate substance. Heavenly Mother is affirmed flatly and in the same breath as the Father. Note the vocabulary sitting on both sides — the spirit “was created yonder” and also “born unto them” — which is normal for the period and not a sign Rich meant anything short of literal birth. The apostrophe in “from' everlasting” is a print artifact confirmed against the page images and left as printed. Compare bh-roberts-tripartite, published the year before, for the same staging worked out at length.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1908/1908-10-rich-testimony-and-mission.md, transcribed from the printed Conference Report of the Seventy-Ninth Semi-Annual Conference (Internet Archive conferencereport1908sa) and Final-Reviewed by full-body collation against the scan page images, leaves n102–n105, printed pp. 101–104, which produced eight scan-confirmed corrections elsewhere in the address and confirmed the surviving oddities inside q1 as artifacts of the print itself; the file is status published. Conference Report, so A. One quote by design: the whole doctrinal content is the closing paragraph, and it arrives after eight paragraphs on the Book of Mormon, the divine origin of the United States government, and the Smoot and Roberts fights — Rich reaches the premortal tripartite model as the answer to “the object God had in placing you here upon this earth,” tells the congregation to live by it, and sits down. Six months earlier, in the April 1908 conference, Heber C. Iverson had credited the Mother to Joseph Smith's inspiration through the hymn (iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908); Rich needs no such licence and offers no source at all.

title: James G. Duffin: parents will “give an account to our Father and Mother in heaven”
speaker: James G. Duffin
office: Elder; former president of the Central States Mission
venue: General conference, Sunday morning overflow meeting (Conference Report, April 1909, pp. 23–25)

quotes.excerpt: The responsibility here at home is not only that the young men may become efficient missionaries, but that they may also be good workers in wards and stakes, in the various organizations established by our Heavenly Father, and, that they may be honored citizens of the great nation of which they form a part, so that when we, as parents, give an account to our Father and Mother in heaven of the manner in which we have conducted ourselves toward the precious souls entrusted to us, how we have dealt with them, that we might bring them all with us, and be able to say to our Heavenly Father, Here are these sacred trusts that you gave unto me while I was upon the earth, I present them to You now spotless, full of faith and integrity, fitted indeed to be members of Thy eternal kingdom.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the whole of its value is that no case is made for it. She is named in a subordinate clause of a sentence about raising missionaries, in a pairing so unremarkable that the next clause reverts to the singular (“be able to say to our Heavenly Father”) without any sense of having changed subject. Compare the surrounding decades, where the doctrine always arrives with a warrant attached — Erastus Snow's inference from anatomy (snow-heavenly-mother-1885), Orson F. Whitney's philosophical dare (whitney-father-and-mother-1907), Heber C. Iverson's appeal to inspiration through Joseph Smith (iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908, from the general conference twelve months before this one). Duffin offers none, because in 1909 none is needed. The claim also does something the hymn does not: she is an addressee of parental accounting, not merely a presence at the reunion.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1909/1909-04-duffin-gospel-rejoicing.md, whose heavyweight pass and Final Review both collated the body against reading-order reconstructions of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1909a, leaves n23–n25); the excerpt was re-checked word-for-word against that scan's djvu text during drafting and matches. Conference Report, so A; the printed Report supplies no formal title and the vault's is supplied. The printed heading gives Duffin as former president of the Central States Mission, which is his standing here — this is not an apostolic statement, and its evidential weight is as a measure of ordinary usage rather than of official teaching. That is what makes the date useful: April 1909, seven months before the First Presidency issued “The Origin of Man” (fp-1909) with its “begotten and born of heavenly parents,” a returned mission president can say “our Father and Mother in heaven” at general conference in passing and move on.

title: First Presidency, “The Origin of Man”
speaker: Joseph F. Smith, John R. Winder, Anthon H. Lund
office: First Presidency
venue: Improvement Era (official statement)

quotes.excerpt: All men and women are in the similitude of the universal Father and Mother and are literally the sons and daughters of Deity… man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father, prior to coming upon the earth in a temporal body to undergo an experience in mortality.
quotes.note: The strongest viviparous statement in the corpus, and the only one that says both begotten and born.

quotes.excerpt: Man is the child of God, formed in the divine image and endowed with divine attributes, and even as the infant son of an earthly father and mother is capable in due time of becoming a man, so the undeveloped offspring of celestial parentage is capable, by experience through ages and aeons, of evolving into a God.
quotes.note: Tagged BACKWARD-MORTALITY per the v2 revision, but flagging a tension for review: as excerpted, the sentence runs forward (man evolving into a God), not backward (God having been man). It reads as a First Presidency forward-progression claim — arguably FORWARD-EUPHEMISM, since no mechanism is named — and only yields a backward claim by running the couplet's inference in reverse. Confirm the exact wording against the 1909 Improvement Era text, then settle the tag. Retag resolved: with BACKWARD-MORTALITY retired, this moves to FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than onto the Father axis. The sentence runs forward — man evolving into a God, no mechanism named — and never claims the Father was mortal. Confirm the Improvement Era wording; if it does contain a backward clause, move it to FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE.

quotes.excerpt: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, basing its belief on divine revelation, ancient and modern, proclaims man to be the direct and lineal offspring of Deity. God Himself is an exalted man, perfected, enthroned, and supreme.
quotes.note: Two paragraphs above the quoted closer, and the answer to the entry's own open question: the 1909 statement does carry a plain Father-status claim, in a different sentence than the one q2 examines. q2 stays FORWARD-EUPHEMISM.

notes: Verify quote 2's wording before relying on it; if confirmed it makes 1909 a stronger forward-progression statement than it is usually remembered as being. The February 2002 Ensign reprint is filed separately as a citation — its timing, five years after the Hinckley interviews, is the datum.

title: Charles A. Callis: the work God is engaged in “accounts for His greatness”
speaker: Charles A. Callis
office: President of the Southern States Mission (ordained an Apostle 1933)
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, April 1910, pp. 75–79)

quotes.excerpt: “For,” said the Lord to the faithful Nephi, “my work is not yet finished; neither shall it be until the end of man; neither from that time henceforth and forever.” What! The Lord God at work? Yes—and I believe that it is this work in which He is engaged that accounts for His greatness, and I do not mean to be sacrilegious in saying that.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the disclaimer is the tell — Callis knows the claim is close to the line and says so (“I do not mean to be sacrilegious”). The greatness of God is not treated as a brute attribute but as something His unending work accounts for, grounded in a Book of Mormon text about work that is never finished. Not a claim about increase in knowledge specifically; closer to the enlargement-of-kingdom form B. H. Roberts published the following year (roberts-progress-of-god-1911), though Callis makes it causal in a way Roberts does not.

quotes.excerpt: He did not limit the attainment of perfection to time, degree, or state. Eternal progression will be along the lines of orderly knowledge, and of law, because the Gospel will be in force in eternity as it is here. It is impossible for a being, mortal or immortal, to progress without a due regard for law and without obeying the mandates of the Almighty.
quotes.note: Context. Callis extends progression-under-law to immortal beings as a general rule — “a being, mortal or immortal” — and refuses to cap perfection by “time, degree, or state.” Stated of creatures rather than of God, so no tag, but it is the same law-governed frame in which he has just placed God's own work.

notes: Both excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1910a, printed pp. 75–79) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1910/1910-04-callis-devotion-to-the-work-of-god.md, whose final review collated leaves n75–n79. Line-break hyphenation closed up; printed em-dash spacing normalised. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Provenance note on office: Callis spoke as a mission president, not a General Authority — he presided over the Southern States Mission from 1908 to 1933 and was then ordained an Apostle. correlationStatus is historical-official because the Conference Report is an official Church publication, not because the speaker held general authority.

title: B. H. Roberts: God's immutability does not exclude advancement or progress of God
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: Member of the First Council of the Seventy (senior President from 1924)
venue: The Seventy's Course in Theology, Fourth Year: The Atonement (Salt Lake City: The Deseret News, 1911), 69–70

witnesses.scribe: Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression: Two Complementary Ways to Talk About God,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 41 (GSA scan p. 43), citing The Seventy's Course in Theology (Deseret News Press, 1911), 69–70
witnesses.note: England's catalogue entry, which is what led here; his reproduction is lowercase OCR and drops the “so” from “should not be so understood.” The excerpts below are from the Roberts volume, not from England.

quotes.excerpt: But God's immutability should not be so understood as to exclude the idea of advancement or progress of God. Thus, for example: God's kingdom and glory may be enlarged, as more and more redeemed souls are added to his kingdom: as worlds and world-systems are multiplied and redeemed and enrolled with celestial spheres, so God's kingdom is enlarged and his glory increased. So that in this sense there may come change and progress even for God.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the ground it stands on matters: Roberts derives divine progress from the enlargement of God's kingdom and glory — the very same “dominions, not knowledge” move that Bruce R. McConkie would later use to *deny* progression (see mcconkie-heresies-1980 and millet-mcconkie-life-beyond-1986). The difference is that Roberts does not stop there; see the next quote.

quotes.excerpt: an absolute immutability would require eternal immobility—which would reduce God to a condition eternally static, which, from the nature of things, would bar him from participation in that enlargement of kingdom and increasing glory that comes from redemption and the progress of men.
quotes.note: The argument stated negatively: an unqualified immutability is not reverence but paralysis. The same stagnation-is-death reasoning runs through Hugh B. Brown's April 1956 conference address (see brown-deify-man-1956), where it has been transferred from God to man.

quotes.excerpt: So with the All-knowing attribute, Omniscience: that must be understood somewhat in the same light as the other attributes considered: not that God is Omniscient up to the point that further progress in knowledge is impossible to him; but that all knowledge that is, all that exists, God knows.
quotes.note: The sharper half of the claim, and the one England does not quote: Roberts takes progression into knowledge, not merely dominion. This is the precise proposition Joseph Fielding Smith calls “very dangerous” forty-three years later (jfsmith-doctrines-salvation-1954) and McConkie calls a deadly heresy in 1980, and it is here in a Church-published quorum study course written by the President of the First Council of the Seventy.

notes: Verified by pulling the printed pages themselves from the Gospel Scholar Archive copy of the collected Seventy's Course in Theology (PDF pp. 802–804 = printed pp. 68–70 of Year Book IV), and confirming from the volume's own title page (PDF p. 727) that the 1911 Deseret News imprint England cites is Fourth Year: The Atonement. Line-break hyphenation has been closed up; one phrase carrying scan damage is elided. The passage sits in a numbered section headed “7. Limitation in the Attributes of God,” immediately after Roberts's treatments of Omnipotence, Omniscience and Omnipresence, and is footnoted to a long quotation from Sir Oliver Lodge — the philosophical provenance England and Matthew Bowman both trace to Herbert Spencer-era British thought. correlationStatus is graded historical-official here because the Year Books were prepared by Roberts as a member of the First Council of the Seventy, so styled on the volume's own title page, issued by the Church's own press, and used as the prescribed course of study for Seventies quorums; note that the existing bh-roberts-tripartite entry grades the same series never-official, and the two should be reconciled by the maintainer rather than left divergent. This entry is deliberately *not* the tripartite-framework entry: bh-roberts-tripartite covers intelligence → spirit → body and still needs its own excerpt pulled from the Year Books; this one covers only the progression claim.

title: Charles W. Penrose: resurrected sexes, posterity without end, and laws of generation that had no beginning
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, April 1911, pp. 30–38)

quotes.excerpt: In a revelation contained in section 132 of the Doctrine and Covenants, we learn a little about the eternity of the marriage covenant. The Lord has revealed, that when a marriage is performed under the sealing ordinance which He has revealed … that a union of that kind will extend beyond the grave; and that when death parts the individuals, the marriage is not dissolved, but continues and goes on, and if the parties are fit for it, worthy of it, it will be continued forever, and of the increase of their posterity there will be no end.
quotes.note: Affirmation: the increase is of posterity, and it has no end. Penrose names D&C 132 as his source and is expounding it rather than reciting it, so the entry stays sourceType original with a citesId edge to dc-132. The elision drops the clause about who is authorised to seal.

quotes.excerpt: In the resurrection, the man will be a man, and the woman will be a woman, with all the faculties and powers with which the sexes are endowed, both of spirit and of body, the body being restored to the spirit, and the spirit to the body. These being living souls, — like Adam and Eve when united in the garden of Eden before death came into the world will go on, increasing in that affection, and love, and admiration, in power, and in dominion, and in the blessings of the family relation.
quotes.note: Marked implied: Penrose describes no gestation and no spirit birth. What he does assert is the physiological premise the viviparous account needs — resurrected beings remain sexed and retain “all the faculties and powers with which the sexes are endowed, both of spirit and of body” — and he places it directly between two statements that their posterity increases without end. The Eden comparison is doing the same work: Adam and Eve as they were before the fall, in a body capable of increase. Flagged for review because the mechanism is supplied by the reader, not the text.

quotes.excerpt: They are waiters upon those who are worthy of this “more exceeding weight of glory” — the exaltation that “continues the seeds forever and ever, wherein the Father is glorified;” … They come forth in the resurrection, according to that revelation to us, “in their saved condition, separately and singly;” therefore, they are not numbered among the Gods, but among the angels, or those that minister unto and are messengers and servants of “the heirs of God and joint heirs with Jesus Christ.”
quotes.note: The euphemism in its canonical form — “continues the seeds forever and ever” quoted straight out of D&C 132 with no gloss on what a seed is — set against its negative: those not sealed “are not numbered among the Gods.” The exegetical target is Matthew 22, and the whole point of the passage is that Christ's “neither marry nor are given in marriage” describes the angels, i.e. the unsealed. Tagged euphemism rather than explicit because the increase is named only in the revelation's own idiom.

quotes.excerpt: Abraham beheld the multiplicity of worlds that the Father had created, as the Lord also showed Enoch. The Lord told Abraham that if he could count them, so he could count his seed; that his seed should be as numerous as the sands on the seashore, and as the stars of the heaven, for multitude. You cannot count them. The multiplicity of the posterity of those who enter into this grand order of family government, sealed on earth and sealed in heaven will go on forever, while the stars shine, while the throne of God endures; while the glory of God, which is intelligence, continues to scintillate and be manifested among the myriads and hosts that inhabit the eternal worlds.
quotes.note: The Abrahamic star-promise read as a measure of eternal posterity, and the worlds and the seed held deliberately in the same frame: Abraham is shown the multiplicity of worlds the Father made, and told his seed will match them for number. Plural worlds under one God, so MANY-WORLDS; and the posterity of the sealed going on forever, so FORWARD-EXPLICIT. No succession of Gods is asserted, and Penrose breaks off — “This opens up a subject too broad and wide for me to enter into fully this morning.” citesId records the Abraham 3 vision he is working from.

quotes.excerpt: I know that He lives, that he is our Father, the Father of our spirits; that our spirits are, in form, like unto Him, and our bodies have been made to conform to the spirit, under the laws of generation that God has established, to which there was no beginning, and of which there shall be no end.
quotes.note: Recorded untagged, on purpose, because it is the passage most likely to be misread as a backward claim. The beginninglessness attaches to the laws of generation — an order God established but which had no beginning — not to a chain of begetters. Penrose names no Father of the Father, no grandfather, and no succession, so BACKWARD-EXPLICIT and INFINITE-CHAIN are both withheld; and the generation clause grammatically governs how our bodies conform to our spirits, not how our spirits came to be, so it is not evidence of spirit birth either. What remains, and is worth having on the record, is an apostle closing a general conference address by making generation a beginningless and endless feature of reality.

notes: All five excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1911a, printed pp. 30–38) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-04-08-charles-w-penrose-remarks-8.md, whose final review collated leaves n30–n38 against the page images. Line-break hyphenation closed up; one raw-OCR corruption in the vicinity of the second excerpt (“the lx>r&” for “the Lord”) falls outside the quoted text. Conference Report, so hearsay A. Two metadata corrections carried over from the vault's heavyweight pass: the filename says 8 April but the printed day headers place this in the second day morning session, 7 April 1911; and Penrose is of the Twelve here, not of the First Presidency — he was not called as a counselor until December 1911. Distinct from penrose-endless-increase-1911, which is the same man six months later in the October 1911 conference. Post-Manifesto, official, and unhedged: this is the full generative package preached in general conference twenty-one years after plural marriage ended.

title: Joseph F. Smith: “it would be inconsistent and impossible for a spirit to beget a man like Christ”
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, October 1911, pp. 2–11)

quotes.excerpt: This same physical, tangible entity called Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary and the Son of God, in His resurrected body, came to Joseph Smith, revealed Himself to Joseph Smith … and, that God, the Father, is like His Son; that it would be inconsistent and impossible for a spirit to beget a man like Christ, and therefore the Father and the Son are the exact resemblance of each other.
quotes.note: Recorded untagged, and the reason is the conflation this dataset exists to prevent. Smith is arguing from procreative necessity to divine embodiment: a spirit could not have begotten a man like Christ, therefore the Father has a body. The begetting in view is Christ's mortal conception, not premortal spirit birth, so SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS would be a retrojection — there is no Mother, no spirit offspring, no regress and no progression anywhere in the argument. What the passage is good evidence for is how a Church President in 1911 grounded the Father's corporeality: not in the couplet, not in King Follett, but in what fatherhood requires.

quotes.excerpt: Now, the Prophet Joseph Smith has also revealed to the world a principle that has been practically kept hid from the foundation of the world. What is it? The union of husband and wife for time and for all eternity. … He has taught to us the principle and the ordinance of the everlasting covenant, the union of parents and children for time and all eternity.
quotes.note: Eternal marriage and the sealed family named as the great restored principle, with nothing said about increase, offspring after this life, or what the sealed become — the eternal-families formula in its bare form, which is what FORWARD-EUPHEMISM is for. Worth reading beside Penrose six months earlier in the same conference series (penrose-laws-of-generation-1911), where the same D&C 132 material is expounded all the way out to endless posterity: the President of the Church stops where the Apostle keeps going.

notes: Both excerpts verified verbatim against the Internet Archive djvu OCR of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1911sa, printed pp. 2–11) and against the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-10-01-joseph-f-smith-remarks-1.md, whose final review collated leaves n2–n13 against an independent reading-order reconstruction. Line-break hyphenation closed up; the elision in the first excerpt drops the restatement “the same God, the same Christ, the same Redeemer of the world that was crucified on Calvary” (the printed page reads “Redeemed,” a compositor's error). Conference Report, so hearsay A. This is the opening address of the October 1911 conference; the bulk of it answers the anti-Mormon press campaign of that year, and the doctrinal material appears as a list of what Joseph Smith revealed that nobody is injured by.

title: Charles W. Penrose: the gift of endless, perpetual increase
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1911, pp. 48–54)

quotes.excerpt: One of the grand things referred to by President Smith as in the revelations of God to the Prophet Joseph, was the eternity of the marriage covenant, by which the man and the woman may be joined together according to God's order, and though death may part them, yet in the resurrection they shall come forth to be husband and wife, to be parents of children, to have the gift of endless, perpetual increase, the beginning of their kingdom and their glory in worlds without end. That is real life, the power to continue and the power to produce and to increase, the power of vitality in the spirit and in the body.
quotes.note: Explicit rather than euphemistic: resurrected couples are named as “parents of children,” and the increase is qualified twice over as endless and perpetual. “Worlds without end” here is the liturgical idiom for eternity, not a claim about plural worlds, so MANY-WORLDS is not applied. The Conference Report OCR prints “bv President Smith”; corrected to “by,” a scan artifact, with no other change to the wording.

quotes.excerpt: And those who follow in the footsteps of Jesus Christ, who is now to all purposes like the Father, will inherit similar glory, and it will never fade away, and it will be exemplified in them to the full. The spirit of life will be within them in body and in spirit, and they will increase forever and ever, and like the blessing that comes to our elder brother, Jesus Christ, of the increase of their kingdom there shall be no end.
quotes.note: The forward chain closed against Christ's own case: the exalted inherit what the Son inherited, and the increase of their kingdom is unending. The vault transcription prints a stray period in “elder .brother,” an OCR artifact of the printed column; removed here, wording otherwise untouched.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-10-15-charles-w-penrose-remarks-15.md. Conference Report, so A. That file has an unusually heavy repair history — two long passages were scrambled by two-column OCR and were later de-interleaved directly against the archive.org page images (leaves n48–n56, printed pp. 48–54) — but neither quoted passage falls inside the repaired blocks, and both read cleanly apart from the two isolated scan artifacts noted on the quotes. Two corrections to how this source is usually described. First the date: the pulpit report gives 6 October, but the vault frontmatter and the printed session heading place it in the second day afternoon session, 7 October 1911. Second the office: he is frequently cited as First Presidency here, but Penrose was not called as a counselor until December 1911, so in October he was still of the Twelve. Why it matters: this is post-Manifesto, official, and undiminished. Twenty-one years after plural marriage ended, the full generative package is preached in general conference without hedging — which is the evidence that the early twentieth century softened the vocabulary of deification, not the doctrine of increase.

title: German E. Ellsworth: a Mother “revealed and taught,” and a poem he retitles “Eternal Motherhood”
speaker: German E. Ellsworth
office: President of the Northern States Mission
venue: General conference, overflow meeting, Assembly Hall, Salt Lake City (Conference Report, October 1911, pp. 74–77)

quotes.excerpt:
It has also been revealed and taught to the Latter-day Saints that, associated with our Father in Heaven we have a Mother there. The poet, in the same verse partly quoted above, gave expression to this beautiful truth:

“In the heavens are parents single?
No; the thought makes reason stare!
Truth is reason; truth eternal
Tells me I’ve a Mother there.”
quotes.note: The epistemic claim in its pre-correlated form, and it is the one that later gets withdrawn and then restored: not inferred, not reasonable, but “revealed and taught.” Compare hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991 eighty years on — “her of whom we have no revealed knowledge” — and renlund-divine-nature-2022, which returns to Ellsworth's ground (“comes by revelation”) while capping the content. The warrant offered here is the hymn, quoted as scripture would be quoted, which is the ordinary situation of the doctrine in this period; see iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908 three years earlier, where the hymn is credited to Joseph Smith's inspiration outright.

quotes.excerpt: In harmony with this idea, one of the present-day poets has expressed the same truth of motherhood in heaven as found in the “O My Father” hymn. I will read this to you, for it illustrates how the spirit of the Gospel is taking hold of the children of our Father, and it is in harmony with the declaration of President Joseph F. Smith concerning light coming into the world through the Prophet Joseph Smith. The poem is entitled “Completion,” by its author, Ella Wheeler Wilcox, but I have called it “Eternal Motherhood,” and it is, as I have said, in harmony with the idea of our having a mother in heaven, and in harmony with the light that has been given to the world, in relation to this subject.
quotes.note: The endorsement, and the retitling, which is the entry's most interesting act. Ella Wheeler Wilcox was a popular American verse writer and spiritualist, not a Latter-day Saint; Ellsworth reads her “Completion” into the conference record, renames it “Eternal Motherhood,” and frames it twice as “in harmony with” the doctrine — a mission president using an outsider's sentimental poem as evidence that the Restoration's light is leaking into the world. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER because the endorsement is explicit and is his own; the poem's own content is handled separately in q3, since what he vouches for is its harmony with a Mother in heaven and not necessarily each of its propositions.

quotes.excerpt:
He must provide for all earth’s cheated mothers
In His vast space of shining sphere on sphere,
And with my son there must be many others —
My spirit children who will claim me here.
quotes.note: Read into the conference record by Ellsworth from Wilcox's poem. The speaker is a woman who lost an infant, addressing “those lesser gods” at the judgment and asking for the motherhood she was denied; the answer she anticipates is spirit children waiting for her beyond death, and the following stanza places them “In God’s great nursery.” Tagged FORWARD-EXPLICIT because post-mortal spirit offspring are named outright, which almost nothing else in the 1911 conference does, and graded hedges rather than affirms for three reasons stated here so a later reader can re-weigh them: the words are a non-member poet's, the mechanism given in the next stanza is creation by thought (“Fair creatures by my loving thoughts created”) rather than begetting, and the children are described as having waited between two worlds until her death rather than as being begotten after it — closer to consolation for the childless than to the Pratt–Ballard physiology. Ellsworth endorses the poem's harmony with a Mother in heaven and does not separately endorse its account of increase. Text note: the vault body carries an OCR intrusion — the running head “ELDER MELVIN J. BALLARD.” and the page number 77 fall between this stanza and the next — which is a scan artifact of the printed column and is excluded here; the excerpt ends where the artifact begins.

notes: Collated word-for-word during drafting against the DjVu text of the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1911sa, printed pages 74–77), read alongside the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-10-24-german-e-ellsworth-remarks-24.md. Three things were confirmed directly in the scan: the session dateline (“An overflow session of the Conference was held in the Assembly Hall, adjoining the Tabernacle, at 10 a. m., Sunday, Oct. 8th, 1911”), which fixes the date against the vault's earlier mis-dating to October 6; the printed byline “(President Northern States Mission.)”; and that the “ELDER MELVIN J. BALLARD.” line appearing mid-poem in the vault body is a running-head bleed rather than text, Ballard's own address beginning several pages later. Conference Report, so A. Same conference as penrose-endless-increase-1911, delivered the previous afternoon, which makes October 1911 a dense pair: Penrose on endless increase in the Tabernacle on the 7th, Ellsworth on eternal motherhood in the Assembly Hall overflow on the 8th. The citesId edge is to o-my-father, quoted twice — the “I had learned to call Thee Father” stanza at the opening and the “parents single” stanza here. Worth flagging for anyone surveying the corpus by speaker rank: this is a mission president at an overflow meeting, not an Apostle, which is exactly the kind of speaker the doctrine's boldest statements tend to come from in this period.

title: Joseph E. Robinson: the couplet credited to Joseph Smith, and grounded on “like begets like”
speaker: Joseph E. Robinson
office: President of the California Mission
venue: General conference, third day overflow meeting (Conference Report, April 1912, beginning p. 78)

quotes.excerpt: The great pagan philosopher, Socrates, said that "this is the whole, end and aim of man, to be like God, and he who follows Him shall become like Him." So the Prophet Joseph Smith, in this age, has added to this truth by the assertion that "As man is God once was, and that as He is man may become," because He is our Father, and like begets like, and inherent within us are the attributes of divinity that shall lead us into perfection, which Christ intended His Saints to attain unto.
quotes.note: Affirmation, with two transmission details worth recording. The couplet is credited to Joseph Smith, not Lorenzo Snow — “the Prophet Joseph Smith, in this age, has added to this truth” — and the wording is a variant, “As man is God once was, and that as He is man may become,” rather than the standard “As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be.” The referent is the Father, fixed by the causal clause Robinson attaches: the couplet is true “because He is our Father, and like begets like.” That clause is the second point. The couplet is not offered as revelation to be accepted but as an inference from literal paternity and heredity, the same inheritance-of-attributes argument George F. Richards would run in richards-obedience-couplet-1913 and richards-gods-in-embryo-1914 — and Robinson sets it as a Latter-day Saint completion of Socrates, an apologetic frame rather than a scandalous one. FATHER-BECAME-GOD is withheld: nothing here narrates an attainment by the Father.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1912/1912-04-23-joseph-e-robinson-remarks-23.md, re-ingested from the correct scan of the official printed Conference Report of the Eighty-Second Annual Conference (Internet Archive conferencereport1912a, internal file conferencereport821chur, leaves n78–n83) and Final-Reviewed against a column-order reconstruction of the same scan, where both flagged candidates proved to be scan-side OCR noise and no body change was needed. Conference Report, so A. Two notes on the metadata: the filename's “1912-04-23” is a talk-order artifact of the ingest and the address was delivered on 7 April 1912, the third day; the vault frontmatter's page anchor is the item root rather than a leaf, and the address begins at leaf n79 with the byline garbled in the running head as “ELDER JOSEPH E.
