venue: General conference, third day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1958)

quotes.excerpt: In after years Joseph referred to God as an “exalted man,” and said that both he and the Son were personages of flesh and bone, as tangible as man.
quotes.note: King Follett compressed to two words and handed to a radio and television audience Romney has just addressed directly as “you who may not be members of the Church.” Marked implied because “exalted man” is adjectival: it states an attained condition without saying who exalted him, when, or from what — the same construction McConkie uses in Mormon Doctrine (“an exalted, glorified, and perfected Man”). Per the Father-status precedent, attainment language without explicit mortality is FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone. Romney supplies no gloss at all; the citation he attaches, D&C 130:22, covers only the flesh-and-bone half of the sentence, and the “exalted man” half is left standing on Joseph Smith's authority with no reference.

quotes.excerpt: Through subsequent revelations he learned that the relationship between God and men is that of parent and children. “The inhabitants” of the “worlds” … “are begotten sons and daughters unto God,” said the Lord to him in one of the revelations. (Ibid., 76:24.) The Prophet further learned through communication from heaven that as the begotten children of God we are endowed with the potential to become like him, even as mortal children may become like their mortal parents.
quotes.note: Untagged, and the reason is the same one that leaves romney-1964-q1 untagged: every clause is about children growing into likeness, and nothing here asserts that the exalted beget spirit children or supplies a mechanism. Two things are worth seeing anyway. First, this is the mortal-parents analogy that Romney will run again six years later in October 1964 — where he does place the Father inside the process (“through this process God himself attained perfection”), which is why that quote is tagged and this one is not. Second, MANY-WORLDS is deliberately withheld: the plural “worlds” survives inside the quotation of D&C 76:24 but carries no weight in Romney's argument, which is about parentage. The ellipsis inside the scripture quotation is Romney's own, as printed. The next sentence names “the doctrine of eternal progression” in a list of things Joseph learned and never defines it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1958/1958-10-romney-my-beloved-brothers-and-sisters-and-friends.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1958sa, leaves n94–n97) and additionally read in full against the reconstructed page order; the final-review pass found no defects. Conference Report, so A. The register is the point of the entry: this is an explanatory address written for outsiders listening on radio and television, a genre in which the Church's more distinctive claims are usually softened, and the “exalted man” sentence goes out unhedged in the middle of it. Companion to romney-1964 and romney-mother-in-heaven-1948 — the same apostle across twenty years, hedging the Mother (“I do not know the process”), stating the Father's attainment plainly, and never once naming a chain.

title: George Q. Morris: “stripped of the greatest power, that of eternal increase”
speaker: George Q. Morris
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1959)

quotes.excerpt: They may be saved in the celestial kingdom, but they cannot be enlarged, and forever and ever they remain a person of a lower degree — a lower order of being, stripped of the greatest power, that of eternal increase.
quotes.note: Morris's own voice, immediately after reading D&C 132:17 aloud — the verse says the unmarried “cannot be enlarged” and “are not gods, but are angels of God forever and ever,” and Morris supplies the gloss the verse does not: what they are stripped of is eternal increase, and increase is “the greatest power.” That identification is the reason the entry exists. It is still FORWARD-EUPHEMISM and not FORWARD-EXPLICIT: increase is ranked and named but never unpacked into offspring, spirit children, or worlds anywhere in the address.

quotes.excerpt: …and they shall pass by the angels, and the gods, which are set there, to their exaltation and glory in all things, as hath been sealed upon their heads, which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever. Then shall they be gods, because they have no end; therefore shall they be from everlasting to everlasting, because they continue; then shall they be above all, because all things are subject unto them. Then shall they be gods, because they have all power, and the angels are subject unto them.
quotes.note: D&C 132:19–20, read to the congregation at length and left entirely unglossed: Morris adds no comment on “a continuation of the seeds” and no comment on “then shall they be gods.” His only remark on the block is procedural — “Now I believe that our teachers, our leaders, and our parents must be taught and must teach these principles. They are as clear as words can make them, as the Lord has explained them.” Recorded per the unglossed-scripture rule, and tagged for what the quoted text says rather than for anything the speaker adds. The excerpt is trimmed at the front (elision marked) and joins the printed paragraph break between verses 19 and 20 without the intervening close-and-open quotation marks; no words are omitted there.

quotes.excerpt: He may enter into the other, but that is the end of his kingdom; he cannot have an increase.
quotes.note: The address closes on D&C 131:4, introduced as “a statement of the Prophet Joseph Smith,” again with no gloss. The negative formulation is the one that recurs across the mid-century conference corpus whenever increase is discussed without being described — compare eldred-smith-no-increase-1948. Between this and q2 the whole doctrine reaches the congregation in the Lord's words and Joseph's, with the apostle's single contribution being the ranking in q1.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1959/1959-10-morris-my-dear-brethren-and-sisters-i-am.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1959sa, leaves n47–n51) and read in full against the reconstructed page order; the pre-pass's low similarity score is accounted for by an adjacent speaker's running head that the vault correctly excludes, not by body drift. Conference Report, so A. The address is a sustained exposition of D&C 132 built as an answer to a youth-divorce statistic cited the day before by Mark E. Petersen, which is why its argument runs through the sealing power rather than through deification: increase enters as the thing the unsealed forfeit. citesId dc-132 for the block quotation.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: “how did we become such, if we had no mother to give us spirit birth?”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Answers to Gospel Questions, vol. 3 (1960), “A Mother in Heaven” (question 35, beginning p. 142); originally a “Your Question” column in the Improvement Era

quotes.excerpt: Question: "Will you please give us the background of the 'theory' advanced of 'a Mother in Heaven'? Some feel that God is great enough to create spirits without any assistance, and if not, why then was not a Mother mentioned among the Godhead?"
quotes.note: The most revealing question in the five volumes. In 1960 a member could write to the senior apostle calling Heavenly Mother a “theory” — the scare quotes are the member's — and could offer, as the live alternative, that God made spirits unassisted. The objection is not modesty about her; it is doubt that she is needed. The answer below is shaped end to end by having to argue that she is.

quotes.excerpt: The fact that there is no reference to a mother in heaven either in the Bible, Book of Mormon or Doctrine and Covenants, is not sufficient proof that no such thing as a mother did exist there. If we had a Father, which we did, for all of these records speak of him, then does not good common sense tell us that we must have had a mother there also?
quotes.note: Conceded scriptural silence, answered from inference rather than revelation — “good common sense,” the same argument-form Brigham Young used in 1862. Conflation warning: this is one of three occurrences of the phrase “had a Father” on this page — the others being “We know that Jesus had a Father” and the section heading JESUS HAD A FATHER AND A MOTHER — and it is the only page in the five volumes where the phrase appears at all. Every occurrence is about our Father or Jesus' Father, not the Father's Father. It is not a regress statement and must not be quoted as one.

quotes.excerpt: If we are his offspring, then how did we become such, if we had no mother to give us spirit birth? … It is my turn to ask a question. How can we be the offspring of God, how can he be the Father of our spirits, unless we had a mother and were born?
quotes.note: Literal spirit birth asserted as the mechanism, and asserted as the reason a Mother must exist — the argument runs from the physiology to the person, not the reverse. “Spirit birth” and “were born” are unhedged. The section heading standing over this text is JESUS HAD A FATHER AND A MOTHER. Note the rhetorical turn: he answers the member's question with a question of his own.

quotes.excerpt: Their children will belong to them, and they will have the gift of "a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever. Then shall they be gods, because they have no end." … Now they will be blessed with the same blessings as those held by our Eternal Father—eternal increase.
quotes.note: The forward chain, and the reason this answer belongs on this timeline rather than only in a Heavenly Mother file: exalted couples receive posterity in eternity and become gods, and the blessing is identified as “the same blessings as those held by our Eternal Father.” The symmetry that produces — the Father presently exercising eternal increase, as we will — is an observation about the shape of the claim, not a backward assertion Smith makes, and is recorded here rather than tagged.

quotes.excerpt: Is it not feasible to believe that female spirits were created in the image of a "Mother in Heaven"?
quotes.note: The closing sentence of the answer, and a register datum: the whole case ends on “is it not feasible to believe,” with the phrase still inside quotation marks. Even the era's most confident defender of the doctrine leaves it at plausibility.

notes: Verified by reading the complete Q&A — question, the untitled opening, the section JESUS HAD A FATHER AND A MOTHER, and the closing Genesis 1:26–27 argument — in the GSA copy. Dated by publication year of volume 3 (1960) at year precision; this edition prints no individual column dates. The printed page anchor is derivable: at volume 4, question 38, Smith cross-references the immediately preceding answer in volume 3 as “‘Elias Is Noah,’ Answers to Gospel Questions, Vol. 3, pp. 138-41,” so “A Mother in Heaven,” which follows it directly, begins at p. 142. The end page is not derivable and is not asserted, and the reflowed digital edition carries no printed pagination of its own. Correlation graded historical-official for the reasons given in jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958. This is the mid-century link between snow-heavenly-mother-1885 / whitney-father-and-mother-1907 and the later hedged treatments (hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, essay-2015): the doctrine is defended, the mechanism is literal, and the whole thing rests on common sense rather than revelation — which is precisely the vulnerability the later retreat exploits. Read against jfs-agq-personal-father-1966, where the same author, asked how a Father of flesh and bone produced spirit children, answers that “this question the Lord has not fully explained.”

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: “such questions should be ignored” — and Abraham's intelligences are begotten spirit children
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Answers to Gospel Questions, vol. 3 (1960), “Why Does Not God Create Intelligence and Prevent Evil?” (question 30); originally a “Your Question” column in the Improvement Era

quotes.excerpt: Question: "If God is all powerful, why is he not able to create intelligence? In the Doctrine and Covenants, Section 93, verse 29, we read that 'intelligence or the light of truth was not created nor indeed can be.' If he is all powerful, why does he permit evil to rule in the world?"
quotes.note: A member pressing on the limits of divine power from D&C 93:29 — if something is uncreatable, in what sense is God omnipotent? The question presses on exactly the seam where uncreated intelligence meets a God who is himself situated in a series.

quotes.excerpt: Perhaps the time will not come while mortality endures that questions of this kind will not be propounded. The first thought that comes is that such questions should be ignored, but as they recur from time to time perhaps it is wisdom to answer them.
quotes.note: The bracketing move performed out loud, in the opening sentences of a column whose entire purpose is to answer members' questions. He answers only after recording that the first instinct was not to — and the stated reason for answering is recurrence, not merit. The same posture, applied to a different question, is what produces the decline in jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958.

quotes.excerpt: Why he cannot create intelligence is simply because intelligence, like time and space, always existed, and therefore did not have to be created. However, intelligences spoken of in the Book of Abraham were created, for these are spirit children of God, begotten sons.
quotes.note: A distinction that matters for the tripartite question and is easily missed: singular “intelligence” (D&C 93:29) is uncreated and co-eternal, while the plural “intelligences” of Abraham 3:22 are not a third pre-spirit tier at all — Smith collapses them into the begotten spirit children. On this reading the framework is two-stage (uncreated intelligence, then begetting as spirit), not the three-stage scheme B. H. Roberts and others built from the same verse; compare bh-roberts-tripartite and madsen-eternal-man-1966. “Begotten sons” is begetting language, but no physiology is stated here, so no spirit-birth category is applied — for that from the same author see jfs-agq-mother-in-heaven-1960.

notes: Verified by reading the complete Q&A — question, the section INTELLIGENCE CO-ETERNAL WITH GOD, and the second half on free agency (OPPOSITION NECESSARY, GOD IS NOT LIMITED BY JUSTICE) — in the GSA copy. Dated by publication year of volume 3 (1960) at year precision; this edition prints no individual column dates. Cited by title and volume sequence number (30); the reflowed digital edition carries no printed pagination and page numbers are not asserted. Correlation graded historical-official for the reasons given in jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958. Carried as sourceType original with citesId to abraham-3 because the value here is Smith's own reading of Abraham 3:22, not the quotation of it. Read alongside jfs-agq-intelligences-1963, where he takes the opposite tack on the same verse and declares the nature of an intelligence unknowable.

title: Delbert L. Stapley: joint-heirship as ascent “to the station of Godhood”
speaker: Delbert L. Stapley
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, April 1961)

quotes.excerpt: In the important doctrinal discourse known as the “King Follett Sermon” the Prophet Joseph Smith, referring to those who “shall be heirs of God and jointheirs with Jesus Christ,” described jointheirship as inheriting the same power, the same glory, and the same exaltation, until an individual ascends to the station of Godhood and rises to the throne of eternal power, sharing the rewards with all the faithful who have preceded him.
quotes.note: Paraphrase, not quotation — Stapley reports what King Follett “described” rather than reading it — and the paraphrase is the datum. What he takes from the sermon is the forward half only: joint-heirs ascend to Godhood. The sermon's backward half, God himself once as we are now, is not mentioned here or anywhere else in the address, though the sermon is named outright and treated as an authority. Untagged, because ascent to Godhood is theosis and nothing more; the entry's tagged claim is in q2.

quotes.excerpt: The everlasting covenant of marriage, ordained of God for man and woman, also is to be entered into and the marriage contract sealed eternally by the authority of the Holy Priesthood of God. Otherwise, the highest degree of the celestial kingdom cannot be attained nor Godhood acquired, which exalted condition assures continuation of the lives forever.
quotes.note: Godhood made conditional on eternal marriage, with “continuation of the lives” — the phrase of D&C 132:22, used without attribution — as what the exalted condition assures. Euphemism rather than explicit: the phrase is the standard veil over posterity, and Stapley never lifts it. Two paragraphs earlier he had stated the premise in the barest possible form, “To become like God we must possess the powers of Godhood,” and then listed the ordinances that convey them — endowment first, then this. Elsewhere in the address he quotes D&C 132:37 (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob “are not angels but are Gods”) and D&C 76:55–59 (“they are gods, even the sons of God”), both without gloss.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1961/1961-04-stapley-my-brothers-and-sisters-as-i-contemplate.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1961a, leaves n65–n69) with the low-similarity leaf checked directly against the BookReader page images; the final-review pass removed three running-head bleeds and confirmed the printed typo “purfied” in the D&C 50:29 quotation as genuine. Conference Report, so A. The address is a joint-heirship sermon in the legal register — Stapley works from the law of equity and the idea that “a joint-heir legally inherits and shares all equities and gifts in equal interest,” which is what makes the Godhood conclusion feel deduced rather than asserted. citesId kfd-1844 for the named paraphrase.

title: Eldred G. Smith: a Father “resurrected … from some previous earth in the long distant past”
speaker: Eldred G. Smith
office: Patriarch to the Church
venue: General conference, first day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1961)

quotes.excerpt: I worship my God who is my Father in heaven, the Father of my spirit, a resurrected, glorified, perfected man, not resurrected from this earth, no, but from some previous earth in the long distant past.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the most specific location of the Father's mortality anywhere in the conference lane of this corpus: not merely that he was once a man but that the body he was raised in was raised somewhere else — “not resurrected from this earth, no, but from some previous earth in the long distant past.” Referent is unambiguous, the sentence names him three ways. Deliberately not tagged MANY-WORLDS: that category is for plural creations under one God, and a prior earth belonging to the Father's own probation is a different claim; and deliberately not BACKWARD-EXPLICIT, since no God above the Father is named here or anywhere in the address — whoever presided over that previous earth goes unmentioned, which is trap #1 holding even at this level of detail.

quotes.excerpt: If men may be resurrected and God is not, then man will have accomplished what God has not and thus become greater than God. This we know is impossible. Hence what men may accomplish, God has accomplished ahead of him. Then the fact that you are now a mortal on this earth is proof that God, too, at one time in the far distant past, has gone through a life of mortality ahead of you. Hence God is a resurrected, glorified man.
quotes.note: The argument, and it is the reason the entry carries both Father-status tags. Mortality is affirmed (“God, too, at one time in the far distant past, has gone through a life of mortality ahead of you”) and so is attainment: “what men may accomplish, God has accomplished ahead of him” predicates a completed ascent, which per the Father-status precedent is FATHER-BECAME-GOD alongside FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE. What is unusual is the warrant. Smith cites neither the King Follett Discourse nor the Snow couplet — neither is named in the address — and derives the Father's mortality a priori from the resurrection instead: man cannot accomplish what God has not, man will be resurrected, therefore God has been. The printed Report sets these as consecutive paragraphs; joined here as continuous prose with no words added, removed, or reordered.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1961/1961-10-smith-i-appreciate-the-honor-of-this-position.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1961sa, leaves n26–n27) with no defects found. Conference Report, so A. Date correction: the filename reads 1961-10, but the 131st Semi-Annual Conference ran 29 September – 1 October 1961 and the Report's own dateline puts this first day afternoon meeting on Friday 29 September. The vault's OCR ingest reflows the printed paragraphs; both excerpts are given as printed prose. This is the sixth Eldred G. Smith entry in the corpus (1948, 1950, 1958, 1961, 1973, 1978) and the sharpest of the backward ones — eldred-smith-fathers-exaltation-1958 says the Father “came to his exaltation,” eldred-smith-spirit-offspring-1973 adds “the same type of experiences they had done,” and here the Patriarch to the Church names a previous earth from the pulpit in the last months of the David O. McKay administration. Read against jfs-progression-1971 ten years later, where the President of the Church is narrowing what may be said about God's own advancement, it is a useful marker of how late the maximal version was still being preached without qualification.

title: Henry D. Taylor: the hymn's closing prayer, mid-century
speaker: Henry D. Taylor
office: Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1961)

quotes.excerpt: We sing a beautiful hymn that is a favorite of mine. It refers to our existence prior to coming to this earth. Sister Eliza R. Snow, the author, poses some very meaningful questions, and in addressing our Father in heaven asks:
quotes.note: The framing, and the reframing. Taylor tells the congregation what the hymn is about — premortal existence — and the Mother is not named in the summary even though she is named in the stanza he is about to read. This is the mid-century handling in miniature: the text is preserved intact and its most distinctive claim is quietly not the point.

quotes.excerpt: "When I leave this frail existence; When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? Then at length, when I've completed All you sent me forth to do; With your mutual approbation, Let me come and dwell with you." ("O My Father")
quotes.note: The Mother addressed directly, in general conference, in 1961. Punctuation follows the Conference Report printing, which uses semicolons where the hymnal has commas. Taylor attributes the hymn by title. See o-my-father.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1961/1961-10-taylor-we-sing-a-beautiful-hymn-that-is.md, whose Final Review collated §0 against conferencereport1961sa, leaves n101–n103, removing two running-head bleeds mid-sentence and making no other body change; the heavyweight pass rebuilt the report's reading order from the scan's DjVu word coordinates and corrected the date and session from the report's own dateline. The vault-supplied title is the talk's opening words, since the printed Report gives none. Conference Report, so A; historical-official — the Church's online archive begins in 1971. A citation and nothing more: Taylor quotes the hymn to introduce a sermon about keeping all the commandments, illustrated by the blind men and the elephant, and never returns to the Mother. It is filed anyway because it is the only located general conference witness to the hymn's Heavenly Mother stanzas in the whole of the 1950s and early 1960s, and because the shape of the citation — full stanza, correct attribution, no comment — is itself the finding for that decade.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith declines a member's man-to-God analogy: “we need not bother about the mysteries”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Answers to Gospel Questions, vol. 4 (1963), “Intelligences and Eternal Life” (question 24); originally a “Your Question” column in the Improvement Era

quotes.excerpt: Question: "… while 'intelligences' were neither made nor created and therefore cannot be destroyed, I have wondered why animals were created for this life only. Is not the difference between man and animals a matter of degree of intelligence, just as the difference between man and God is? Why then should animals be for this life only?"
quotes.note: The question that makes this entry worth keeping. The member states, as something the Church has taught him, that the difference between man and God is one of degree and not of kind — and states it in passing, as an uncontroversial premise on the way to asking about animals. That is how thoroughly the ladder cosmology had been absorbed by ordinary members by 1963.

quotes.excerpt: Some of our writers have endeavored to explain what an intelligence is, but to do so is futile, for we have never been given any insight into this matter beyond what the Lord has fragmentarily revealed. We know, however, that there is something called intelligence which always existed. It is the real eternal part of man, which was not created nor made. This intelligence combined with the spirit constitutes a spiritual identity or individual.
quotes.note: “Some of our writers” is a swipe at the tripartite theorists — B. H. Roberts and his successors — without naming them; compare bh-roberts-tripartite and madsen-eternal-man-1966. What he retains is thinner than what he rejects: an uncreated something combined with spirit, with the combining left unexplained. Note the drift from his 1960 answer (jfs-agq-create-intelligence-1960), where he was willing to say what Abraham's intelligences were.

quotes.excerpt: There are so many things in the gospel which are essential for us to know and observe, that we need not bother about the mysteries which have never been revealed. There are many things that we will know when we receive the resurrection and attain to the glories of the kingdom of our Eternal Father, which we cannot understand in this mortal state even if they were revealed to us.
quotes.note: The mysteries-are-not-your-business reframe, in the mid-century idiom. Its force here is what it silently covers: the member's premise that man differs from God in degree is never engaged, endorsed, or corrected anywhere in the answer. The analogy that would license the whole ladder simply drops.

notes: Verified by reading the complete Q&A — the full question (abridged in the excerpt above with an ellipsis at the front; the member also rehearses D&C 76:24, Acts 17, and Moses on the creation of animals), the section “MAN WAS ALSO IN THE BEGINNING WITH GOD,” ALMA'S WORDS TO ZEEZROM, and the second half on the resurrection of animals — in the GSA copy. Dated by publication year of volume 4 (1963) at year precision; this edition prints no individual column dates. Cited by title and volume sequence number (24); the reflowed digital edition carries no printed pagination and page numbers are not asserted. Correlation graded historical-official for the reasons given in jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958. Smith quotes his own earlier book The Progress of Man, p. 11, inside the answer. The pattern this entry documents with jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958 and jfs-agq-personal-father-1966 is consistent across the lane: members supply the speculative frame, and the senior apostle answers the tractable half of the question and lets the frame pass in silence.

title: Marion G. Romney: a process infinitely repeated in nature
speaker: Marion G. Romney
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session (Conference Report, October 1964)

quotes.excerpt: We all know that like begets like and that for the offspring to grow to the stature of his parent is a process infinitely repeated in nature. We can therefore understand that for a son of God to grow to the likeness of his Father in heaven is in harmony with natural law. We see this law demonstrated every few years in our own experience. Sons born to mortal fathers grow up to be like their fathers in the flesh. This is the way it will be with spirit sons of God. They will grow up to be like their Father in heaven. Joseph taught this obvious truth.
quotes.note: Spirit sons of God growing to the stature of their parent, argued from natural law. Untagged: every clause is about growth into likeness, and nothing in it asserts that the exalted beget spirit children or supplies a mechanism — the generative reading is supplied by the reader, not by Romney.

quotes.excerpt: As a matter of fact, he taught that through this process God himself attained perfection. From President Snow's understanding of the teachings of the Prophet on this doctrinal point, he coined the familiar couplet: “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.” This teaching is peculiar to the restored gospel of Jesus Christ.
quotes.note: “This process” is the one just called “infinitely repeated in nature,” with the Father placed inside it — a chain is implicit by symmetry, but per the no-retrojection principle it is not tagged INFINITE-CHAIN: Romney never states the backward direction. “God himself attained perfection” is the clearest FATHER-BECAME-GOD statement in the set.

notes: The only located instance in the twentieth-century conference corpus (~10,000 addresses, 1897–1970 plus the modern era) where the parent-offspring mechanism is called infinitely repeated and God Himself is placed within it. Verified against the Internet Archive scan of the October 1964 Conference Report. Collated against the Internet Archive scan conferencereport1964sa at leaf n50 (running head “Saturday, October 3”); title page gives the conference dates as October 2, 3, 4, 1964.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: contraception and “the blessings of eternal increase”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, first day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1965)

quotes.excerpt: If the love of the world and the wicked practices of the world mean more to a man and a woman than to keep the commandment of the Lord in this respect, then they are shutting themselves off from the eternal blessing of increase. … If the responsibilities of parenthood are willfully avoided here, then how can the Lord bestow upon the guilty the blessings of eternal increase? It cannot be, and they shall be denied such blessings.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “The Curse of Prevention.” The structure of the argument is what earns the entry: mortal fertility is made the qualifying test for eternal increase, so the two are treated as the same power exercised in two states — the premise that makes the doctrine operative in a talk about contraception rather than a talk about deification. Increase itself is never described; no offspring, no mechanism, no worlds, hence FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. The elision covers three sentences on small families and covenant-breaking; nothing about increase is omitted.

quotes.excerpt: May I make this personal remark: I am the father of eleven children, and to this day every one is a faithful member of the Church and all are active, for that is the way they were taught, and they were obedient. They will belong to me forever and are the foundation stones of my kingdom. My posterity reaches today over the one-hundred mark.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “The Blessing of Increase,” which is what fixes the reading: a man's sealed mortal posterity is described as “the foundation stones of my kingdom,” the kingdom being the eternal dominion of an exalted being. That is increase in its domesticated form — no future begetting is claimed, only that this posterity continues and constitutes the kingdom — so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. Worth pairing with jfs-agq-temple-marriage-1954, where the same man defines eternal lives as “eternal increase—the continuation … of the seeds forever.”

quotes.excerpt: In no other way, other than through birth into this life and the resurrection, can spirits become like our Eternal Father.
quotes.note: Untagged context, and the sentence the rest of the address hangs on: becoming like the Father is gated on embodiment, which is why denying a spirit its body is treated as an offence against the plan rather than a private choice. Theosis only — no claim about how the Father came to be what he is, and none about offspring — so no category, on the same reading that leaves romney-1964-q1 untagged.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1965/1965-10-smith-my-dear-brethren-and-sisters-i-hope.md, whose body was collated against the DjVu column-order reconstruction of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1965sa, leaves n27–n30, printed pp. 27–30) in the final-review pass, which repaired a two-column interleaving defect in the opening lines and restored seven printed side-heads. The tagged passages are well clear of the repaired opening. Conference Report, so A. Distinct from the several Answers to Gospel Questions entries by the same author: this is the doctrine delivered as pulpit instruction on birth control to the whole Church, five years before he became President of the Church, and the argument only works because eternal increase is assumed to be continuous with mortal parenthood. The address quotes Brigham Young and Joseph F. Smith on preparing tabernacles for waiting spirits; neither passage has a dataset entry, so no citesId.

title: Sterling W. Sill: God, angels, spirits and men “all of the same species”
speaker: Sterling W. Sill
office: First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, second day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1965)

quotes.excerpt: Someday we will more clearly know who we are. We will understand the great scriptural teaching that God, angels, spirits, and men are all of the same species in different stages of righteousness and development.
quotes.note: Species identity stated as flatly as the corpus has it, and called “the great scriptural teaching” with no scripture named. Left untagged on the reading applied to brown-deify-man-1956-q2, the closest parallel in the corpus (“Father and children, belong to the same society of eternal intelligences … he is the most advanced”): placing God at the top of a developmental scale implies an ascent, but Sill does not state one, and the no-retrojection rule keeps the inference out of the categories. Recorded because the implication is unusually bare here — “different stages of … development” distributes across a list whose first member is God.

quotes.excerpt: God placed the gold and silver in the earth, but he endowed his children with his own attributes and made them heirs to his potentialities. And according to his own immutable laws of heredity, the children may hope sometime to become like the parents.
quotes.note: The heredity argument, printed under the side-head “The Handiwork of God.” It is the same like-begets-like move Romney makes in October 1964 and Hugh B. Brown makes in October 1966, and by itself it asserts likeness, not offspring — untagged for the same reason romney-1964-q1 is. Sill runs it twice: earlier, under “Partake of the Divine Nature,” he asks “why should we call God our Heavenly Father and at the same time fail to believe his promise that the offspring of God may someday become like the parent?”

quotes.excerpt: Then what may not be done in eternity by one of these Godmen? Remove from his path the incident of death; or, better yet, contemplate him as raised from the dead; and give to him in the full splendor of manhood's estate, immortality, endless existence, what may we not hope that he will accomplish? What limits can you venture to fix as marking the boundary of his development, of his progress? … Why should there be any limits thought of?
quotes.note: B. H. Roberts, The Mormon Doctrine of Deity (1903), pp. 33–35, as Sill cites it — read to general conference at extraordinary length, roughly a full printed page of the Report. Not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: the unbounded progress is predicated of resurrected men, Roberts's “Godmen,” not of God. Contrast roberts-progress-of-god-1911, where the same author does predicate it of God and Joseph Fielding Smith later calls the proposition dangerous. The ellipsis inside the passage is Sill's, as printed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1965/1965-10-sill-my-brothers-and-sisters-i-appreciate-very.md, whose body was collated line by line against the DjVu column-order reconstruction of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1965sa, leaves n55–n60, printed pp. 55–60) in the final-review pass, which fixed three mechanical OCR artifacts and restored the printed side-heads. Conference Report, so A. Every quote here is deliberately untagged: the address is theosis at full volume — a three-act framing of existence, species identity with God, heredity, and a long reading from Roberts on limitless progress — and it never asserts eternal increase, spirit offspring, or a backward claim about the Father. That is exactly why it belongs in a comprehensive corpus: it is the shape of the mid-century deification sermon with the generative and genealogical halves absent, and the untagged rows are the evidence for that absence rather than an oversight. Sill's three-stage framing (premortal, mortal, eternal) is the standard three estates and not the intelligence→spirit→body staging, so no TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK tag.

title: Truman G. Madsen: an imaginary Joseph Smith on how God became God
speaker: Truman G. Madsen
office: Professor of Philosophy, Brigham Young University
venue: Eternal Man (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1966), ch. “Evil and Suffering,” pp. 55–57

quotes.excerpt: Now the Creeds say that God has always been God. But this well-motivated expression of reverence is a solemn travesty. The truth is infinitely more inspiring: that God Himself became God (whose power now extends in and through all things) by the mastery of the same ultimate and unchanging conditions to which you and I are subject. So, likewise, did His Firstborn Son, Jesus the Christ.
quotes.note: These words are not Madsen speaking in his own voice. They are assigned to a character labelled “The Prophet” in an invented dialogue between Joseph Smith and the mother of a blind baby — see the next quote. The content itself is past attainment plus subjection to conditions God did not create; Madsen does not say God was mortal, and he asserts no chain of any length. The always-God tag marks a denial: the passage calls the creedal always-God position a travesty while asserting attainment.

quotes.excerpt: The dialogue is imaginary, but the ideas are not. The “Mother” poses questions that have been raised numberless times. For every sentence in the Prophet's “replies” there is a first-hand counterpart in his writings or sermons.
quotes.note: Madsen's own footnote 5 on the device, printed at p. 55, before the dialogue begins. Any citation of the passage above has to carry this sentence. Note also the limit of Madsen's own claim: he asserts that a first-hand counterpart exists for every sentence, but he supplies no such counterpart for the “God Himself became God” line — his note there points instead to the King Follett Discourse with B. H. Roberts's footnotes, and to a list of finite-God philosophers.

quotes.excerpt: The rare notion that God is in a sense finite, limited by the nature of His environment, has been taught in some form by such men as William James, A. N. Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne, E. S. Brightman, and A. C. Garnett.
quotes.note: Madsen's footnote 11, attached to the “became God” line. It fixes the genre: this is a finite-God theodicy in conversation with process and personalist philosophy, not a genealogical claim about heavenly grandfathers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the printed text at pp. 55–57 (the dialogue passage runs from p. 56 onto p. 57; footnote 5 sits at the foot of p. 55, footnote 11 at the foot of p. 57). The scan's OCR is poor and mangles “but” to “hut” and “William” beyond recognition in the notes; those are scanner artifacts of an otherwise clear text and are silently corrected here. The framing caveat is not optional: the speaker is a fictional Joseph Smith, ventriloquized by Madsen for a theodicy, and quoting “God Himself became God” as though Madsen or Joseph Smith said it flatly is the single most common misuse of this book. Never-official: a BYU philosopher's trade book from Deseret Book. Adjacent interest for the Roberts/James strand — Madsen aligns his position with James, Whitehead, Hartshorne and Brightman by name.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith on how a Father of flesh and bone begot spirits: “this question the Lord has not fully explained”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Answers to Gospel Questions, vol. 5 (1966), “Personal Father and Spiritual Offspring” (question 54); originally a “Your Question” column in the Improvement Era

quotes.excerpt: Question: "If God has a body of flesh and bones plus spirit, how is it that his children were spirits, in the pre-existence?"
quotes.note: The spirit-birth mechanism question in its bluntest form: an embodied Father is supposed to have produced non-embodied offspring, and the member wants to know how. The title the volume gives the answer — “Personal Father and Spiritual Offspring” — names the problem exactly.

quotes.excerpt: This is a very proper question, and perhaps we cannot give an answer that will satisfy these people who have been traditioned in the doctrine that God is a Spirit. … This question the Lord has not fully explained, but there are sufficient reasons why we should believe that he does have a tabernacle of flesh and bones.
quotes.note: Concession and pivot in a single sentence. He grants the question is proper, states that the mechanism has not been revealed, and then answers a different question — whether the Father is embodied — for the remainder of the column. The rest of the answer argues from Christ's begetting and resurrected body that the Father must have a body; the spirit-birth mechanism the member asked about is never returned to. Note also the reframing of the questioner: a doctrinal question from within becomes a problem belonging to “these people who have been traditioned” outside.

notes: Verified by reading the complete Q&A in the GSA copy; it is short, running about one page, and the whole of it after the sentence quoted here is an argument from Hebrews 1:3, John 14:9, Zechariah 13:6 and D&C 45:51–54 that the Father has a body of flesh and bones. Dated by publication year of volume 5 (1966) at year precision; this edition prints no individual column dates. Cited by title and volume sequence number (54); the reflowed digital edition carries no printed pagination and page numbers are not asserted. Correlation graded historical-official for the reasons given in jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958. The reason to keep this entry is the contrast with jfs-agq-mother-in-heaven-1960: in 1960 the same author answered a closely related question with a confident mechanism — “how did we become such, if we had no mother to give us spirit birth?” — and here, six years later, tells a member that the Lord has not fully explained it. Whether that is a shift in position or a difference in what each question made convenient to say is not resolvable from the texts, and is not asserted; both are recorded so the pair can be read together.

title: Paul H. Dunn: “His eternal, primal self was born into a spirit body”
speaker: Paul H. Dunn
office: First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, first day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1966)

quotes.excerpt: Second, he believes that he has a divine heritage. His eternal, primal self was born into a spirit body of which God is the eternal father. Thus men and women are truly sons and daughters of God.
quotes.note: Real staging, compressed into one sentence: an eternal primal self, then birth into a spirit body, then the mortality the rest of the list assumes — the intelligence→spirit→body model rather than the ordinary three estates. What is born is the body; what inhabits it was never made, which is exactly the distinction bh-roberts-tripartite-q2 spends a printed page establishing. SPIRIT-BIRTH-ADOPTION is hedged, not affirmed: Dunn keeps the birth language and calls God the eternal father of the spirit body, so he is not denying begetting the way abraham-3 and kfd-1844 do — he is relocating it from the self to the body.

quotes.excerpt: First, the Latter-day Saint knows himself to be an eternal being. He is challenged by a divine plan of progression that can make both mortality and the eternities to come an ongoing experience of purpose and meaning.
quotes.note: The immediately preceding item in the same list of five, kept because it establishes the eternity of the self that q1 then has born into a body. Untagged on its own: eternal existence plus a plan of progression, with nothing said about offspring or about the Father's own past.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1966/1966-10-dunn-folks-accept-new-customs-because.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1966sa, leaves n15–n16, similarity 0.9687) and read in full against the reconstructed page order; the final-review pass found no body defects. The heavyweight pass also corrected the speaker attribution, which an earlier ingest had taken from an OCR-garbled running head (“ELDER PAUL H. DUNN” read as a bare “Pal”). Conference Report, so A. The talk is a five-point summary of distinctive Latter-day Saint belief written for a general and partly non-member audience, which is what makes the phrasing notable: the tripartite model is not being argued for, it is being reported as the plain content of point two.

title: Hugh B. Brown: “crowned with immortality, eternal life, and eternal increase”
speaker: Hugh B. Brown
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, third day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1966)

quotes.excerpt: We point out, moreover, that we, as his children, are the only creations of the Father to be blessed with his image. It follows that under the divine law of “like begets like,” our progress through the eternities may be limitless.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “In His image.” Untagged: “like begets like” is doing work on likeness and human progress, not on offspring, and the inference Brown draws from it is explicitly about our progress rather than about anything we will beget. The same maxim is the hinge of romney-1964-q1, which is untagged for the same reason. Note what precedes it — Brown has just conceded to “orthodox Christianity” every attribute of God it claims, calling him all powerful, all knowing, and perfect, which is the concession his 1956 address made in the opposite direction.

quotes.excerpt: All who are faithful to the teachings of the gospel will continue as a family into the highest degree of the celestial kingdom and will be crowned with immortality, eternal life, and eternal increase.
quotes.note: The bare formula from a member of the First Presidency: increase as the third term of a triad, undefined, in a sentence whose subject is the sealed mortal family continuing. Compare kimball-godhood-1952, the same construction with Godhood as the final term.

quotes.excerpt: President Lorenzo Snow gave an intimation of what eternal marriage meant: “A man and a woman in the other life, having celestial bodies, free from sickness and disease, glorified and beautified beyond description, standing in the midst of their posterity, governing and controlling them, administering life, exaltation and glory, world without end.” And President Joseph F. Smith told us, “The very foundation of the Kingdom of God, of righteousness, of progress, of development, of eternal life, and eternal increase in the Kingdom of God is laid in the divinely ordained home.”
quotes.note: The strongest passage in the address, printed under the side-head “Divinely ordained home,” and still short of explicit. The Snow relay puts a resurrected couple in the other life amid their posterity “administering life … world without end,” which is generative language in everything but name; what it never says is that the posterity are newly begotten spirits, so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than FORWARD-EXPLICIT. Provenance caveat: Brown supplies no citation for either quotation, and the Snow passage as he gives it is an uncited pulpit relay of a nineteenth-century statement — the Conference Report is a faithful record of what Brown said, which is a separate question from whether Snow said it in these words. Neither quoted text corresponds to an existing dataset entry, so no citesId.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1966/1966-10-brown-god-centered-homes-for-children.md, whose body was collated against the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1966sa, leaves n103–n107, printed pp. 100–105, similarity 0.9629) with the page images checked directly; the final-review pass restored one dropped line and recovered the address's true closing, which had been misfiled at the head of the following speaker's file. All three excerpts fall in the body, not in the recovered closing. Conference Report, so A. Distinct from brown-deify-man-1956, and the pair is the interesting thing: in 1956, as an Assistant to the Twelve, Brown read Widtsoe aloud on God's own growth and then drew a boundary around it; here, ten years later and in the First Presidency, the God-facing half is gone entirely — the address is about juvenile delinquency and the family, and eternal increase arrives as a crown on the sealed home.

title: William J. Critchlow, Jr.: the seven-act drama ends in “the power of eternal increase”
speaker: William J. Critchlow, Jr.
office: Assistant to the Council of the Twelve
venue: General conference, second day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1967, pp. 87–91)

quotes.excerpt: It is our Father's way of providing his billions of spirit children with mortal, flesh and bone bodies. … It provides his children with powers of procreation for the first time.
quotes.note: Two items from the six-item list of what mortality is for; the elision covers the two intervening items (a fulness of joy, and probationary testing). Untagged, but the second item is the premise the nineteenth-century mechanism arguments are built on — spirits do not have procreative power, embodiment confers it — stated here as a bare fact about the plan. Compare pratt-people-worlds-1871-q1, which runs the identical premise (“Can spirits do this? No, they remain single”) straight through to spirit offspring and worlds. Critchlow does not; he draws no conclusion from it at all, which is why nothing is tagged.

quotes.excerpt: Life is eternal. Faithful members of the cast, after their resurrection, may attain a state of exaltation in God's kingdom in a glory called celestial. That glory holds a promise of eternal life, the power of eternal increase, a continuation of the seeds.
quotes.note: The formula in its most compact form, three terms in apposition, delivered as the answer to the question the address has just posed about what happens to the cast when the drama ends. “A continuation of the seeds” is D&C 132:19 quoted without quotation marks or citation, and Critchlow adds nothing to it — no offspring, no mechanism — so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. citesId dc-132 records the unmarked borrowing.

notes: Verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1967/1967-10-critchlow-all-the-worlds-a-stage.md. Provenance is worth stating in full: the address had never been ingested into the vault at all, and was transcribed in a heavyweight pass directly from the DjVu word-coordinate reading order of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1967sa, leaves n87–n91, printed pp. 87–91); its closing section — which contains both excerpts here — had additionally been misfiled onto the front of Gordon B. Hinckley's file by a running-head bleed and was split back out in the same pass. A later final-review collation of leaves n87–n91 confirmed the body against the scan, with the only flagged candidates being OCR garbles in the independent scan text rather than vault errors. Conference Report, so A. The address's own staging — “Act 1 I would call the pre-mortal act, involving the cast in their spirit state,” then the mortal act, then the immortal act — is the standard three estates and not intelligence→spirit→body, so no TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK tag despite the three-stage vocabulary.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: “a continuation of the seeds forever, and perhaps … the opportunity of building worlds and peopling them”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles; Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, third day morning meeting (Conference Report, October 1967, pp. 121–122)

quotes.excerpt: We are in school, the mortal school, to gain the experiences, the training, the joys, and the sufferings that we partake of, that we might be educated in all these things and be prepared, if we are faithful and true to the commandments of the Lord, to become sons and daughters of God, joint heirs with Jesus Christ; and in his presence to go on to a fullness and a continuation of the seeds forever, and perhaps through our faithfulness to have the opportunity of building worlds and peopling them.
quotes.note: Both tags, for the two halves of the sentence, on the precedent of sdyoung-creators-of-worlds-1969. “A continuation of the seeds forever” is D&C 132:19 recited with no mechanism attached — hedges. “Building worlds and peopling them” satisfies the explicit category's world-making clause outright, and it is the stronger reading of the two because peopling is not creating: worlds are to be furnished with inhabitants, which is as close to the generative claim as the correlated era gets without naming spirit children. Note the qualifier: “perhaps.” The seeds are promised; the worlds are offered as a possibility, and the hedge falls on the half that is explicit rather than on the half that is coded.

quotes.excerpt: We are in the mortal life to get an experience, a training, that we couldn’t get any other way. And in order to become gods, it is necessary for us to know something about pain, about sickness, and about the other things that we partake of in this school of mortality.
quotes.note: Untagged, and the restraint is the point. This is the King Follett symmetry premise stated in its bare form — godhood requires a mortal probation — by the speaker who spent his career policing what could be inferred from it. He applies it forward, to us, and never once backward, to the Father, in this address or anywhere near it. Tagging FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE here would be exactly the retrojection the taxonomy's first conflation trap warns against; recorded instead as the premise the corpus keeps supplying without drawing the conclusion. Compare jfs-agq-as-man-is-1958, where the same speaker, asked directly about the Snow couplet, answers about the Father without leaving the couplet's own terms.

notes:
Collated word-for-word during drafting against the DjVu text of the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1967sa, printed pages 121–122), read alongside the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1967/1967-10-smith-but-undergirding-and-overarching-all-that-i.md. The scan's OCR reads “that we might he educated”; the vault's final-review pass corrected it to “be educated” against the page image, and that correction is carried here — it is the only difference between this excerpt and the raw OCR. The printed byline gives his office as of the Twelve Apostles and the First Presidency. The vault file's slug is inherited from a mis-ingested fragment and does not describe the address; the address itself is an extemporaneous talk on the Fall, opening “My dear brethren and sisters, I made a few notes and thought I would present them here on this occasion, but I have changed my mind.” Conference Report, so A.

The reason this entry matters is the speaker. Joseph Fielding Smith is the corpus's most disciplined restrictor on the backward and progression axes — jfs-progression-1971 (“not in gaining more knowledge”), jfs-agq-create-intelligence-1960 (“such questions should be ignored”), jfs-agq-intelligences-1963 — and in 1951 he had flattened “continuation of the seeds” into mere endurance of the couple (jfs-continuation-of-seeds-1951). Here, sixteen years later and three years before becoming President of the Church, he states the forward chain at close to full strength from the general conference pulpit: seeds forever, and worlds built and peopled. The pattern the corpus keeps showing is confirmed in the sharpest available case — the forward direction was never the one under discipline. What is still absent is any backward inference: nothing in the address suggests our Father did the same, and the “in order to become gods” sentence that would license it is left standing on its own.

title: Spencer W. Kimball: knowledge “in order to create worlds and to furnish them”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1968)

quotes.excerpt: We shall need all of the accumulated secular knowledge in order to create worlds and to furnish them, but only through the “mysteries of God” and these hidden treasures of knowledge may we arrive at the place and condition where we may use that knowledge in creation and exaltation.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “Secular and spiritual knowledge,” and the world-making is not the sermon's subject — it arrives as the unargued premise of an argument about study. That is what makes it useful: exaltation is given concrete content (the exalted create worlds, plural, and furnish them) in the course of saying something else entirely. MANY-WORLDS alone; the peopling half of the forward chain is absent, so no FORWARD-* tag, and nothing is said about the Father's own past. Compare kimball-godhood-1952, the same speaker sixteen years earlier ending an address on “eternal increase, perfection, and with it all — Godhood,” and kimball-1976, where as President he warns the Church against disseminating doctrines “alleged to have been taught by some of the General Authorities of past generations.”

quotes.excerpt: Spiritual knowledge gives the power to live eternally and to rise and overcome and develop and finally to create.
quotes.note: Printed under the side-head “Knowledge not unfindable,” about two-thirds of the way through the address and well before q1. Untagged context, kept because it shows the creation claim is not a slip at the close: creating is named as the terminal item in a progression of powers the first time the subject comes up, and then made specific at the end.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1968/1968-10-kimball-president-alvin-r-dyer-the-tabernacle-choir.md, collated in the final-review pass against the DjVu column-order reconstruction of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1968sa, leaves n129–n133). Provenance caveat a maintainer should know: this file's closing had been missing — the vault text broke off mid-sentence at “since he would not humbly” — and the continuation, which contains q1, had been misfiled as the entire body of the Alma Sonne file for the same session. The final-review pass confirmed the join by direct scan continuity across the leaf 132/133 page break and appended the recovered text here, and the recovered portion carries Kimball's own closing testimony and “Amen.” The reading is sound but q1 sits in recovered text, so it is worth a glance at the page image before publication. Conference Report, so A. The printed Report supplies no title; the vault's placeholder is taken from the opening line.

title: Alma Sonne reads Mormon Doctrine from the pulpit: “Man and God are of the same race”
speaker: Alma Sonne
office: Assistant to the Council of the Twelve
venue: General conference, third day afternoon meeting (Conference Report, October 1968)

quotes.excerpt: “Man and God are of the same race,” said President Bruce R. McConkie. (Mormon Doctrine, pp. 465-66.) Man's destiny is godlike, for he has the opportunity to reach the heights of a glorious exaltation.
quotes.note: Untagged, deliberately. Species identity plus theosis is the whole of the inference Sonne draws — no increase, no offspring, no claim about the Father's past — and per the reading applied to brown-deify-man-1956-q2 that earns no category. Two things are recorded by the row itself rather than by a tag: that Mormon Doctrine is being quoted by name and page from the general-conference pulpit ten years after its contested first edition and two years after the second, by an Assistant to the Twelve expounding the Articles of Faith; and that “President” here is the style for McConkie as one of the seven Presidents of the First Council of the Seventy, not a First Presidency title. The attribution and page reference are reproduced as Sonne gives them; whether the sentence appears in those words at those pages has not been checked against the book for this entry.

notes: Verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1968/1968-10-sonne-bow-in-baptism-the-holy-ghost-is.md. Provenance is unusual and should be read before the entry is relied on: the file under this name previously contained none of Sonne's words at all — its body was the misfiled closing of Spencer W. Kimball's address from the same session (see kimball-create-worlds-1968) — and Sonne's real address was ingested from scratch in the final-review pass from leaves n133–n135 of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1968sa) via the DjVu column-order reconstruction, with the closing boundary confirmed against the narrator's line that follows. The excerpt here is from that fresh ingest of the printed Report, so A, but it has been through one transcription pass rather than a transcription plus an independent collation, and a maintainer should check it against the page image before publication. sourceType citation because the transmission is the entry's whole value: what the row records is Mormon Doctrine reaching a general-conference audience under its own title, not a new doctrinal claim by Sonne.

title: Hugh B. Brown: the spirit “a self-existing entity, uncreated and eternal”
speaker: Hugh B. Brown
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, second day morning meeting (Conference Report, April 1969)

quotes.excerpt: We believe that before the creation of the body, all men existed as intelligences. These intelligences were not created or made, neither indeed can they be; the intelligent entity in man which we call spirit or soul is a self-existing entity, uncreated and eternal. Thus man is crowned with the dignity which belongs to his divine and eternal nature.
quotes.note: Denial, on the abraham-3 and kfd-1844 reading — no beginning means no begetting — and stated by a counselor in the First Presidency in general conference, printed under the side-head “Man's eternal nature.” The middle clause is the sharp one: Brown identifies the uncreated intelligence with “spirit or soul,” which collapses the staging rather than building it. That is why no TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK tag, despite the intelligences vocabulary and despite the source he is working from — the whole point of bh-roberts-tripartite is that the intelligence is a tier prior to the spirit, and here they are the same thing, leaving two stages (uncreated spirit, then body) rather than three. Attribution: Brown introduces the passage as “The late President Brigham H. Roberts, in one of his later writings … I shall quote and paraphrase him,” so the wording is his rendering of Roberts and the boundary between quotation and paraphrase is not marked.

quotes.excerpt: The Church teaches that when God created man in his own image, he did not divest himself of that image. He is still in human form and is possessed of sanctified and perfected human qualities, which we all admire. … In other words, he is an exalted, perfected, and glorified Being.
quotes.note: Marked implied. The work this sentence is doing is anthropomorphism — the surrounding paragraphs are an argument against the creedal God “without body, parts or passions” — and the attainment reading rides on an adjective rather than a verb: an exalted Being, with nothing said about who exalted him, from what, or when. Per the Father-status precedent that is FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone, no mortality claim attached; it is the identical phrase McConkie applies to the Father in Mormon Doctrine (“an exalted, glorified, and perfected Man,” see mcconkie-mormon-doctrine-q1), where the same reading is noted and then left to an explicit quote. Brown has no explicit quote to defer to — the address never returns to the Father's origin — so the tag lands here, marked implied. The elision covers three sentences on the separateness of the Father and the Son and on the scriptural warrant for the image claim.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-04-brown-the-apostle-peter-writing-to-the-saints.md, whose body was independently re-collated in the final-review pass against leaves n52–n56 of the Church History Library preservation scan (conferencereport1969a) rather than trusting the prior stamps; that pass fixed one accidental mid-name paragraph split and converted twelve printed side-heads, and left two shared OCR artifacts (“Pirst Peter,” “]esus Christ”) untouched because both witnesses agree on them. Neither artifact falls in the excerpts here. Conference Report, so A. This is Brown's Saturday-morning general-session address, distinct from his priesthood-session address later in the same conference and from brown-deify-man-1956 and brown-eternal-increase-1966. The address is an apologia for Latter-day Saint distinctiveness aimed outward (“we are a peculiar people”), which is the frame worth keeping in view: the uncreated-spirit claim and the exalted-Being claim are both offered as selling points to outsiders, not as mysteries. citesId bh-roberts-tripartite for the acknowledged Roberts source; the James E. Talmage passage Brown also reads (“What is man in this boundless setting of sublime splendor?”) is not from The Articles of Faith and has no dataset entry, so it is not linked.

title: S. Dilworth Young: “not just gazers into the wonders of the heavens, but creators of them”
speaker: S. Dilworth Young
office: First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1969; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1969a, leaves n79–n81)

quotes.excerpt: How much greater is the love of the Christ, who becomes our Father by our acceptance of his offer to us not only of earthly development but also of salvation, exaltation, and eternal lives. In the gospel of Christ he offers us the opportunity to become not just gazers into the wonders of the heavens, but creators of them.
quotes.note: Two moves in two sentences. "Eternal lives" is the D&C 132 term of art for eternal increase, used here with no mechanism attached at all — the euphemism in its purest correlated-era form. Then the very next sentence supplies a gloss, and it is not the usual one: what the exalted become is creators of heavens, not parents of spirits. Both tags are carried because both moves are present, and the difference between them is the point of the entry. (The Christology is also unusual and is left untagged: Christ, not the Father, is the one who "becomes our Father" by covenant.)

quotes.excerpt: It is wondrous to know that the most magnificent of God's creations may be duplicated — not by technical knowledge gained here, although this may be of help, but by such simple acts as being kind to and honest with all people. By obeying the first principles and ordinances, one places himself in harmony with eternal teachings that will lead him to the presence of the Creator, and from him he will learn to take part in the acts of creation. We understand that these wondrous accomplishments will not come without work. We know we must learn all we can of the truth of things in this life, and that we shall have to conquer eternal physics, eternal chemistry, eternal biology, and all eternal arts to give eternal science beauty.
quotes.note: The forward claim at full strength: God's creations "may be duplicated," the exalted will "take part in the acts of creation," and the curriculum for it is named — eternal physics, eternal chemistry, eternal biology. Tagged FORWARD-EXPLICIT on the world-making half of the category definition, on the precedent of pratt-key-theology-1855-q3. What is conspicuously absent, and the reason this entry is worth having, is offspring: no spirit children, no heavenly parents, no begetting, no continuation of the seeds anywhere in the address. SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS would be pure retrojection. The address is a standing counterexample to the assumption that a mid-century "we shall become creators" statement is shorthand for eternal increase — here the forward chain runs through creation rather than procreation, and "eternal biology" is as close as it comes to the generative register.

quotes.excerpt: Hear the witness of their Creator, for it is God who speaks: "And by the word of my power, have I created them, which is mine Only Begotten Son, who is full of grace and truth. "And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose; and by the Son I created them, which is mine Only Begotten." (Moses 1:32-33.)
quotes.note: Moses 1:32–33 quoted with no gloss beyond the attribution of creation to the Son, which the surrounding paragraphs develop from Colossians 1 and 3 Nephi 9. Plural worlds under one God; nothing successive is claimed or implied. The astronomical opening of the address — "uncountable island universes" — is the same point made from the telescope rather than the scripture.

notes: Re-read in full and quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1969/1969-04-young-many-years-ago-in-our.md, independently collated at final review against leaves n79–n81 of the Church History Library preservation scan (Internet Archive conferencereport1969a). Conference Report, so A. Speaker disambiguation matters here: this is S. Dilworth Young of the First Council of the Seventy, not Brigham Young and not Levi Edgar Young. The address is filed because of how it distributes the forward axis — "eternal lives" as a bare formula in one paragraph, world-creation as a fully stated destiny in another, and spirit offspring never mentioned at all — which makes it a clean control on the eternal-increase question rather than another witness for it.

title: Harold B. Lee answers a member who cannot believe “God himself was once as we are now”
speaker: Harold B. Lee
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, April 1969; Internet Archive scan conferencereport1969a, leaves n131–n135)

quotes.excerpt: Another man wrote: "If a member cannot believe the concept that God himself was once as we are now, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens," is this justification for excommunication from the Church? … The reasoning of Joseph Smith, in the partial statement from which he has quoted, "that God was once as we are now," is given additional strength if our brother will recall the words of the Master: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do; for what things soever he [the Father] doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise." (John 5:19.) When we consider the fact that our Lord and Master, Jesus of Nazareth, one of the Godhead, came to tabernacle in mortality, then this quoted statement, taken literally, is of great significance.
quotes.note: The occasion is the entry's value: a member has written in to ask whether disbelieving the King Follett statement is grounds for excommunication, and an apostle answers by defending the statement rather than by softening it. Lee's argument is the Christological one — John 5:19, the Son does what he has seen the Father do, plus the fact of Christ's own mortality — which is the same engine that drives kfd-1844-q1 and the Snow couplet. "Taken literally" is Lee's own adverb. FATHER-BECAME-GOD is deliberately not tagged: the member's letter quotes "was once as we are now, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens" but omits the attainment clause "and is an exalted man," and Lee never supplies it. Referent is the Father throughout — Lee's subject is "God, the Eternal Father, also known as the Father of our spirits."

quotes.excerpt: Commenting on this same teaching, President Brigham Young had this to say: ". . . it must be that God knows something about temporal things, and has had a body and been on an earth; were it not so He would not know how to judge men righteously, according to the temptations and sins they have had to contend with." (Journal of Discourses, Vol. 4, p. 271.)
quotes.note: A relay: Young's words reach the 1969 congregation through the Journal of Discourses, so the sentence is Watt-shorthand secondhand inside a first-person Conference Report address. It is quoted here as Lee printed it, ellipsis and all. Journal of Discourses 4:271 has no entry of its own in this dataset, so no citation edge is set for it; if that sermon is ever added, this quote should acquire the edge.

quotes.excerpt: Those who can attain to this highest degree of glory are spoken of in a revelation we know as Doctrine and Covenants 131:1-4: "In the celestial glory there are three heavens or degrees; "And in order to obtain the highest, a man must enter into this order of the priesthood [meaning the new and everlasting covenant of marriage] ; "And if he does not, he cannot obtain it. "He may enter into the other, but that is the end of his kingdom; he cannot have an increase."
quotes.note: D&C 131:1–4 quoted with one interpolation and no gloss on the word that matters. The bracket "[meaning the new and everlasting covenant of marriage]" is Lee's, printed in the Conference Report; "increase" is left standing unexplained, which is the standard correlated-era handling of this passage. What is not standard is what Lee does next — he immediately supplies the explanation from Brigham Young (q4), which is the strongest available one. Tagged euphemism for the scripture itself; the explicit tag belongs to q4. OCR note: the printed spacing "marriage] ;" and the run-in quotation marks are reproduced as the scan has them.

quotes.excerpt: President Young again expands upon the meaning of this quotation: ". . . The kingdoms he possesses and rules over are his own progeny. Every man who is faithful and gets a salvation and glory, and becomes a king of kings and Lord of Lords, or a father of fathers, it will be by the increase of his own progeny. Our Father and God rules over his own children. Wherever there is a God in all the eternities possessing a kingdom and glory and power it is by means of his progeny. . . ." (Journal of Discourses, Vol. 11, p. 262.)
quotes.note: The gloss Lee chooses for D&C 131's "increase": an exalted man's kingdom is literally his own posterity, and — Young generalises — every God's kingdom anywhere is his progeny. That is eternal increase stated as offspring rather than as formula, read into the 1969 Conference Report by an apostle. Two precision points. First, the generalisation is about the class of Gods, not about a line of them: "wherever there is a God in all the eternities" asserts plurality and a shared pattern, not succession, so INFINITE-CHAIN is withheld. Second, the sentence "Our Father and God rules over his own children" applies the pattern to the Father, which is a claim about who populates his kingdom, not about who fathered him. The Conference Report breaks the citation across a column ("Journal of Discourses, Vol. / 11, p. 262."); it is closed up here.

quotes.excerpt: There are those who would think to go beyond that which God has revealed. It was to such as these, who would seek to penetrate that curtain of revealed truth, that inspired writers of our early leaders posed a profound question that was later given a musical setting in one of our most beloved hymns: "If you could hie to Kolob In the twinkling of an eye, And then continue onward With that same speed to fly, D'ye think that you could ever, Through all eternity, Find out the generation Where Gods began to be? … The works of God continue, And worlds and lives abound; Improvement and progression Have one eternal round. There is no end to matter; There is no end to space; There is no end to spirit; There is no end to race." (Hymns, No. 257.)
quotes.note: The clearest statement in the corpus of what the hymn is for when a General Authority reaches for it: it is deployed against "those who would think to go beyond that which God has revealed," as a bar on the question rather than an answer to it.
