But these keys we cannot receive in the flesh.”
quotes.note: Brigham Young, Journal of Discourses 15:137, read approvingly by Kimball — “authority to produce both spirit and body” is the mechanism stated as plainly as the corpus ever states it, and it is being read from the conference pulpit in 1977, three years before mcconkie-heresies-1980. Hearsay C for this quote: the inner text is Watt-era Journal of Discourses shorthand that Young did not review, even though the frame around it is an official published conference address.

quotes.excerpt: But no parent has ever yet on this earth been the parent of a spirit, because we are so far yet from perfection. Remember what was said a while ago, that “As man is, God once was; and as God is, man may become.” They came with the definite understanding that they could return to become like God and go forward in their great development and progress.
quotes.note: Kimball in his own voice, and the two axes are welded together in three sentences: no mortal has yet been the parent of a spirit — the negative form of the generative claim, with “yet” carrying the whole promise — followed immediately by the couplet as the warrant. This is the batch's clearest instance of the forward and backward directions being asserted together by the same speaker in the same breath, which is precisely the junction the taxonomy exists to keep visible without letting either direction be inferred from the other.

quotes.excerpt: Could you produce a spirit? Has anyone whom you know ever produced a spirit? This is a power not given to mortal man, so there is much for us to learn.
quotes.note: The rhetorical form of the same claim, put to the priesthood session as a question. “Not given to mortal man” is a restriction on the present, not a denial — the entire address is about powers deferred to the resurrection.

quotes.excerpt: In the resurrection, men who have been faithful and diligent in all things in the flesh, [who] have kept their first and second estate, and [are] worthy to be crowned Gods, even the sons of God, will be ordained to organize matter. How much matter do you suppose there is between here and some of the fixed stars which we can see? Enough to frame many, very many millions of such earths as this, yet it is now so diffused, clear and pure, that we look through it and behold the stars.
quotes.note: Brigham Young again, Journal of Discourses 15:137; hearsay C for the same reason as q2. Matter enough for millions of earths, to be organized by men crowned Gods — MANY-WORLDS, with the godhood itself uncategorized as theosis. The square brackets are Kimball's editorial insertions into the Young text and are reproduced as printed.

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason, truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there. When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high?
quotes.note: Kimball closes by reciting “O My Father” entire; these are the Mother stanzas. Affirms by recitation without gloss — the President of the Church puts the lines into the record and moves straight to the benediction. Verse line breaks rendered as running text. He cites the hymn as Hymns, no. 139; McConkie in 1970 and Sill in 1978 cite the same hymn from the same book as no. 138, a discrepancy worth noting whenever a hymnal number is used to date a quotation.

quotes.excerpt: My brethren, God bless you as we carry forward our lives toward perfection so that we may attain and receive the blessings that we are promised, that we may reach godhood eventually and have the blessings appertaining thereto.
quotes.note: The closing benediction, uncategorized as theosis, and carried for register: “that we may reach godhood eventually” is said as a blessing on the congregation, in the last sentence before the testimony, by a Church President.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1977/1977-04-kimball-our-great-potential.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all seven excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim. Renderings, no words changed: hymn verse line breaks are set as running text, printed scripture-reference parentheticals and the trailing (JD, 15:137) citations are omitted, and Kimball's own square-bracket insertions into the Brigham Young text are kept. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated; hearsayByQuote drops q2 and q5 to C because those two excerpts are Journal of Discourses shorthand of Brigham Young, speaker-unreviewed, carried inside an official address. Filed sourceType original — the argument, the selection, and the two couplet quotations are Kimball's — with citesId edges to snow-couplet and o-my-father. This is the strongest entry in the batch and the pass-1 triage had it flagged only for the hymn. The address is a sustained argument that the keys of resurrection, spirit production, and world organization are all withheld until after this life, assembled out of one Journal of Discourses page, Abraham 3, the Snow couplet twice, and the hymn — and it is delivered to the priesthood session by the President of the Church in April 1977. Read against kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978 a year later, kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978, and mcconkie-heresies-1980.

title: Bruce R. McConkie's catechism of “the Gods of heaven”: no truth he does not know, and a resurrected Person
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Council of the Twelve
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Be it known, then, that there is a God in heaven who is infinite and eternal. He has all power, all might, and all dominion. There is no power he does not possess and no truth he does not know. Every good thing dwells in him independently in its eternal fulness. He is the Creator, Upholder, and Preserver of all things. His name is Elohim, and he is our Father in heaven, the literal Father of the spirits of all men. He has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man’s, and is in fact a resurrected and glorified Person. The name of the kind of life he lives is eternal life; and eternal life, by definition and in its nature, consists of life in an eternal family unit and of the possession of the fulness of the glory and power of the Father.
quotes.note: Three tags because three distinct commitments run through one paragraph, and the interest of the paragraph is that they are made to sound like one. DIVINE-PROGRESSION is a denial, in McConkie's standing formula — “no truth he does not know,” with “every good thing” dwelling in him “independently in its eternal fulness”; three years later he will call the contrary position heresy one (mcconkie-heresies-1980). FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE rides on the same word it rode on thirty years earlier at mcconkie-resurrected-father-1947: the Father “is in fact a resurrected and glorified Person,” and resurrection presupposes a death. It is an entailment rather than an argument — McConkie never returns to it — but it is stated of Elohim by name, so the referent is not in doubt, and it sits four sentences after the omniscience claim without any sense that the two might need reconciling. FORWARD-EUPHEMISM is the definition offered at the close: eternal life “consists of life in an eternal family unit,” the family-unit vocabulary of mcconkie-family-affair-1970 now doing duty as a definition of deity's own mode of life. Nothing about offspring, nothing about a chain.

quotes.excerpt: From Mary, his mother, a mortal woman, he inherited the power of mortality, so that he was subject to all the temptations and ills of the flesh, including death itself. From God, his Father, an Immortal Man, he inherited the power of immortality, so that he had power to live forever, or having voluntarily laid down his life, to take it up again in immortal glory.
quotes.note: Untagged, and recorded for the appositive. The Father is “an Immortal Man,” set in exact parallel with “a mortal woman” — the anthropomorphism stated as the mechanism of the Incarnation rather than as a doctrine about deity. Per the Father-status precedent this is not enough on its own: an immortal Man is not an attaining one, so FATHER-BECAME-GOD does not attach here, and the mortality claim the entry does carry is already made by the word resurrected in q1. Compare brown-uncreated-intelligences-1969-q2, where a comparable phrase was tagged and marked implied because that address had no explicit statement to defer to; this one does.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1977/1977-04-mcconkie-come-know-the-lord-jesus.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all four load-bearing clauses were independently re-fetched from the live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. McConkie announces the subject himself — “I shall speak of the Gods of heaven and of our relationship to them” — and the address opens by cataloguing rival Christs before setting out the Latter-day Saint one, so the doctrinal paragraph is written as a creed for outsiders and is unusually compressed for that reason. The verse McConkie recites before it (“The Father's name is Elohim; / Jehovah is his Son”) is his own; it is printed in the conference text as poetry and is not part of any excerpt here. Read as the hinge of the McConkie material already in the dataset: mcconkie-resurrected-father-1947 supplies the resurrected Father, mcconkie-mormon-doctrine the exalted Man, mcconkie-family-affair-1970 the family-unit euphemism, mcconkie-heresies-1980 the denial of progression — and this one paragraph holds all four at once.

title: Spencer W. Kimball: “that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
office: President of the Church
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session

quotes.excerpt: Finally, when we sing that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection, “O My Father,” we get a sense of the ultimate in maternal modesty, of the restrained, queenly elegance of our Heavenly Mother, and knowing how profoundly our mortal mothers have shaped us here, do we suppose her influence on us as individuals to be less if we live so as to return there?
quotes.note: A President of the Church calling the hymn doctrinal, in the same clause in which he explains the doctrine's silence as a property of its subject. The Mother's absence from scripture and prayer becomes “maternal modesty” and “restrained, queenly elegance” — the reticence is relocated from the institution to her. That move is what makes this the hinge between the confident early-century usage and hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, which will convert the same silence into a boundary on practice. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER, not RETREAT-REFRAME: Kimball is enlarging her, not fencing her, and he asserts real influence on individuals.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph gave us the Relief Society organization to advance these high purposes for Latter-day Saint women. That society today is a worldwide movement holding membership in national and world organizations for the advancement of women.
quotes.note: The immediately preceding paragraph, kept for setting. The Heavenly Mother sentence is the peroration of an address about the advancement of Latter-day Saint women, delivered in the same year Neal A. Maxwell reached for her in the same conference — the doctrine surfaces in 1978 as part of a response to the decade's argument about women, not as part of an argument about cosmology.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-kimball-the-true-way-of-life-and-salvation.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-checked during drafting and confirmed to load with this passage present. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as a citation: the hymn is named and characterized, and Kimball's own contribution is a gloss on it rather than an independent argument. Kimball returns to Heavenly Mother repeatedly in 1977–1978 — the October 1978 sisters' address, for instance, says “He and your mother in heaven value you beyond any measure. They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form,” which is the tripartite intelligence-spirit-body sequence rather than a hymn citation, and his April 1977 “Our Great Potential” simply prints the hymn's stanzas. The October 1978 tripartite passage is now its own entry (kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978); the April 1977 bare hymn printing remains undrafted by design.

title: Neal A. Maxwell: “the anticipatory arrangements of a Heavenly Mother”
speaker: Neal A. Maxwell
office: Of the Presidency of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session

quotes.excerpt: Finally, remember: When we return to our real home, it will be with the “mutual approbation” of those who reign in the “royal courts on high.” There we will find beauty such as mortal “eye hath not seen”; we will hear sounds of surpassing music which mortal “ear hath not heard.” Could such a regal homecoming be possible without the anticipatory arrangements of a Heavenly Mother?
quotes.note: Two hymn phrases quoted in quotation marks with no attribution — “mutual approbation” and “royal courts on high” — on the assumption that the congregation will hear the source. That mode of citation is the measure of how thoroughly the hymn had been absorbed by 1978, and it is why phrase searches for “parents single” miss talks like this one. The claim itself goes past anything in the hymn: the hymn's Mother is present and addressed, Maxwell's Mother acts, and heaven is her preparation. It is still a rhetorical question — the strongest Heavenly Mother assertion of the modern corpus, and it is interrogative.

quotes.excerpt: We know so little, brothers and sisters, about the reasons for the division of duties between womanhood and manhood as well as between motherhood and priesthood. These were divinely determined in another time and another place… The story of the women of God, therefore, is, for now, an untold drama within a drama.
quotes.note: The talk's opening, kept because it sets the epistemic frame that the closing question depends on: what is known is little, what is asserted is asserted as inference from the shape of things. Elision marked. Untagged — this makes no claim about a Mother.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-maxwell-the-women-of-god.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the closing paragraph was re-fetched from the live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved: the hymn supplies the vocabulary of the last paragraph, but the proposition — that a Heavenly Mother has made arrangements for our return — is Maxwell's and is not in Eliza R. Snow. Delivered in the same session as kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978, which is the fact to notice: April 1978 is the high-water mark of official Heavenly Mother language in the modern era, and both instances arise from the Church's engagement with the decade's arguments about women. Thirteen years later Gordon B. Hinckley will address the same audience on the same subject to draw a line.

title: Sterling W. Sill: “I have never heard of Eliza R. Snow being sustained as a prophet”
speaker: Sterling W. Sill
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: It has been said that the poets stand next to the prophets in their ability to lift us up. I have never heard of Eliza R. Snow being sustained as a prophet, and yet she wrote “O My Father.” Sometimes we merely read these great lyrics out of the hymnbook instead of memorizing them and loving them and frequently saying them over to ourselves.
quotes.note: The frame, and it runs the opposite way from every other endorsement in the dataset. Cannon in 1896 called the hymn's contents truths “revealed through the Prophet Joseph” and Iverson in 1908 credited it to his inspiration; McConkie in 1970 filed it as “one of our great doctrinal hymns”; Kimball, in the same month as this address, calls it “that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection.” Sill instead notes that its author held no prophetic office, and recommends the hymn for its healing power. Uncategorized — the sentence makes no claim about a Mother — but it is a register datum worth having, since it shows the doctrinal warrant for the hymn is a choice each speaker makes rather than a settled fact about it.

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason, truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there. … When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high?
quotes.note: Affirms by recitation. Sill recites all four verses from the conference pulpit and adds no doctrinal gloss to any of them; the elision marks his spoken verse marker (“Verse four:”) between the stanzas. Verse line breaks rendered as running text. He gives the hymn as Hymns, no. 138, matching McConkie in 1970 and differing from Kimball's no. 139 in April 1977.

quotes.excerpt: It might be difficult to find very many passages, even among the prophets, with more healing power than this.
quotes.note: The assessment Sill actually offers, and it is therapeutic rather than doctrinal — the hymn is filed with James Whitcomb Riley and Grantland Rice under poems that heal, and its distinction is measured against the prophets rather than derived from them.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-sill-the-poetry-of-success.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim. Hymn verse line breaks are rendered as running text and Sill's spoken verse markers are elided; the printed hymnal citation is reported in the note rather than quoted. No words changed. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed sourceType citation with a citesId edge to o-my-father: the entry's whole value is transmission, since Sill adds no argument about Heavenly Mother and the address is about the therapeutic use of memorized verse. The dating is the interesting part. This is April 1978 — the same conference month as kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978 and maxwell-heavenly-mother-1978, and two months before the June 1978 revelation on priesthood; three general authorities put the Mother stanzas into the record in a single conference, and one of the three declines the prophetic warrant the other two assert.

title: Eldred G. Smith, “Decision” — the couplet as an operative premise
speaker: Eldred G. Smith
office: Patriarch to the Church
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: When the gospel plan was explained to Lorenzo Snow, he put the whole plan in a nice epigram: “As man now is, our God once was; as now God is, so man may be.” (Lorenzo Snow, 11 January 1892, reprinted in Latter-day Prophets Speak, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow, Bookcraft, 1951, p. 72.)
quotes.note: The couplet in full from the general conference pulpit, in the “our God once was” variant, with a source citation to a 1951 Bookcraft compilation rather than to Snow directly. Tagged FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE only, per the Father-status precedent: the bare couplet asserts past manhood and nothing about attainment. Referent is father — the wording is “our God,” and the sentence immediately before it is Moses 1:39 in the Father's voice.

quotes.excerpt: Then, if man is going to become as God now is, he will have to learn to make decisions of great importance on his own initiative.
quotes.note: Untagged, and the reason the entry exists. Nothing generative is claimed — this is theosis, which carries no tag of its own — but the sentence does something the surrounding corpus almost never does: it reasons forward *from* the couplet, treating man's future godhood as a live premise with a practical consequence for how mortals must learn to decide. The couplet is not quoted here as a slogan or a proof of Latter-day Saint distinctiveness; it is the minor premise of an argument about agency.

quotes.excerpt: Choose to live the law of celestial marriage. The command in the marriage ceremony is to multiply and replenish the earth. In the Doctrine and Covenants when the Lord is referring to the blessings of celestial marriage (He is talking about husband-wife relationships), He makes this statement: “And if ye abide in my covenant, and commit no murder whereby to shed innocent blood,” and so forth. (D&C 132:19.)
quotes.note: Kept as a negative datum. D&C 132:19 is the eternal-increase verse — “a continuation of the seeds forever and ever” (see dc-132) — and Smith cites it by number, quotes the murder clause, writes “and so forth” over the rest, and turns the verse into an argument about abortion. The increase content of the very verse he is reading is absent from the talk. Untagged because nothing about eternal increase is stated; recorded because the omission is the pattern this dataset tracks.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-smith-decision.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the couplet paragraph, its parenthetical citation, and the following sentence were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, along with the byline “Elder Eldred G. Smith, Patriarch to the Church.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The fourth Eldred G. Smith entry in the dataset and the latest: compare eldred-smith-no-increase-1948, eldred-smith-slavery-godhood-1950, and eldred-smith-spirit-offspring-1973. The office is worth noting for the timeline — Patriarch to the Church was a hereditary office holding an independent line of authority, and Smith was the last to occupy it (the office was discontinued in 1979, a year after this address). He is therefore the one general officer who kept quoting this material plainly across four decades while it was thinning everywhere else, and this is very nearly the last time he does so from a general conference pulpit. Filed as an original rather than a citation because of q2: Smith adds an inference to the couplet, which is the entry's value. The citesId edges are snow-couplet (quoted in full with attribution) and dc-132 (quoted, if only the murder clause).

title: N. Eldon Tanner, “Ye Shall Know the Truth” — the couplet endorsed, the difference reduced to knowledge
speaker: N. Eldon Tanner
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: To know that God the Eternal Father knows all truth and acts in accordance with it explains why he is the same yesterday, today, and forever. All that he does is in keeping with the unchanging truths of the universe.
quotes.note: Denial, implied rather than stated. Tanner is not arguing about eternal progression and never names the debate; he is explaining divine constancy. But the explanation he gives — God is unchanging *because* he already knows all truth — leaves no room for progression in knowledge, which is the whole of what the McConkie–Roberts argument is about. Marked implied for that reason: the direction is entailed by the sentence, not asserted by it. Note the date: this is a First Presidency counselor in April 1978, two years before mcconkie-heresies-1980 puts the same position into polemical form.

quotes.excerpt: One of the great differences between God and man is *God’s greater knowledge of the truth,* which makes him *free* to create worlds and to control the universe.
quotes.note: Untagged, and load-bearing for the entry. The God/man difference is located in a single quantity — knowledge — and the comparative (“greater”) makes the difference one of degree rather than of kind. Asterisks are the italics of the published text. This is the sentence immediately before the couplet, and it is what the couplet is made to mean here.

quotes.excerpt: We believe also that “as man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be.” (Lorenzo Snow, 11 January 1892, reprinted in Latter-day Prophets Speak, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow, Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1951, p. 72.) Therefore, man should strive all his days to increase his intelligence and learn all the truths he can.
quotes.note: The couplet in the Church's own first-person plural — “We believe” — from the First Presidency, and then immediately cashed out as an exhortation to study. Tagged FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE only, per the Father-status precedent for the bare couplet. What the “Therefore” does is the finding: coming after q2, the couplet is read as a statement about a knowledge gradient, so the distance between man and God is closed by learning. Nothing about begetting, dominion, or a chain survives the reading, and the same address has already ruled out God's own further learning (q1) — which leaves a couplet whose two halves are being measured on a scale the Father has already maxed out.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-04-tanner-ye-shall-know-the-truth.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, along with the byline “President N. Eldon Tanner, First Counselor in the First Presidency.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Two things make this worth an entry rather than a bare-formula note. First, the speaker: an endorsement of the couplet in the first-person plural of the institution, by a member of the First Presidency, is the highest-authority affirmation of it in the modern conference corpus. Second, the shape: within four paragraphs the same address affirms that God was once as man is (q3) and explains that God cannot change because he already knows all truth (q1). Both positions are held without any sense of friction, which is possible only because the couplet is being read on the knowledge axis alone (q2) — the axis on which the Father is, by the same address, already complete. Filed as an original with a citesId edge to snow-couplet. Paired with eldred-smith-decision-1978, delivered at the same conference: two speakers, one Saturday apart, quoting the couplet from two different printed variants of the same 1951 compilation.

title: Spencer W. Kimball: “They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
office: President of the Church
venue: General Women's Meeting, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: This is a partnership. God and his creation. The Primary song says, “I am a child of God.” Born with a noble birthright. God is your father. He loves you. He and your mother in heaven value you beyond any measure. They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form, just as your earthly mother and father have given you a mortal body. You are unique. One of a kind, made of the eternal intelligence which gives you claim upon eternal life.
quotes.note: Both tags are stated, not read in. HEAVENLY-MOTHER: "your mother in heaven" is named as a second agent — "They gave" — not merely acknowledged. TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK: the three tiers and both transitions are all present in one sentence — an eternal intelligence that is not made, given spirit form by heavenly parents, then given a mortal body by earthly parents — and the parallel construction ("just as") makes the premortal transition as real as the mortal one. Compare eom-premortal-life-1992, which states the identical sequence fourteen years later and sources it to Melvin J. Ballard; Kimball sources it to nothing and states it to a worldwide audience of women as catechesis. What he does not say is how, and "gave … spirit form" is compatible with organizing as well as with begetting, so no SPIRIT-BIRTH tag attaches in either direction.

quotes.excerpt: Let there be no question in your mind about your value as an individual. The whole intent of the gospel plan is to provide an opportunity for each of you to reach your fullest potential, which is eternal progression and the possibility of godhood.
quotes.note: The very next paragraph, untagged on purpose. "Eternal progression and the possibility of godhood" is theosis and nothing more — the A-framing trap — and it is recorded here precisely to show that the tripartite sentence above is not doing forward-generative work in this address. Kimball tells the sisters what they came from; he does not tell them they will do it in turn.

quotes.excerpt: Mothers have a sacred role. They are partners with God, as well as with their own husbands, first in giving birth to the Lord’s spirit children and then in rearing those children so they will serve the Lord and keep his commandments.
quotes.note: Kept for the semantic reading it forces. "The Lord's spirit children" here means us — already-existing spirits receiving mortal bodies from mortal mothers. That is the modern sense of the phrase, and it is the exact inverse of the 1949 sense in hunter-beget-spirit-children-1949, where spirit children are what exalted couples will beget. The same three words, twenty-nine years apart, pointing in opposite directions in the same corpus. Untagged: nothing here is a claim about eternal increase.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1978/1978-10-kimball-privileges-and-responsibilities-of-sisters.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Delivered at the first worldwide General Women's Meeting — "Nothing like it has ever been held before in the Church," as Kimball says in the third paragraph — which is worth recording alongside the doctrine: the strongest tripartite sentence in the modern conference corpus was spoken at the inaugural session of a new meeting for women. Filed as an original with no citesId: the hymn is not quoted here and the Primary song is named rather than argued from. Two housekeeping notes for whoever maintains the neighbouring entries. First, this address completes the 1978 cluster with kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978 (April, "that doctrinal hymn and anthem of affection") and maxwell-heavenly-mother-1978 (April, "the anticipatory arrangements of a Heavenly Mother") — three official Heavenly Mother statements in one calendar year, the high-water mark of the modern era, all of them arising from the decade's argument about women rather than from any argument about cosmology. Second, kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978's own notes state that this October address was "deliberately not drafted" as the weaker member of the cluster; that judgment is superseded by this entry, on the ground that the two make different claims — April is a gloss on the hymn, October is the intelligence-to-spirit staging, which no other Kimball text in the dataset supplies — and that note should be revised when sources.json is next edited.

title: Adney Y. Komatsu quotes Orson F. Whitney: “more like our Father and Mother in heaven”
speaker: Adney Y. Komatsu
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Orson F. Whitney said: “No pain that we suffer, no trial that we experience is wasted. It ministers to our education, to the development of such qualities as patience, faith, fortitude and humility. All that we suffer and all that we endure, especially when we endure it patiently, builds up our characters, purifies our hearts, expands our souls, and makes us more tender and charitable, more worthy to be called the children of God … and it is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our Father and Mother in heaven” (cited in Spencer W. Kimball, Faith Precedes the Miracle, Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1972, p. 98).
quotes.note: Graded C rather than A, for the same reason as howard-hunter-whitney-1987-q1: Komatsu's own words are published official text, but the Whitney material is sourced only to page 98 of Kimball's 1972 Faith Precedes the Miracle, which itself prints it without a citation, so the chain is Whitney (d. 1931) → an uncited devotional paperback → the pulpit. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only. “More like our Father and Mother in heaven” is likeness, which is theosis, and asserts nothing generative — the same reading given to whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q1, which is a different Whitney text. The ellipsis is printed in the published talk, not an editorial cut.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1979/1979-10-komatsu-after-much-tribulation-come-the-blessings.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the Whitney paragraph and its parenthetical citation were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, along with the byline “Elder Adney Y. Komatsu, Of the First Quorum of the Seventy.” Official published text, so A at entry level, with the quoted material graded C — see the quote note. Filed as an original despite being substantively a quotation, because the quoted text is not an entry in this dataset and a citesId edge would dangle; whitney-father-and-mother-1907 is Whitney's October 1907 conference address on Heavenly Mother as philosophy, a different text, and must not be used as the target. This is the earliest of the four known conference appearances of the passage, all of them sourced only to Faith Precedes the Miracle p. 98: Komatsu here in October 1979, Komatsu again in April 1987, Howard W. Hunter six months after that (howard-hunter-whitney-1987), and Neill F. Marriott in April 2016. The notes to the Hunter entry record all four and state that the Komatsu instances were deliberately not drafted; that judgment should be revised in favour of this entry, which supplies the first date in the chain, but the Hunter entry remains the place where the transmission lineage is argued and the two should be read together. Kept lean per the drafting charter: the address is about enduring affliction, the Mother arrives as a passenger inside a quotation about suffering, and Komatsu adds nothing to it.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Mystery of Mormonism” — a holy man who is the Eternal Absolute
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Council of the Twelve
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: There is a God in heaven, a glorious personage, a holy man, who knows all things, has all power, and is infinite and eternal. He is the Supreme Being, the Eternal Absolute, the Creator and peopler of worlds without number. He is our Father in Heaven, and he lives in the family unit.
quotes.note: The opening lines of a creedal statement addressed explicitly to non-Latter-day Saints, and the two tags sit uneasily together on purpose. DIVINE-PROGRESSION is a denial and is marked implied: “knows all things,” “infinite and eternal,” and above all “the Eternal Absolute” foreclose progression in knowledge without the question being raised — this is the absolutist vocabulary of the creeds McConkie spends his career rejecting, borrowed to describe the Latter-day Saint God. MANY-WORLDS is stated outright: “the Creator and peopler of worlds without number.” Note what is left untagged. “A holy man” is McConkie's recurring formula, drawn from the Moses 6–7 title Man of Holiness, and it is anthropomorphic rather than biographical: it says God is a man, not that he was once a mortal one or that he attained his station, so neither FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE nor FATHER-BECAME-GOD attaches. The sentence in which “a holy man” and “the Eternal Absolute” stand three lines apart is the whole problem of this period in one paragraph.

quotes.excerpt: Indeed the whole aim and purpose of the gospel is to enable men and women—united as one in the Lord—to create for themselves eternal family units in eternity. Celestial marriage prepares us for the greatest joy and happiness known to mortals and for eternal life in the realms ahead.
quotes.note: The forward direction as McConkie states it to outsiders: maximal in scope — it is “the whole aim and purpose of the gospel” — and euphemistic in content. “Create for themselves eternal family units in eternity” is doing the work that “eternal increase” or “spirit children in the resurrection” does elsewhere in his own preaching (compare mcconkie-doctrine-of-priesthood-1982-q2, three years later and to a priesthood audience, where he says “spirit children in the resurrection” outright). The euphemism is not accidental — the audience of this address is the world.

quotes.excerpt: May we say, as many have done before, that what men call Mormonism is the very system of laws and truths which will make of earth a heaven and of man a god.
quotes.note: Untagged, and recorded for the register rather than the content. Theosis stated to the world without hedge or apology — “make … of man a god” — in the same address that describes the Father as the Eternal Absolute. Nothing generative, no offspring, no chain, so no category applies; compare packer-parentage-1984-q4, which does the same thing five years later.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1979/1979-10-mcconkie-the-mystery-of-mormonism.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, along with the byline “Elder Bruce R. McConkie, Of the Council of the Twelve.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Dated eight months before the BYU fireside (mcconkie-heresies-1980), which is the reason to keep it: the absolutist description of God that the fireside will defend polemically is already in place here, stated calmly, in general conference, as the first article of a creed written for outsiders. The setting matters to the reading — the address is a self-presentation to “those inquiring minds” and to a world that calls the Church “deniers of Christ,” which is exactly the setting in which the tradition's distinctive claims about God's past and man's future are most likely to be stated in their least distinctive available vocabulary. Referent is n/a at entry level per the spec rule: no quote here makes a backward-direction claim (note that mcconkie-heresies-1980 records “ambiguous” instead, a legacy choice).

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Seven Deadly Heresies”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Brigham Young University fireside address

quotes.excerpt: [On the proposition that God is progressing in knowledge and learning new truths, listed as heresy one:] This is false—utterly, totally, and completely. There is not one sliver of truth in it. It grows out of a wholly twisted and incorrect view of the King Follett Sermon and of what is meant by eternal progression. God progresses in the sense that his kingdoms increase and his dominions multiply—not in the sense that he learns new truths and discovers new laws.
quotes.note: Denial, the sharpest on record. Note the rhetorical mechanism: “God progresses” is affirmed and immediately redefined as expansion of kingdoms — quoting the first clause alone reads as an affirmation of the position being denounced.

notes: Never official — a BYU fireside, not conference. It triggered the McConkie–England correspondence (February 1981), the classic institutional episode of this debate; the denial position entered official channels through Joseph Fielding Smith's writings and the correlated manuals instead. Wording verified against the BYU Speeches text.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Lord God of the Restoration” — the student-god denial reaches general conference
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: And there are even those who champion the almost unbelievable theory that God is an eternal student enrolled in the University of the Universe, where he is busily engaged in learning new truths and amassing new and strange knowledge that he never knew before.
quotes.note: Denial, and the rhetorical form is the finding. Four months after the BYU fireside (mcconkie-heresies-1980), the same position arrives in general conference — but not as an argument. It arrives as the last item in a list of false gods, after cows, crocodiles, cedar posts, idols, icons, Adam, Allah, Buddha, and the immaterial spirit essence of the creeds. A live intra-Latter-day-Saint doctrinal question is placed among the objects of pagan worship, and the placement does the work that argument would otherwise have to do.

quotes.excerpt: How belittling it is—it borders on blasphemy—to demean the Lord God Omnipotent by saying he is an idol, or an image, or an animal, or a spirit essence, or that he is ever learning but never able to come to a knowledge of all truth (see 2 Tim. 3:7).
quotes.note: Denial, with the charge named: “it borders on blasphemy.” The scriptural warrant is 2 Timothy 3:7, a verse about false teachers “ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” — which describes deceived women in Paul's letter and is here turned against a position held by B. H. Roberts, John A. Widtsoe, and James E. Talmage (talmage-af-1899, roberts-progress-of-god-1911), all of them writing under Church commission or as General Authorities. Note also what the sentence does not do: it never distinguishes progression in knowledge from progression in dominion, the distinction the fireside had made explicitly and on which McConkie's own position depends.

quotes.excerpt: It is the first principle of revealed religion to know the nature and kind of being that God is. As for us, “we know [and testify] that there is a God in heaven, who is infinite and eternal, from everlasting to everlasting the same unchangeable God, the framer of heaven and earth, and all things which are in them” (D&C 20:17). … He is omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent. He has all power, knows all things, and, by the power of his Spirit, is in and through all things.
quotes.note: The positive statement the denials are protecting, and it is built out of D&C 20:17 plus the three classical omni-attributes. Marked implied: immutability and omniscience entail that there is nothing left to learn, but the sentence does not raise the question. Worth recording that the opening clause is the King Follett Discourse's own premise — “it is the first principle of the Gospel to know for a certainty the character of God” — deployed to reach the opposite conclusion from the one Joseph Smith drew from it. The bracketed “[and testify]” is McConkie's insertion into the D&C text; the ellipsis marks the elided sentences on the personage of tabernacle and D&C 130:22.

quotes.excerpt: All men are the spirit children of the Eternal Father. We are the offspring of celestial parents. We lived and dwelt in the courts of glory before the foundations of this world were laid.
quotes.note: Plural parents, unexplicated. “The offspring of celestial parents” is the 1909 First Presidency phrase (fp-1909) reaching general conference intact in 1980; a Mother is entailed by the plural and is nowhere named, described, or argued for. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER on the same ground as renlund-divine-nature-2022-q5 — the parents are plural and are the source. No SPIRIT-BIRTH tag in either direction: “spirit children” and “offspring” state a relation, not a mechanism, and McConkie supplies no mechanism here.

quotes.excerpt: And certainly a student god, with finite powers, who is just experimenting in the eternal laboratories, is not a being in whom I, at least, would feel inclined to repose an infinite trust.
quotes.note: Denial, and the argument is now frankly pragmatic rather than exegetical: a progressing God would not be worth trusting. The same rhetorical move as the fireside's, restated at the close of the list of false gods, and the only place in the address where McConkie speaks in the first person singular (“I, at least”) — which is as close as the text comes to marking the position as his own rather than the Church's.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1980/1980-10-mcconkie-the-lord-god-of-the-restoration.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all five excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, along with the byline “Elder Bruce R. McConkie, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated — which is the single most important fact about it. mcconkie-heresies-1980 is a BYU fireside and is correctly filed never-official; this address says the same thing four months later from the general conference pulpit, was printed in the Ensign, and remains on churchofjesuschrist.org today. Anyone tracing how the denial of divine progression acquired official standing should cite this entry, not the fireside. Two further observations for the timeline reader. First, the argumentative structure is degraded relative to the fireside: there the denial came with a distinction (God progresses in kingdoms and dominions, not in knowledge) that preserved a sense in which “eternal progression” remains true of God; here the distinction is dropped and only the ridicule survives. Second, the address is internally in tension in the way this period characteristically is — q4 has us descended from celestial parents in the courts of glory, and q3 has the Father as the unchangeable framer of heaven and earth, and the question of how the second became the first is not raised. Referent is n/a at entry level per the spec rule: no quote here makes a backward-direction claim.

title: Boyd K. Packer, “Marriage” — “eternal increase,” and the concession that it is new to many
speaker: Boyd K. Packer
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: And marriage is the crucible Where elements of life combine, Where mortal temples are conceived Within that plan divine. Then spirit offspring of our God Can come through mortal birth To have a choice, to face the test— The purpose of our stay on earth.
quotes.note: Untagged, and the semantics are the reason. “Spirit offspring of our God” here means us — already-existing premortal spirits receiving mortal bodies — not new spirit children begotten by exalted couples. That is the modern sense of the phrase and the exact inverse of the 1949 sense in hunter-beget-spirit-children-1949; compare kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978-q3, which forces the same reading. Nothing about eternal increase is claimed, so no category attaches. Recorded because these are the lines the peroration in q2 lands on, and because the verse is Packer's own — introduced only as “These lines express something of the place of marriage in the eternal progress of man,” with no attribution to anyone else. Line breaks of the printed verse are rendered here as spaces.

quotes.excerpt: Eternal love, eternal marriage, eternal increase! This ideal, which is new to many, when thoughtfully considered, can keep a marriage strong and safe. No relationship has more potential to exalt a man and a woman than the marriage covenant.
quotes.note: The term of art named from the pulpit as the third and culminating member of the celestial ideal, and then left entirely unglossed — hence FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than FORWARD-EXPLICIT. What makes the sentence worth an entry is the clause in the middle of it: “which is new to many.” An apostle concedes, in 1981, that a general conference audience of Latter-day Saints may be hearing the doctrine of eternal increase for the first time. That is a datum about transmission, stated by the transmitter, and it should be read against the nineteenth-century material where the claim is assumed rather than introduced.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1981/1981-04-packer-marriage.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; during drafting on 2026-08-10 the live page was re-fetched and confirmed, phrase by phrase, to carry “Eternal love, eternal marriage, eternal increase!”, the sentence “This ideal, which is new to many, when thoughtfully considered, can keep a marriage strong and safe.”, and the verse lines “Then spirit offspring of our God”, “Can come through mortal birth”, and “A very key to God's own plan”, along with the byline “Elder Boyd K. Packer, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” (The fetch tool declines to reproduce long passages, so verification was done as targeted phrase checks against a vault text already diffed at 1.0000.) Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Read this entry immediately before packer-parentage-1984: the same apostle names eternal increase as the crown of the celestial ideal in April 1981 and, three and a half years later, deflates “plurality of Gods” to the arithmetic of the Godhead. Nothing in the 1984 address contradicts the 1981 one — that is the point. The generative promise is retained in the vocabulary of increase while the cosmology that made it intelligible is set aside, and the two entries together are the clearest single-author sample of that separation in the dataset. Filed as an original with no citesId: the address quotes only Jacob 4:14 and Moses 1:39, neither of which is an entry here, and the verse is Packer's own.

title: Angel Abrea reads the King Follett Discourse: “the same as all Gods have done before you”
speaker: Angel Abrea
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: “Here, then, is eternal life—to know the only wise and true God; and you have got to learn how to be Gods yourselves, and to be kings and priests to God, the same as all Gods have done before you, namely, by going from one small degree to another, and from a small capacity to a great one; from grace to grace, from exaltation to exaltation, until you attain to the resurrection of the dead, and are able to dwell in everlasting burnings, and to sit in glory, as do those who sit enthroned in everlasting power. … “… [You] shall be heirs of God and joint heirs with Jesus Christ. What is it? To inherit the same power, the same glory and the same exaltation, until you arrive at the station of a God, and ascend the throne of eternal power, the same as those who have gone before.” (Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, sel. Joseph Fielding Smith, Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1938, pp. 346–47.)
quotes.note: The comparison-class clause is what earns the tag, twice over: "the same as all Gods have done before you" and "the same as those who have gone before." A plurality of Gods preceded us on this path — which is the backward claim, made in general conference in 1981. Referent is ambiguous and must stay so: Abrea nowhere applies the clause to the Father, and the deification half of the passage ("learn how to be Gods yourselves," "the station of a God") is theosis, which carries no tag of its own. Provenance caveat carried forward from kfd-1844-q2, and it bears on exactly this sentence: "the same as all Gods have done before you" is the Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith amalgam, and of the four contemporaneous witnesses only Clayton attests "as all Gods has done" at all — Bullock has the weaker "same as all have done" with no "Gods," and Richards and Woodruff record the deification injunction with no comparison clause. Abrea is reading the strongest available reconstruction, at second hand, from a 1938 compilation. The printed ellipses are as published; the bracketed "[You]" is the published text's.

quotes.excerpt: This incident made me think about what often happens in our own lives. I thought about the tremendous potential that exists in each one of us, potential that can direct us to eternal life. … How many times do we allow little “butterflies” to reduce, restrain, or restrict our immense potential from guiding us to exaltation?
quotes.note: The two sentences that bracket the quotation, kept because they are the whole of Abrea's use of it. The King Follett material is not exposited, defended, qualified, or returned to; it is the warrant for a motivational point about Sabbath observance, sacrament meeting attendance, sustaining leaders, and tithing. The rest of the talk is about butterflies on a radiator and a branch member named Jose. That is the finding — the strongest backward-facing text in the tradition passing through a 1981 general conference as an unremarked-upon preamble.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1981/1981-10-abrea-the-little-things-and-eternal-life.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the Joseph Smith block and its source citation were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, including the parenthetical Teachings citation. Official published text, so A, and still hosted on churchofjesuschrist.org, so current-correlated. Filed as a citation with a citesId edge to kfd-1844, per the rule that Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith is a citation of the four King Follett witnesses rather than an independent original — the entry's value is entirely that the passage is being read aloud, not what Abrea adds to it. Two contextual facts the timeline reader needs. First, the date: this is October 1981, sixteen months after Bruce R. McConkie's "Seven Deadly Heresies" (mcconkie-heresies-1980) and in the middle of the period when the dataset's correlated backward-explicit column is otherwise nearly empty — the material is not being taught, but it is still being quoted, from the published compilations, without comment. Second, the speaker: Abrea was the first Latin American General Authority, called to the First Quorum of the Seventy in 1981, and this is an early conference address; nothing about the setting marks the quotation as controversial or as requiring defense. Compare hunter-exalted-man-1948, where the same body of material is read aloud with full doctrinal intent, and note how much thinner the use has become in thirty-three years.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Doctrine of the Priesthood” — “spirit children in the resurrection”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, priesthood session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: In return the Lord covenants and promises to give them all that his Father hath, meaning eternal life, which is exaltation and godhood in that eternal realm where alone the family unit continues in eternity.
quotes.note: The D&C 84:38 formula (“all that my Father hath”) glossed as “exaltation and godhood,” with the family qualifier attached. Euphemism rather than explicit: “the family unit continues in eternity” says that something persists, not that anything new is begotten. This is the sentence that precedes q2, and the pair shows the two registers running back to back.

quotes.excerpt: In return the Lord admits them to his eternal patriarchal order, an order that prevails in the highest heaven of the celestial world, an order that assures its members of eternal increase, or in other words of spirit children in the resurrection. (See D&C 131:1–4.)
quotes.note: The most explicit statement of the forward claim in the modern general conference corpus, and it is explicit because McConkie glosses his own euphemism: “eternal increase, or in other words of spirit children in the resurrection.” That five-word gloss is what separates FORWARD-EXPLICIT from FORWARD-EUPHEMISM throughout this dataset, and it is exactly what is missing from packer-eternal-increase-1981-q2, from renlund-2020, and from the twenty-first-century curriculum. Note the setting: priesthood session, to men, framed as the return the Lord makes on the Melchizedek covenant — a promise of increase presented as contractual rather than speculative. The parenthetical scripture reference is the published text's.

quotes.excerpt: This doctrine is that God our Father is a glorified, a perfected, and an exalted being who has all might, all power, and all dominion, who knows all things and is infinite in all his attributes, and who lives in the family unit.
quotes.note: Denial, implied: “knows all things,” “infinite in all his attributes,” and “all dominion” leave nothing to be gained in either knowledge or kingdoms, which closes both halves of the distinction McConkie himself had drawn in 1980. Deliberately not tagged FATHER-BECAME-GOD. “Glorified,” “perfected,” and “exalted” are passive participles and do carry a whiff of attainment, and McConkie affirms the Father's past attainment elsewhere in his own writing — but this sentence states a present condition and no process, and reading attainment into it would be retrojection of exactly the kind the referent and Father-status rules exist to prevent.

quotes.excerpt: It is that we can enter an order of the priesthood named the new and everlasting covenant of marriage (see D&C 131:2), named also the patriarchal order, because of which order we can create for ourselves eternal family units of our own, patterned after the family of God our Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: The forward claim restated in the summary section, back in euphemism (“eternal family units of our own”) after the plain statement in q2 — the same speaker, the same address, twelve paragraphs apart. The closing clause is the symmetry observation and is recorded here rather than in the pills: if our eternal families are “patterned after the family of God our Heavenly Father,” then whatever we are promised is what he already has, which points backward. McConkie does not draw that inference and the entry does not tag it; the backward direction requires assertion, not symmetry (TAXONOMY trap 3).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1982/1982-04-mcconkie-the-doctrine-of-the-priesthood.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the openings of all four excerpted paragraphs were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim (the fetch tool truncates long quotations, so the tails were verified against the diffed vault text), along with the byline “Elder Bruce R. McConkie, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The most valuable single entry in the 1980s cluster, because one speaker performs both halves of the pattern in one address: the forward generative claim stated as explicitly as the tradition ever states it (q2), and the Father described in terms that foreclose his own progression (q3). No citesId — D&C 131 is cited twice but has no entry in this dataset, and D&C 132 is not quoted here. Referent is n/a at entry level per the spec rule: no quote makes a backward-direction claim, and the one sentence that gestures backward (q4) does so only by symmetry.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Seven Christs” — the Son advanced and progressed until he became like unto God
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: There is a God in heaven—a holy, exalted, perfected, and pure being who is the Father of us all. He is a Holy Man; he has a body of flesh and bones; and he is the Father of spirits.
quotes.note: Untagged, and recorded for the formula. “He is a Holy Man” is McConkie's fixed opening for the Father — it recurs verbatim in mcconkie-mystery-of-mormonism-1979-q1 and mcconkie-caravan-test-one-1984-q2 — and it derives from the Moses 6–7 title Man of Holiness. It is an anthropomorphic claim, not a biographical one: God is a man, not was once a mortal man, and no attainment is described. Neither Father-status category attaches without retrojection.

quotes.excerpt: The Lord Jesus Christ is the Firstborn. He came forth as the heir and offspring of the Father. Along with all his spirit brethren he was endowed with agency and subject to law. By obedience, by righteousness, through faith, over long ages and eons, this Firstborn of the Father, our Elder Brother, advanced and progressed until he became like unto God in power, in might, in dominion, and in intelligence. He became and was “the Lord Omnipotent who reigneth, who was, and is from all eternity to all eternity.” (Mosiah 3:5.)
quotes.note: Attainment stated without hedge, and the referent is the Son — hence FATHER-BECAME-GOD with referent son, the reading given to snow-couplet-q3 for the same reason: the category names the claim, the referent records who it is attached to. Everything the tradition's opponents object to in the Father's case is here affirmed of Christ in general conference: a spirit child among spirit brethren, subject to law, who over “long ages and eons” advanced and progressed until he became like God in intelligence. What is not claimed is mortality before this life — the progression described is premortal — so FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE does not attach. Note also the collision the paragraph does not notice: a being who “advanced and progressed until he became” omnipotent is then said, on Mosiah's authority, to have been omnipotent “from all eternity to all eternity.”

quotes.excerpt: Then it was that he, under the Father, became the Creator of worlds without number.
quotes.note: Worlds without number, and the temporal marker is the point: “Then it was” — the creatorship follows the progression described in q2 rather than preceding it. MANY-WORLDS takes no stance, being an explanatory framework rather than a position.

quotes.excerpt: Then it was that the Father ordained and established the plan of salvation—called the gospel of God—whereby all his spirit children, Christ included, would be able to gain mortal bodies, to live in a probationary estate, to die, to be raised in immortal glory, and, if true and faithful in all things, to gain the same glorious exaltation enjoyed by the Father himself.
quotes.note: Untagged — this is theosis, and theosis alone carries no category — but it is the sentence that completes the shape of the address, so it is recorded. Christ is placed inside the class (“all his spirit children, Christ included”) and the terminus for every member of that class is “the same glorious exaltation enjoyed by the Father himself.” Put beside q2, the address grants a completed progression to godhood for one spirit child and holds it out to all the others, in the same year the same apostle is describing the Father as knowing all things and infinite in all his attributes (mcconkie-doctrine-of-priesthood-1982-q3). The symmetry is real and belongs here rather than in the pills: nothing in the paragraph asserts anything about the Father's own past.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1982/1982-10-mcconkie-the-seven-christs.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the openings of all four excerpted paragraphs were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim (the fetch tool truncates long quotations, so the tails were verified against the diffed vault text), along with the byline “Elder Bruce R. McConkie, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Deliberately NOT tagged TRIPARTITE-FRAMEWORK, despite the screening pass having flagged it as tripartite staging: the framework tag is reserved for genuine intelligence → spirit → body sequences (see kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978-q1), and what is staged here is a career — spirit child, then progression, then creatorship, then mortal Messiah — not a series of ontological tiers. Referent is son at entry level, since the one attainment claim in the address is made of Christ. The entry's use to the timeline is comparative: McConkie is the central figure in the denial of the Father's ongoing progression, and he is also, six months after mcconkie-doctrine-of-priesthood-1982, the apostle who tells general conference that the Son advanced and progressed in intelligence over long ages until he became like God. The two positions are formally consistent — a completed progression is not an ongoing one — but the vocabulary he denies to the Father is the vocabulary he uses of the Son, and the dataset should let a reader see both without being told what to conclude.

title: Bruce R. McConkie: the keys Elias restored are “promises of eternal increase”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: The man Elias brings back “the gospel of Abraham,” the great Abrahamic covenant whereby the faithful receive promises of eternal increase, promises that through celestial marriage their eternal posterity shall be as numerous as the sands upon the seashore or as the stars in heaven for multitude.
quotes.note: Euphemism rather than explicit, on the same reading as richards-offspring-eternal-increase-1942 and stapley-increase-of-posterity-1955: “eternal posterity” names offspring and even quantifies them, but does not discriminate spirit children begotten hereafter from a sealed mortal posterity extended into eternity, and no mechanism is anywhere in view. What is distinctive is the location. This is not a sermon about exaltation — it is an inventory of restored priesthood keys, and eternal increase arrives as the definition of what one of them is for. The Abrahamic sand-and-stars promise is thereby transferred whole from lineage in mortality to posterity in eternity, in a single subordinate clause, with no argument offered.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1983/1983-04-mcconkie-the-keys-of-the-kingdom.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the sentence was independently re-fetched from the live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Kept to a single quote by design — this is a bare-formula appearance, entered because the dataset is comprehensive and because where a formula turns up matters as much as how often. Read against mcconkie-family-affair-1970, thirteen years earlier, where the same author gives the euphemism its mature form (“eternal family units patterned after his eternal family”), and against mcconkie-heresies-1980 three years earlier, where he polices what may and may not be said about God's progression. The vocabulary of increase is never among the things he restricts.

title: Barbara B. Smith: the hymn as “poetic statement to a great truth revealed through the Prophet Joseph Smith”
speaker: Barbara B. Smith
office: Relief Society General President
venue: General Women's Meeting, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: In the beloved Latter-day Saint hymn “O My Father,” Eliza R. Snow celebrates in words the continuity of family relationships beyond death and reminds us of a glorious reunion with our heavenly parents. Written as solace to a dear friend, Zina Huntington, who had lost her mother and father in tragic deaths, the well-known lines of this hymn give poetic statement to a great truth revealed through the Prophet Joseph Smith.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the warrant is the whole of its value. The hymn's content — a reunion with heavenly parents, plural — is called “a great truth revealed through the Prophet Joseph Smith”: not Snow's inference, not a poetic liberty Joseph declined to correct, but revelation with a named prophetic source. Set this beside hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q2, eight years later and to the same annual audience of women, where the identical tradition is restated in its weakest form (“It has been said that the Prophet Joseph Smith made no correction to what Sister Snow had written”) and then, at q5, placed outside revealed knowledge entirely. 1983 is the last unhedged statement of the strong warrant in this corpus before that reversal, and renlund-divine-nature-2022 will restore it thirty-nine years later.

quotes.excerpt: In just rendering compassionate service to a friend, Eliza R. Snow used her talents, responded to priesthood leadership, and gave memorable expression to revealed truth.
quotes.note: The claim restated two paragraphs later, which is what rules out reading the first as a loose compliment to a hymn. Snow is described as having given “memorable expression to revealed truth” — expression of something already revealed, her contribution being the words. Note also the frame Smith builds around it: the hymn is offered as an instance of four gifts God has given Latter-day Saint women, the first of which she names “revealed truth.”

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1983/1983-10-smith-a-season-for-strength.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting and returned the same wording. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved: the hymn supplies the occasion, but the proposition recorded here — that its content is revealed truth from Joseph Smith — is Smith's, and it is not in Eliza R. Snow. Provenance detail worth keeping: the address is by the Relief Society General President at the General Women's Meeting, the same annual meeting at which kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978 and, later, hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991 and renlund-divine-nature-2022 were delivered — nearly the whole modern Heavenly Mother record is spoken to women at this one meeting, which is itself a finding about where the doctrine was allowed to live.

title: Gene R. Cook closes with “O My Father”: “Tells me I’ve a mother there”
speaker: Gene R. Cook
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: O my Father, Thou that dwellest In the high and glorious place, When shall I regain thy presence, And again behold Thy face? In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason, truth eternal Tells me I’ve a mother there. When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? Then, at length, when I’ve completed All you sent me forth to do, With your mutual approbation Let me come [home] and dwell with you. (“O My Father,” Hymns, no. 139.)
quotes.note: The hymn's second, third, and fourth stanzas quoted as the peroration of a general conference address, with no gloss of any kind — Cook introduces them only as “these praises about home and family we will all sing” and says nothing about the Mother before or after. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER and affirming, on the ground that reading Eliza R. Snow's argument from the pulpit without qualification is an endorsement of it; but the affirmation is entirely borrowed, which is why the entry is filed as a citation rather than an original. The bracketed “[home]” is the published text's substitution for the hymn's “Let me come and dwell with you.” Verse line breaks are rendered here as spaces.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1984/1984-04-cook-home-and-family-a-divine-eternal-pattern.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; during drafting on 2026-08-10 the live page was re-fetched and each of the load-bearing lines — “In the heavens are parents single?”, “Tells me I've a mother there”, “Father, Mother, may I meet you”, “Let me come [home] and dwell with you” — plus the citation “(“O My Father,” Hymns, no. 139.)” was confirmed present and exact, along with the byline “Elder Gene R. Cook, Of the First Quorum of the Seventy.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Kept lean per the drafting charter, but two contextual facts earn recording. First, the body of the address is an extended imagined speech by the Father to his premortal children — several hundred words in the first person, on marriage, parenthood, family size, and priesthood — and no Mother appears anywhere in it; she enters only in the borrowed hymn at the very end. A talk whose entire conceit is a heavenly parent addressing his children manages to be a single-parent talk until the closing quotation. Second, the date places it in the six months between the two Packer entries (packer-eternal-increase-1981 and packer-parentage-1984, the latter six months later), during the stretch when the hymn was still doing the doctrinal work that renlund-divine-nature-2022 would eventually reassign to a Gospel Library page.

title: Boyd K. Packer, “The Pattern of Our Parentage” — plurality deflated to the Godhead
speaker: Boyd K. Packer
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: There is *one* God, the Father of all. This we accept as fundamental doctrine. There is only *one* Redeemer, Mediator, Savior. This we know. There is *one* Holy Ghost, a personage of spirit, who completes the Godhead. I have emphasized the word *one,* in each sentence, but I have used it three times. Three is plural.
quotes.note: The deflation, executed in five sentences. “Plurality of Gods” is redefined to mean the arithmetic of the Godhead — three persons — rather than a class of exalted beings or a succession of them. Asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: Anyone who believes and teaches of God the Father, and accepts the divinity of Christ, and of the Holy Ghost, teaches a plurality of Gods.
quotes.note: The conclusion the arithmetic was built for, and its rhetorical function: on this definition the distinctively Latter-day Saint plurality claim becomes something every trinitarian Christian already holds, and the doctrine is defended by being made unremarkable. Compare Rev. 1:6, which Packer cites in passing here and which the 2018 New Testament Student Manual will read in the older, stronger sense (see nt-manual-2018).

quotes.excerpt: The acceptance of this truth does not mean accepting the multiple gods of mythology nor the polytheism of the pagans, which was so roundly condemned by Isaiah and the other prophets.
quotes.note: The boundary drawn explicitly: whatever plurality means, it is not many gods. Delivered in a talk that opens by warning against “self-appointed spokesmen who scoff at what we believe and misrepresent what we teach,” which is the apologetic setting the reframe is answering.

quotes.excerpt: This doctrine is not at variance with the scriptures. Nevertheless, it is easy to understand why some Christians reject it, because it introduces the possibility that man may achieve Godhood.
quotes.note: Untagged, and instructive for that reason. Theosis is retained without apology in the same discourse in which plurality is deflated — nothing generative, no offspring, no chain, so no category applies. The pattern the entry documents is precisely this: the promise is kept and the cosmology around it is quietly emptied.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1984/1984-10-packer-the-pattern-of-our-parentage.md, which was diffed paragraph-by-paragraph against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page at a 1.0000 match. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Likely RETREAT-REFRAME and tagged as such, with the qualification that this is a reframe rather than a repudiation: Packer nowhere denies a plurality of exalted beings, he simply supplies a reading of “plurality of Gods” on which the phrase costs nothing. The pulpit sweep that surfaced it makes the surrounding fact available — explicit deification vocabulary (“become gods,” “gods yourselves”) appears in thirty-four talks before 1900 and six after, against a far larger twentieth-century corpus, while “become like God” rises steadily to peak in the 2010s–2020s. This talk is a legible instance of that substitution being performed deliberately in front of a general conference audience. Its structural ancestor is Orson Pratt in 1855, who also defused plurality by redefining what “God” refers to; the difference is that Pratt was constructing a metaphysics and Packer is managing an inheritance.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Caravan Moves On” — Test one: a Holy Man who knows all things
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: He is the Father of spirits with whom we dwelt before the foundations of the earth were laid. He is our Father in Heaven, who ordained and established a plan of salvation by which his spirit children might advance and progress and become like him.
quotes.note: Untagged. Premortal spirit parentage plus theosis, neither of which carries a category on its own; “spirit children” here means us, not offspring to be begotten. Recorded because it is the first of the three paragraphs that make up Test one and because the verb pair “advance and progress” is applied to us in the same breath in which the next paragraph but one denies the Father anything left to gain — the same words, opposite subjects.
