quotes.excerpt: He is a Holy Man, a personage of tabernacle, having a body of flesh and bones; and he created mortal man in his own image, “male and female created he them.” … He is a glorified and exalted being in whom all fulness and perfection dwell, who knows all things and has all power, all might, and all dominion.
quotes.note: Denial, implied, and stated as a test of orthodoxy rather than as a doctrinal argument: the reader is being told what he must believe in order to “gain the full blessings of the gospel in this life and inherit eternal life.” “All fulness and perfection,” “knows all things,” “all power, all might, and all dominion” close knowledge and dominion alike — again without the 1980 fireside's distinction between them. As at mcconkie-doctrine-of-priesthood-1982-q3, “glorified and exalted” is not tagged FATHER-BECAME-GOD: it describes a present condition, and the attainment reading would be supplied by the reader, not by McConkie. The ellipsis marks the elided Gen. 1:27 citation between the two paragraphs.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1984/1984-10-mcconkie-the-caravan-moves-on.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; both excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and confirmed exact, along with the byline “Elder Bruce R. McConkie, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The genre is what distinguishes this from the neighbouring McConkie entries: mcconkie-lord-god-restoration-1980 is a proclamation and mcconkie-mystery-of-mormonism-1979 is a creed for outsiders, but this is a catechism with a pass mark — ten questions “all of which must be answered correctly” — and the omniscience of the Father is question one. That is the strongest available form of the claim short of a First Presidency statement: not taught, but tested. The address is otherwise best known for its ninth test and its closing image, and for the sentence “No Latter-day Saint who is true and faithful in all things will ever pursue a course, or espouse a cause, or publish an article or book that weakens or destroys faith,” delivered three and a half years after the McConkie–England correspondence over precisely this doctrine — context that a reader of Test one should have, and which is recorded here rather than tagged. Referent is n/a at entry level per the spec rule: no quote makes a backward-direction claim.

title: Millet and McConkie: God's development “has brought him to the point at which he now presides”
speaker: Robert L. Millet and Joseph Fielding McConkie
office: Professors of Ancient Scripture, Brigham Young University
venue: The Life Beyond (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1986), 148–49

witnesses.scribe: David L. Paulsen and R. Dennis Fisher, FARMS Review 15/2 (2003), 429–30 n. 22
witnesses.note: Quotes the passage in full with page citation, and states its function: Millet and McConkie “argue for the same understanding of this attribute as do Bruce R. McConkie and Joseph Fielding Smith.”

witnesses.scribe: Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), n. 42
witnesses.note: Recorded as quoting the same passage to the same effect. The archive's scan of that issue is too badly OCR'd to re-collate, so England is listed as a witness rather than as a second verification. England's reproduction reads “to a point at which he now presides” against Paulsen and Fisher's “to the point”; the excerpt here follows Paulsen and Fisher, and the reading is not independently confirmed.

quotes.excerpt: Our Father's development and progression over an infinitely long period of time has brought him to the point at which he now presides as God Almighty, He who is omnipotent, omniscient, and, by means of his Holy Spirit, omnipresent: he has all power, all knowledge, and is, through the Light of Christ, in and through all things.
quotes.note: Denial, not affirmation. The verb is the tell: development “has brought him to the point at which he now presides,” and the payoff clause is “he has all power, all knowledge.” The progression is finished. Note also that “over an infinitely long period of time” is a claim about duration, not about a line of ancestors — the sentence contains no Father of God and no chain.

notes: The book itself is not in the collated corpus; the text was verified verbatim against Paulsen and Fisher's block quotation with page citation in the FARMS Review 15/2 (2003), 429–30 n. 22, where the note runs across the two printed pages. Recorded here because the sentence circulates as regress evidence when both scholarly sources that quote it read it as the opposite — a divine-progression denial, placing Millet and McConkie with Bruce R. McConkie and Joseph Fielding Smith against the Brigham Young–Woodruff–Roberts–Widtsoe side of the intra-LDS debate. Under this project's taxonomy it belongs outside category C entirely. Never-official: a Bookcraft trade book by two BYU religion faculty.

title: Ardeth G. Kapp reads a Heavenly Mother into the 1986 conference record — and names “our heavenly home and parents” in her own voice
speaker: Ardeth G. Kapp
office: Young Women General President
venue: General Women's Meeting, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: “They always say something must happen in your life so you want to change. Well, that something has happened. I still have a long way to go. I finally realized that my Father in Heaven is on my side, even though I have betrayed him in a way. I am trying awfully hard to get my life in order and do what is right. I am bound and determined to, no matter how long it takes—but it is so hard. I just wish of all things I could go up and give Heavenly Father and Heavenly Mother a big hug and tell them that I made it back.”
quotes.note: The caveat first, because it governs the reading: this is a letter from an unnamed young woman, read aloud by Kapp without comment on the Mother clause. Kapp does not author the sentence and does not gloss it. What the entry documents is therefore not an assertion by a general officer but a decision by one — to select this letter, read it into general conference, and publish it in the Ensign with the phrase intact. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER and graded at the entry's A rather than downgraded, because the datum is the reading, not the letter: the fact in evidence is that in October 1986 “Heavenly Father and Heavenly Mother” could be said from that pulpit in that form. Five years later hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991 will address a comparable audience to say that praying to her is not the pattern, and thereafter no comparable sentence appears in the women's sessions for a generation.

quotes.excerpt: You see, this brief time away from our heavenly home and parents is a time when we are given our agency for the purpose of being tried and tested in every way (see 2 Ne. 2:24–28).
quotes.note: Kapp in her own voice, and the reason the entry is not merely a record of quoted correspondence. “Our heavenly home and parents” is plural and unhedged, offered as the ordinary premise of the plan of salvation rather than as a claim requiring defense — the same casual register as the letter she has just read, from the officer rather than the correspondent. It asserts nothing beyond her existence and our origin with her; no mechanism, no generative claim, hence HEAVENLY-MOTHER alone.

notes: Quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1986/1986-10-kapp-a-time-for-hope.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline (“Ardeth G. Kapp, Young Women General President”) and both excerpts verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Useful chiefly as a dateable point on the pre-1991 side of the modern Heavenly Mother line, from the office that spoke to young women, and as a reminder that the doctrine's ordinary habitat in this period was pastoral rather than doctrinal — a letter about coming back, and a sentence about agency. The address never argues for a Mother in Heaven and never mentions eternal increase; the two sentences above are the whole of the axis-bearing content.

title: Adney Y. Komatsu reads Orson F. Whitney's “Father and Mother in heaven” into the April 1987 record
speaker: Adney Y. Komatsu
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt:
In closing, may I quote Orson F. Whitney, who said:

“No pain that we suffer, no trial that we experience is wasted. It ministers to our education, to the development of such qualities as patience, faith, fortitude and humility. All that we suffer and all that we endure, especially when we endure it patiently, builds up our characters, purifies our hearts, expands our souls, and makes us more tender and charitable, more worthy to be called the children of God … and it is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our Father and Mother in heaven” (in *Faith Precedes the Miracle,* p. 98).
quotes.note: Graded C rather than the entry's A for the same reason howard-hunter-whitney-1987-q1 is: Komatsu's own words are published official text, but the Whitney material is sourced to nothing except page 98 of Spencer W. Kimball's Faith Precedes the Miracle (1972), which itself prints the passage without a citation. The chain is Whitney (d. 1931) → Kimball's uncited paperback → the pulpit. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only: “more like our Father and Mother in heaven” is likeness, which is theosis, and asserts nothing generative. The ellipsis is printed in the published talk; the asterisks are its italics. Note the position — this is the address's closing paragraph, given the last word before the Savior's own.

quotes.excerpt: Elder James E. Talmage wrote, “No pang that is suffered by man or woman upon the earth will be without its compensating effect … if it be met with patience” (in Spencer W. Kimball, “Tragedy or Destiny,” *Faith Precedes the Miracle,* Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1972, p. 98).
quotes.note: Two paragraphs earlier, from the same page of the same book, and it settles how the Whitney passage got here. Komatsu is working from p. 98 of Faith Precedes the Miracle and lifting both of its quotations in order; the Heavenly Mother clause arrives as a passenger on a devotional page about adversity. Untagged — nothing here concerns a Mother — but it is the strongest available evidence that the transmission is mechanical rather than doctrinal.

notes:
Quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1987/1987-04-komatsu-looking-to-the-savior.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline (“Elder Adney Y. Komatsu, Of the First Quorum of the Seventy”) and the closing Whitney quotation with its parenthetical source verbatim. Official published text, so A at entry level, with the Whitney quotation graded C — see the quote note. Filed as an original rather than a citation for the reason given in howard-hunter-whitney-1987: the quoted source is not an entry in this dataset and a citesId edge would dangle, and whitney-father-and-mother-1907 is a different Whitney text making a different argument and must not be used as the target.

This entry supersedes a housekeeping decision recorded elsewhere. The notes on howard-hunter-whitney-1987 state that “the Komatsu and Marriott instances are recorded here rather than drafted as entries of their own”; that judgment should be revised when sources.json is next edited, because the Komatsu instances are dateable pulpit events of their own and this one is the nearer antecedent of Hunter's — April 1987, six months before Hunter's October 1987 address, from the same quorum, ending on the same clause.

The full lineage, for whoever maintains these entries: the identical Whitney passage, always closing on “our Father and Mother in heaven” and always sourced only to Faith Precedes the Miracle p. 98, is read in general conference by Komatsu in October 1979 (“After Much Tribulation Come the Blessings”), by Komatsu again here, by Howard W. Hunter six months later, by Neill F. Marriott in April 2016 (“What Shall We Do?”), and — this is the part worth verifying against the primary rather than repeating — by Brian K. Taylor in April 2024 (“Swallowed Up in the Joy of Christ”), where the closing clause is printed as “which will make us more like our [heavenly parents].” The bracket is the 2024 published text's own; the phrase “Father and Mother in heaven” has been replaced, in square brackets, with the correlated modern term. Taylor's version also trims the passage with four ellipses and inserts “[patiently].” Read against this entry it is a documented reframing of a fixed quotation across thirty-seven years, which is why the pair belongs in the corpus even though neither speaker is arguing about a Mother. Verified during drafting against the vault file talks/english/modern/2024/2024-04-taylor-swallowed-up-in-the-joy-of-christ.md, whose heavyweight pass also matched the live page at 1.0000. Taylor 2024 is not itself drafted here; it is outside this batch and should be entered separately, tagged RETREAT-REFRAME, when someone works that file.

title: Howard W. Hunter quotes Orson F. Whitney: “more like our Father and Mother in heaven”
speaker: Howard W. Hunter
office: Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session

quotes.excerpt: I share the view expressed by Orson F. Whitney in these words: “No pain that we suffer, no trial that we experience is wasted. It ministers to our education, to the development of such qualities as patience, faith, fortitude, and humility. All that we suffer and all that we endure, especially when we endure it patiently, builds up our characters, purifies our hearts, expands our souls, and makes us more tender and charitable, more worthy to be called the children of God … and it is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our Father and Mother in heaven” (as quoted in *Faith Precedes the Miracle,* p. 98).
quotes.note: Graded C rather than A on its own, and the reason is the attribution the talk gives. Hunter's own words are published official text; the Whitney material is not sourced to any Whitney publication but only to page 98 of Spencer W. Kimball's 1972 Faith Precedes the Miracle, which itself prints the passage without a citation. No conference address that uses it — and there are four — supplies a primary source, so the chain is Whitney (d. 1931) → Kimball's uncited book → the pulpit. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only: "more like our Father and Mother in heaven" is likeness, which is theosis, and asserts nothing generative — the same reading given to whitney-father-and-mother-1907-q1, which is a different Whitney text. The ellipsis is printed in the published talk, not an editorial cut; the asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: President Spencer W. Kimball, who knew a good deal about suffering, disappointment, and circumstances beyond his control, once wrote: “Being human, we would expel from our lives physical pain and mental anguish and assure ourselves of continual ease and comfort, but if we were to close the doors upon sorrow and distress, we might be excluding our greatest friends and benefactors. Suffering can make saints of people as they learn patience, long-suffering, and self-mastery” (*Faith Precedes the Miracle,* Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1972, p. 98).
quotes.note: Earlier in the same address, and from the same page of the same book. Kept because it shows the mechanism of transmission exactly: Hunter is working from a single page of a devotional paperback on adversity, and the Heavenly Mother clause arrives as a passenger on a quotation about suffering. Untagged — nothing here concerns a Mother.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1987/1987-10-hunter-the-opening-and-closing-of-doors.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-checked during drafting on 2026-08-10 and confirmed to load with the Whitney paragraph present and with the attribution reading "as quoted in Faith Precedes the Miracle, p. 98." Official published text, so A at entry level, with the Whitney quote graded C — see the quote note. Filed as an original despite being substantively a quotation, because the quoted source is not an entry in this dataset and a citesId edge would dangle: whitney-father-and-mother-1907 is Whitney's October 1907 conference address on Heavenly Mother as philosophy, a different text making a different argument, and it must not be used as the target here. What this entry actually documents is a quotation lineage, and the lineage is larger than it first appears. The identical Whitney passage, always with the "Father and Mother in heaven" clause and always sourced only to Faith Precedes the Miracle p. 98, is read in general conference by Adney Y. Komatsu in October 1979 ("After Much Tribulation Come the Blessings"), by Komatsu again in April 1987 ("Looking to the Savior"), by Hunter here six months later, and by Neill F. Marriott in April 2016 ("What Shall We Do?", footnote 5: "Orson F. Whitney, in Spencer W. Kimball, Faith Precedes the Miracle (1972), 98"). Marriott's version silently trims the passage with four ellipses but keeps the closing clause intact. Four conference appearances across thirty-seven years, none of them arguing for a Heavenly Mother and none of them able to cite Whitney directly — which is how the doctrine kept surfacing in official discourse during the decades when almost no one taught it: not as doctrine but as a fixed phrase inside a quotation about adversity. Per the drafting charter, the Komatsu and Marriott instances are recorded here rather than drafted as entries of their own. (Update: the April 1979 Komatsu instance is now its own entry, komatsu-father-and-mother-1979.)

title: Vaughn J. Featherstone: “carry a little one under her breast either in this life or in the eternal worlds”
speaker: Vaughn J. Featherstone
office: Of the First Quorum of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: Women are endowed with special traits and attributes that come trailing down through eternity from a divine mother. A young woman has special God-given feelings about charity, love, and obedience. Coarseness and vulgarity are contrary to their natures. They have a modifying, softening influence on young men. Young women were not foreordained to do what priesthood holders do. Theirs is a sacred, God-given role, and the traits they received from heavenly mother are equally as important as those given to the young men.
quotes.note: Twice in one paragraph, in his own voice, with no hedge and no citation: “a divine mother,” then “heavenly mother.” Stronger than the era's norm on one specific point — she is not merely affirmed to exist but assigned a causal role, as the source from which particular traits descend to particular living women. Note also what the argument is doing: the Mother is introduced to ground a claim about the differentiation of male and female roles, which is where nearly all modern Heavenly Mother language originates (compare maxwell-heavenly-mother-1978 and kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978, both arising from the decade's argument about women).

quotes.excerpt: Sometimes misguided women or men direct our youth away from their divinely appointed role. Worlds without end, men will never be able to bear children. Every young woman may be a procreator with God and carry a little one under her breast either in this life or in the eternal worlds. Motherhood is a wonderful, priceless blessing, no matter what all the world may say. Priesthood ordination is a blessing to men. There are serious consequences when either motherhood or priesthood is abused or laid aside.
quotes.note: The most physical statement of post-mortal childbearing in the modern conference corpus, and it is worth being precise about what it does and does not say. FORWARD-EXPLICIT is stated outright: childbearing is located “in the eternal worlds” as an alternative to this life, on the same construction johnson-2025 will use thirty-eight years later (“whether we are sealed and bear children in this life or the next”). SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS is marked implied, and the marker is doing real work — gestation is unmistakably in view (“carry a little one under her breast”), but Featherstone never says the offspring are spirits, so the viviparous reading is supplied by the reader from the mechanism rather than from the object. “A procreator with God” is his own phrase and is left unexplained; read strictly it makes God the partner in the act, which is not the Ballard-style physiology of ballard-increase but a looser devotional formula. Stance review flagged on the viviparous tag for that reason.

notes: Quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1987/1987-10-featherstone-a-champion-of-youth.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline (“Elder Vaughn J. Featherstone, Of the First Quorum of the Seventy”) and both paragraphs verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The context is worth recording because it is so unlike the doctrine: this is a Scouting-and-youth address, largely anecdotal, and the two paragraphs above arrive in the middle of praise for the Young Women presidency. Nothing prepares them and nothing follows from them. That is the pattern of the late twentieth century — the generative doctrine surfaces in conference as an aside inside an argument about women's roles, never as a topic. Same conference year as howard-hunter-whitney-1987 and komatsu-whitney-1987, which makes 1987 an unusually dense year on the Heavenly Mother axis and worth reading as a set. Still hosted on churchofjesuschrist.org as of drafting, which is the surprising fact about it.

title: Boyd K. Packer: spirit children of a Father God, of an existence that “could [not] have been” begun
speaker: Boyd K. Packer
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Truth: We are spirit children of a Father God. We lived with him in our premortal existence, of which it must be said that there was not, neither could there have been, a beginning. The revelations speak of things “from before the foundation of the world” and “before the world was” (see D&C 124:33–41).
quotes.note: Two clauses that most of the corpus keeps apart, welded into one item on a list headed “Truth.” Packer affirms spirit childhood of a Father God and, in the same sentence, forecloses any origin for the relationship — not merely that it had no beginning, but that “there was not, neither could there have been” one, a modal claim rather than a historical one. Read the way brown-uncreated-intelligences-1969 was read, an existence that could not have begun cannot have been begotten, which is why the tag sits on the organization side of the spirit-birth question rather than the viviparous side; read the way dunn-primal-self-1966 was read, the birth language survives and only the thing born has moved. The stance is recorded as hedges and flagged for review because Packer is not arguing the mechanism at all — he is establishing that the hearer's existence is unbounded in both directions so that a disabled body will read as a brief episode in it. What makes the sentence worth the entry is its register: this is stated as doctrinal “Truth” by an apostle, in the flat catechetical mood of the three-item list it belongs to.

quotes.excerpt: Every quarter of an inch of physical and mental improvement is worth striving for. The Prophet Joseph Smith said that “all the minds and spirits that God ever sent into the world are susceptible of enlargement” (*Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith,* sel. Joseph Fielding Smith [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1938], p. 354).
quotes.note: Untagged, and kept for the citation rather than the claim. TPJS p. 354 is King Follett material — the same printed page eom-premortal-life-1992 quotes for “a privilege to advance like himself” — so the King Follett Discourse is being read from the general conference pulpit in 1991, seven years after packer-parentage-1984 deflated plurality and four years before the Proclamation. What it is read for is the point: not theogony, not advancement toward godhood, but a pastoral assurance that impaired minds are enlargeable. Asterisks are the italics of the published text.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1991/1991-04-packer-the-moving-of-the-water.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting and returned the same content. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Markdown scripture links in the vault body are rendered here as the plain parenthetical citations of the published page. The address is about disability, not cosmology, which is exactly why the sentence is worth recording: the eternity of the hearer is deployed as consolation, and the doctrinal commitments come out flat and unguarded because nothing in the sermon depends on defending them. Filed as an original with a citesId edge to kfd-1844 for the TPJS quotation in q2. Read against packer-parentage-1984 by the same apostle seven years earlier, where plurality of Gods is redefined down to the Godhead: the deflation there and the unbounded premortal existence here are the same instinct — keep the promise, drop the machinery.

title: Gordon B. Hinckley, “Daughters of God” — the Mother affirmed and fenced
speaker: Gordon B. Hinckley
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General Women's Meeting, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: I am therefore on this occasion going to take the liberty of rereading that portion of the talk which pertains to a matter over which some few women of the Church appear to be greatly exercised. I give it to all, in this forum, because of the activities of a few who evidently are seeking to lead others in the paths which they are following. I speak of those who advocate the offering of prayers to our Mother in Heaven.
quotes.note: The occasion, stated. Everything that follows is Hinckley rereading his own April 1991 address to the regional representatives, verbatim and in quotation marks, to a general audience of women — so the boundary is being set twice, once in a training meeting and once, deliberately, in public. Provenance is still first-person and A: the inner quotation is the same speaker quoting himself from six months earlier, not a relay.

quotes.excerpt: “It was Eliza R. Snow who wrote the words: ‘Truth is reason; truth eternal / Tells me I’ve a mother there.’ (*Hymns,* 1985, no. 292.) “It has been said that the Prophet Joseph Smith made no correction to what Sister Snow had written. Therefore, we have a Mother in Heaven. Therefore, [some assume] that we may appropriately pray to her.
quotes.note: The hymn cited by author and hymnal number, and the traditional warrant for the doctrine restated in its weakest available form: not that Joseph revealed it, but that he did not correct it. Compare iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908, where the same doctrine is credited to “inspiration flowing first through the mind of the Prophet Joseph Smith.” Eighty-three years have converted a revelation claim into an argument from silence. The bracketed “[some assume]” is Hinckley's own interpolation as printed; asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: “Logic and reason would certainly suggest that if we have a Father in Heaven, we have a Mother in Heaven. That doctrine rests well with me.
quotes.note: The affirmation, and the ground it stands on. This is Erastus Snow's inference and Rudger Clawson's rhetorical question arriving intact in 1991 — logic and reason, not revelation and not scripture. “Rests well with me” is a personal endorsement rather than a doctrinal declaration, and the sentence is placed so that the concession precedes the restriction. See snow-heavenly-mother-1885 and clawson-mother-there-1929.

quotes.excerpt: “However, in light of the instruction we have received from the Lord Himself, I regard it as inappropriate for anyone in the Church to pray to our Mother in Heaven.… “I have looked in vain for any instance where any President of the Church, from Joseph Smith to Ezra Taft Benson, has offered a prayer to ‘our Mother in Heaven.’
quotes.note: The restriction, and the two arguments for it: the scriptural pattern of prayer to the Father, and an argument from the absence of precedent among Church presidents. Elision marks the omitted run of scriptural citations from Matthew 6 and 3 Nephi. Note what is not said — the doctrine is nowhere denied, and no claim is made that she does not exist or is not a person. What is fenced is practice.

quotes.excerpt: “I suppose those … who use this expression and who try to further its use are well-meaning, but they are misguided. The fact that we do not pray to our Mother in Heaven in no way belittles or denigrates her.” That is the end of the quotation from the talk I gave earlier, to which I may add that none of us can add to or diminish the glory of her of whom we have no revealed knowledge.
quotes.note: The closing sentence is the most consequential clause in the modern corpus on this subject: “her of whom we have no revealed knowledge.” The Mother is affirmed as real and simultaneously placed outside revelation altogether — which retroactively reclassifies the whole nineteenth- and early twentieth-century tradition, including Iverson's claim that the doctrine came by inspiration through Joseph Smith and Kimball's description of “O My Father” as a doctrinal hymn, as something other than revealed. The ellipsis in the first sentence is printed in the published text, not an editorial cut. Carries both tags: the reframe is executed and the doctrine is affirmed in the same breath, which is precisely the pattern the category exists to capture.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1991/1991-10-hinckley-daughters-of-god.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; three of the five excerpts were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting and returned verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved — the hymn is quoted and attributed, but the entry's substance is Hinckley's own ruling on what may be done with it. The pivotal modern boundary text, and its structure is worth stating plainly, because both critics and defenders routinely collapse it: the doctrine is affirmed (q3), the practice is prohibited (q4), the affirmation is then hollowed by the epistemic claim that nothing about her is revealed (q5). Nothing here repudiates Heavenly Mother, and nothing here leaves room for anyone to say much more about her. Read forward to essay-2015, which restates the doctrine while citing this address, and back to maxwell-heavenly-mother-1978, delivered to a comparable audience thirteen years earlier with no fence at all.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “God the Father: Overview”
speaker: Stephen E. Robinson
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:548–550

quotes.excerpt: This doctrine is stated concisely in a well-known couplet by President Lorenzo Snow: “As man now is, God once was: as God now is, man may be”… This principle is clearly demonstrated in the person of Jesus Christ, a God who became mortal, and yet a God like whom mortals may become… But the maxim is true of the Father as well. As the Prophet Joseph Smith said, “God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens! That is the great secret”… Thus, the Father became the Father at some time before “the beginning” as humans know it, by experiencing a mortality similar to that experienced on earth.
quotes.note: Both tags earned under the Father-status precedent: past mortality (“was once as we are now,” “by experiencing a mortality similar to that experienced on earth”) *and* attainment (“the Father became the Father at some time before ‘the beginning’”). Note the order of the argument — the couplet is first demonstrated on Christ, then extended to the Father by the word “also.” That is precisely the referent move the 2014 Gospel Topics essay would later exploit in the other direction; here in 1992 the extension to the Father is made explicit and without hedging. Elisions drop parenthetical scripture and TPJS citations only.

quotes.excerpt: There has been speculation among some Latter-day Saints on the implications of this doctrine, but nothing has been revealed to the Church about conditions before the “beginning” as mortals know it. The important points of the doctrine for Latter-day Saints are that Gods and humans are the same species of being, but at different stages of development in a divine continuum, and that the heavenly Father and Mother are the heavenly pattern, model, and example of what mortals can become through obedience to the gospel.
quotes.note: The 1992 snapshot's handling of the regress: it does not deny that the Father has a Father, it declares the prior conditions unrevealed and reclassifies the question as “speculation… on the implications.” Five years ahead of Hinckley's 1997 “I don't know that we teach it,” and the same shape of move — but note the difference: Robinson keeps the mortality claim itself (q1) fully intact and quarantines only what lies behind it.

quotes.excerpt: The Father, Elohim, is called the Father because he is the literal father of the spirits of mortals (Heb. 12:9). This paternity is not allegorical. All individual human spirits were begotten (not created from nothing or made) by the Father in a premortal state, where they lived and were nurtured by Heavenly Parents.
quotes.note: Tagged viviparous on the viviparous-versus-adoption axis: the article insists on literal begetting against creation ex nihilo (“This paternity is not allegorical”). It does not describe physiology — no gestation, no spirit-matter mechanics of the Pratt/Ballard kind — so the grade of explicitness is well below B4 in the working taxonomy.

quotes.excerpt: The Father existed prior to the Son and the Holy Ghost and is the source of their divinity. In classical terms, LDS theology is subordinationist; that is, it views the Son and the Holy Ghost as subordinate to and dependent upon God the Eternal Father. They are his offspring… The Son and the Holy Spirit were “in the beginning, with God,” but the Father alone existed before the beginning of the universe as it is known.
quotes.note: Context, not a category claim — but the tension is worth recording. One page before the article says the Father “became the Father,” it says he “alone existed before the beginning of the universe as it is known” and is “ultimately the source of all things.” Robinson never reconciles the two; the reconciliation is exactly what q2 declares unrevealed.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF pp. 126–128 = printed 2:548–550); the article is signed “Stephen E. Robinson” on p. 550. Small-capital cross-reference styling in the printed text has been normalized to ordinary case; wording is unaltered. On status: the Encyclopedia is the semi-official 1992 snapshot, not an official publication. Its own Preface (1:lxii, signed by editor in chief Daniel H. Ludlow) states that “The Encyclopedia of Mormonism is a joint product of Brigham Young University and Macmillan Publishing Company, and its contents do not necessarily represent the official position of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. In no sense does the Encyclopedia have the force and authority of scripture,” and that contributors' “statements and opinions remain their own.” At the same time the Acknowledgments (1:lxiii) record that the General Authorities designated BYU as the contractual Author, and that the First Presidency appointed Elders Neal A. Maxwell and Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve as advisers to the project — which is why correlationStatus is never-official but the entry should be read as an authorized-adjacent reference work rather than a private book.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Eternal Progression”
speaker: Lisa Ramsey Adams
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:465–466

quotes.excerpt: No official Church teaching attempts to specify all the ways in which God progresses in his exalted spheres; “there is no end to [His] works, neither to [His] words” (Moses 1:38). God's glory and power are enhanced as his children progress in glory and power (see Moses 1:39; Young, JD 10:5). Ideas have been advanced to explain how God might progress in knowledge and still be perfect and know all things (see Foreknowledge of God; Omnipotent God).
quotes.note: The agnosticism, verbatim, and it is carefully built. Three moves in three sentences: (1) presuppose that God progresses while declaring the manner unspecified by official teaching; (2) grant the safe, McConkie-compatible version — enlargement of glory and power through the progress of his children, i.e. dominions rather than knowledge; (3) acknowledge progression *in knowledge* as a live question — “Ideas have been advanced to explain how God might progress in knowledge and still be perfect” — and refuse to adjudicate it, routing the reader to two other articles instead. Twelve years after Bruce R. McConkie called progression in knowledge one of the seven deadly heresies (see mcconkie-heresies-1980), the standard reference work declines to follow him and leaves the D question open. The direction here is neither affirmation nor denial; the tag marks the question.

quotes.excerpt: At the Resurrection and Judgment, people will be assigned a degree of glory. Further progress is believed possible within each degree. Marriage and family life, however, continue only in the celestial kingdom, allowing “eternal increase” through having spirit children (see Eternal Lives, Eternal Increase).
quotes.note: Spirit children after this life, printed plainly and without euphemism in a general-audience reference work. Note also the flat statement that further progress is possible “within each degree” — the post-1917 Talmage line (see talmage-af-kingdom-excision-1917), inter-kingdom progression conspicuously not asserted.

quotes.excerpt: The principle of eternal progression cannot be precisely defined or comprehended, yet it is fundamental to the LDS worldview. The phrase “eternal progression” first occurs in the discourses of Brigham Young. It embodies many concepts taught by Joseph Smith, especially in his King Follett Discourse. It is based on the proposition that “there is no such thing as principle, power, wisdom, knowledge, life, position, or anything that can be imagined, that remains stationary—they must increase or decrease” (Young, JD 1:350).
quotes.note: Context for the genealogy the article draws for itself: Brigham Young for the phrase, the King Follett Discourse for the content. Worth recording that the article routes the reader to the King Follett Discourse by cross-reference and quotes none of it — the “God himself was once as we are now” material appears in this Encyclopedia under God the Father, not under Eternal Progression.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF pp. 43–44 = printed 2:465–466); signed “Lisa Ramsey Adams” on p. 466. Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. The article's sole bibliography item is John A. Widtsoe, “Is Progress Eternal or Is There Progress in Heaven?,” Improvement Era 54 (Mar. 1951):142, plus Evidences and Reconciliations — that is, the pro-progression side of the twentieth-century debate is the only authority cited, while the text itself stays neutral. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Mother in Heaven”
speaker: Elaine Anderson Cannon
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:961

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints infer from authoritative sources of scripture and modern prophecy that there is a Heavenly Mother as well as a Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: The article's opening sentence, and the verb is doing work: “infer.” Compare Lorenzo Snow in 1885 (snow-heavenly-mother-1885), “it is not said in so many words in the Scriptures… It is left for us to infer this.” A century on, the reference work uses the same epistemic register.

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints believe that all the people of earth who lived or will live are actual spiritual offspring of God the Eternal Father (Num. 16:22; Heb. 12:9). In this perspective, parenthood requires both father and mother, whether for the creation of spirits in the premortal life or of physical tabernacles on earth. A Heavenly Mother shares parenthood with the Heavenly Father. This concept leads Latter-day Saints to believe that she is like him in glory, perfection, compassion, wisdom, and holiness.
quotes.note: The argument for Heavenly Mother here is an argument from the mechanics of spirit birth: “parenthood requires both father and mother, whether for the creation of spirits in the premortal life or of physical tabernacles on earth.” That parity between spirit begetting and mortal begetting is the viviparous model, stated as a premise rather than defended.

quotes.excerpt: As early as 1839 the Prophet Joseph Smith taught the concept of an eternal mother, as reported in several accounts from that period. Out of his teaching came a hymn that Latter-day Saints learn, sing, quote, and cherish, “O My Father,” by Eliza R. Snow. President Wilford Woodruff called it a revelation (Woodruff, p. 62). In the heav'ns are parents single? No, the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there. When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? [Hymn no. 292]
quotes.note: The Encyclopedia prints both stanzas in full and grades the hymn's authority twice over — Joseph Smith as origin (“as early as 1839… as reported in several accounts”), Wilford Woodruff calling it a revelation. Line breaks in the printed hymn quotation are run together here; wording is unaltered.

quotes.excerpt: In 1909 the First Presidency, under Joseph F. Smith, issued a statement on the origin of man that teaches that “man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father,” as an “offspring of celestial parentage,” and further teaches that “all men and women are in the similitude of the universal Father and Mother, and are literally the sons and daughters of Deity”.
quotes.note: The 1909 First Presidency statement (fp-1909) carried into a 1992 reference work with the “begotten and born” language intact. Two of these three phrases are quoted again on the facing page under Motherhood (2:962) — the “begotten and born of heavenly parents” and “similitude of the universal Father and Mother” clauses, though not “offspring of celestial parentage” — so the Encyclopedia reproduces the core of the 1909 language twice.

quotes.excerpt: Belief that there is a Mother in Heaven who is a partner with God in creation and procreation is not the same as the heavy emphasis on Mariology in the Roman tradition.
quotes.note: “Procreation,” unhedged, in a Macmillan reference work aimed partly at non-Mormon readers. The sentence exists to distinguish the doctrine from Marian devotion, and in doing so states the doctrine more baldly than the disclaimer around it.

quotes.excerpt: Today the belief in a living Mother in Heaven is implicit in Latter-day Saint thought. Though the scriptures contain only hints, statements from Presidents of the Church over the years indicate that human beings have a Heavenly Mother as well as a Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: The closing paragraph, and the softest thing in the article: “implicit,” “only hints,” authority relocated from scripture to the accumulated statements of Presidents. Read against q2 and q5 in the same column, this is the article hedging its own confidence at the end rather than a change of doctrine.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF p. 539 = printed 2:961); signed “Elaine Anderson Cannon.” Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. The article's bibliography is two items: Linda P. Wilcox, “The Mormon Concept of a Mother in Heaven,” in Sisters in Spirit (Urbana, 1987), and Durham's Discourses of Wilford Woodruff — notable for citing Wilcox, a Dialogue-lineage feminist historian, in an official-adjacent reference work. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Premortal Life”
speaker: Gayle Oblad Brown
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 3:1123–1125

quotes.excerpt: There is indeed indication that the intelligence dwelling in each person is coeternal with God. It always existed and never was created or made (D&C 93:29). In due time that intelligence was given a spirit body, becoming the spirit child of God the Eternal Father and his beloved companion, the Mother in Heaven. This spirit, inhabited by the eternal intelligence, took the form of its creators and is in their image (Ballard, p. 140).
quotes.note: The cleanest tripartite statement in the 1992 Encyclopedia: uncreated coeternal intelligence → spirit body begotten by Heavenly Parents → mortal body. It is sourced not to scripture but to Melvin J. Ballard's collected sermons (see ballard-increase), which is where the viviparous physiology lives; the Encyclopedia takes the structure and leaves the mechanics behind the citation.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph Smith taught that “God himself, finding he was in the midst of spirits and glory, because he was more intelligent, saw proper to institute laws whereby the rest [of the intelligences] could have a privilege to advance like himself” (TPJS, p. 354). His plan included sending his sons and daughters to earth (the second estate), to obtain a body of flesh and bones and learn by experience through earthly vicissitudes, with no memory of the first estate and with the agency to fail or succeed.
quotes.note: King Follett material (TPJS p. 354) quoted verbatim, but only the half that runs forward: intelligences advancing to be like God. The neighbouring King Follett claim — that God himself was once as we are — is absent from this article and appears in this Encyclopedia only under God the Father. “Advance like himself” is left unglossed, hence euphemism rather than explicit.

quotes.excerpt: Thus, to Latter-day Saints premortal life is characterized by individuality, agency, intelligence, and opportunity for eternal progression. It is a central doctrine of the theology of the Church and provides understanding to the age-old question “Whence cometh man?”
quotes.note: Context — the article's closing summary. Recorded because the framing question it answers is the backward one (“Whence cometh man?”), answered entirely at the level of human origin and never extended to the origin of the Father.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 3 (PDF pp. 153–155 = printed 3:1123–1125); signed “Gayle Oblad Brown” on p. 1125. Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. Drafted in place of the “Pre-existence” heading named in the charter: the Encyclopedia's PRE-EXISTENCE (PRE-EARTHLY EXISTENCE) heading at 3:1123 is not an article at all but a bracketed index note listing the articles that treat the subject, so it carries no claims of its own; Premortal Life is the substantive article behind it. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Spirit Body”
speaker: Wilson K. Andersen
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 3:1405–1406

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints believe that each person was born in premortal life as a spirit son or daughter of God. The spirit joins with a physical body in the process of birth on the earth. At death the spirit and the body separate until they reunite in the resurrection.
quotes.note: Birth language (“was born in premortal life”) with no parentage beyond “of God” — this short article never mentions a Mother in Heaven, and never says who bore the spirit. Contrast the immediately preceding article, Spirit (Jay E. Jensen, 3:1404): “human spirits are the literal offspring of perfected, exalted parents, a Father and a mother in heaven.” Two adjacent columns of the same reference work, one explicit and one silent.

quotes.excerpt: Latter-day Saints believe that “all spirit is matter,” but this matter is so fine that it cannot be discerned by mortal eyes (D&C 131: 7-8). The Doctrine and Covenants explains that “the spirit of man [is] in the likeness of his person, as also the spirit of the beast; and every other creature which God has created” (D&C 77:2).
quotes.note: Context — the materialist premise the viviparous model rests on. Recorded because the 1992 article keeps spirit-as-refined-matter while dropping every trace of the nineteenth-century physiology built on it.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 3 (PDF pp. 435–436 = printed 3:1405–1406); signed “Wilson K. Andersen” on p. 1406. Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. This is a thin entry by design — the Spirit Body article is roughly one column and makes only the one category claim — but it is worth holding for the contrast with the Spirit and Premortal Life articles noted on q1. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, “Eternal Lives, Eternal Increase”
speaker: Shirley S. Ricks
office: Signed contributor, Encyclopedia of Mormonism (Brigham Young University / Macmillan)
venue: Encyclopedia of Mormonism, ed. Daniel H. Ludlow (New York: Macmillan, 1992), 2:465

quotes.excerpt: “Eternal lives” is a term that refers to the right and power to beget children after the resurrection, granted to those who are exalted in the highest degree of the celestial kingdom. This is an aspect of eternal progression.
quotes.note: The opening definition, and about as explicit as the forward direction ever gets in print: “the right and power to beget children after the resurrection.” No euphemism, no “eternal increase” shorthand — the mechanism is named in the first clause of the article.

quotes.excerpt: Except a man and his wife enter into an everlasting covenant and be married for eternity, while in this probation, by the power and authority of the Holy Priesthood, they will cease to increase when they die; that is, they will not have any children after the resurrection. But those who are married by the power and authority of the priesthood in this life, and continue without committing the sin against the Holy Ghost, will continue to increase and have children in the celestial glory.
quotes.note: Joseph Smith at Ramus, Illinois, 16–17 May 1843, quoted by the Encyclopedia from TPJS, pp. 300–301 — the doctrinal root of D&C 131. Note it is the negative form that carries the force: those not sealed “will not have any children after the resurrection.”

quotes.excerpt: In 1864 he elaborated: “In like manner, every faithful son of God, becomes, as it were, Adam to the race that springs from his loins, when they are embraced in the covenants and blessings of the Holy Priesthood… in the progress of eternal lives.… We have not yet received our kingdoms, neither will we, until we have finished our work on the earth, passed through the ordeals, are brought up by the power of the resurrection, and are crowned with glory and eternal lives” (JD 10:355).
quotes.note: Brigham Young's forward chain quoted at length in 1992: each exalted man becomes “Adam to the race that springs from his loins,” each with his own kingdom. Not tagged MANY-WORLDS: the passage distributes kingdoms across every faithful son, which implies a plurality of peopled dominions, but it never says “worlds” — the inference belongs here rather than in the pills. Read with the Adam-God material (young-adam-god-chain-1854) this is the surviving, sanitized half of that framework.

notes: Verified by reading the printed article in the Gospel Scholar Archive scan of Encyclopedia of Mormonism vol. 2 (PDF p. 43 = printed 2:465); signed “Shirley S. Ricks.” Small-capital cross-reference styling normalized to ordinary case; wording unaltered. Not among the articles named in the drafting charter, but included because the Encyclopedia gives the timeline's own subject its own signed heading and states the forward claim more explicitly than any of the charter articles do — the maintainer should drop it if the scope was meant to be strictly the four named entries. On status: never-official; see the Preface disclaimer quoted in the notes to eom-god-the-father-1992.

title: Russell M. Nelson, “Constancy amid Change” — unchangeableness as constant number one
speaker: Russell M. Nelson
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Our Heavenly Father has a glorified body of flesh and bone, inseparably connected with His spirit. Scriptures state that He is “infinite and eternal, from everlasting to everlasting the same unchangeable God” (D&C 20:17).
quotes.note: The weak form of the denial, and the stance is flagged for review because the weak form is genuinely contestable. D&C 20:17 is quoted, not glossed, and immutability of character is compatible with progression in dominions on McConkie's own 1980 distinction — so a reviewer could reasonably read this as no stance at all. It is recorded as a denial because of the use Nelson puts it to: the sentence is the opening of an address whose thesis is that certain things do not change, and God's unchangeableness is listed first among them. Marked implied throughout. Compare mcconkie-lord-god-restoration-1980-q3, which quotes the same verse to the same end and adds omniscience to it explicitly. Superscript footnote markers (2 and 3 in the published text) are elided from the excerpt.

quotes.excerpt: Unchanging principles are so because they come from our unchanging Heavenly Father. Try as they might, no parliament or congress could ever repeal the law of earth’s gravity or amend the Ten Commandments. Those laws are constant.
quotes.note: The thesis sentence, and the direction of the inference is what to notice: the Father's unchangeableness is the premise, and the fixity of moral law is the conclusion drawn from it. That makes divine immutability load-bearing for an argument about the Church's position on contested moral questions in 1993 — the year of the September Six — rather than a claim about eternal progression at all. Tagged and flagged on the same reasoning as q1: the entailment is real, the topic is not raised, and a reviewer may prefer no stance.

quotes.excerpt: “If a man marry a wife by my word, which is my law, and by the new and everlasting covenant, and it is sealed unto them … [they] shall inherit thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, dominions, … exaltation and glory in all things, … which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever” (D&C 132:19). A promise like that is worth your personal effort and endurance.
quotes.note: D&C 132:19 quoted at length to a general conference audience, and Nelson adds no gloss whatsoever — the only comment is “A promise like that is worth your personal effort and endurance.” “A continuation of the seeds forever and ever” is the canonical euphemism for eternal increase and is tagged FORWARD-EUPHEMISM here to match dc-132-q1, which reads the same clause the same way and likewise records the stance as hedges. The three ellipses are Nelson's own, printed in the published text; the bracketed “[they]” is his too. The paragraph appears under the heading “Family,” at the end of a list that runs priesthood, moral law, judgment, tithing, truth, family — the increase promise arriving as the closing sweetener of a talk about constancy.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1993/1993-10-nelson-constancy-amid-change.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently confirmed against that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10, along with the byline “Elder Russell M. Nelson, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Two flagged stances on one entry is unusual and deliberate: this is the weak-form immutability affirmation, and the dataset needs it recorded without pretending it is mcconkie-heresies-1980. What makes it worth including at all is the position of the speaker in the later corpus — Nelson becomes President of the Church in 2018 — and the pairing inside the address itself, which affirms an unchanging Father in section I and quotes “a continuation of the seeds forever and ever” in section III without either passage acknowledging the other. Filed as an original with a citesId edge to dc-132, earned by the quotation in q3. The square-bracketed “[D&C 132:19]” in q3 renders the published text's inline scripture reference, which the source page carries as a hyperlink.

title: Boyd K. Packer, “For Time and All Eternity” — the two-keys parable and a treasure never diminished
speaker: Boyd K. Packer
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Dear brethren and sisters, the scriptures and the teachings of the Apostles and prophets speak of us in premortal life as sons and daughters, spirit children of God. Gender existed before, and did not begin at mortal birth.
quotes.note: Untagged, and kept as the frame the parable depends on. “Spirit children of God” means us; the published footnote for the second sentence cites D&C 132:63 and the 1909 First Presidency statement “The Origin of Man” (fp-1909), which is the source of the entry's only citesId edge. Nothing generative is claimed here — this is premortal parentage and the eternity of sex, not eternal increase. Superscript footnote markers (1 and 2 in the published text) are elided from the excerpt.

quotes.excerpt: Once a man received as his inheritance two keys. The first key, he was told, would open a vault which he must protect at all cost. The second key was to a safe within the vault which contained a priceless treasure. … He was promised that if he used the treasure worthily, it would be replenished and never be diminished, not in all eternity.
quotes.note: The parable's central promise, and the tag depends entirely on an identification the text never makes explicit. Read in the setting of the address — an hour on gender, marriage, procreation, and the First Presidency's 1942 message on begetting children — the treasure that only a man's key and a woman's key together can unlock is the joint procreative power, and a power “replenished and never … diminished, not in all eternity” is eternal increase under a different figure. Marked implied and flagged for review on exactly that ground: a reviewer who declines the identification should read the quote as an allegory about chastity and downgrade the entry. Stance is hedges, not affirms, because a parable withholds the claim it carries. The ellipsis marks the elided warning about those who would rob him of his inheritance.

quotes.excerpt: With great joy they found that they could pass the treasure on to their children; each could receive a full measure, undiminished to the last generation.
quotes.note: The forward chain in figure. If the identification in q2 holds, this sentence distributes the same undiminished power down the generations without limit — the shape of B3, the forward chain, arriving in a general conference in 1993 as a bedtime story. “To the last generation” is the one phrase that resists a purely chastity-focused reading: a caution about misusing sex does not need a claim about what every descendant inherits in full measure. Flagged with q2 and standing or falling with it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1993/1993-10-packer-for-time-and-all-eternity.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all three excerpts were independently confirmed against that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10, along with the byline “Elder Boyd K. Packer, Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The weakest entry in this batch and marked as such: two of its three quotes are flagged for stance review, and the tagging rests on identifying the parable's treasure with the procreative power. A reviewer may reasonably rule the entry REDUNDANT against packer-eternal-increase-1981, which states in three words (“eternal increase!”) what this address encodes in a parable. It is drafted rather than dropped because the encoding is itself the datum: the same apostle who named the doctrine plainly in 1981 renders it twelve years later as an allegory of keys, locks, and an inheritance, in an address delivered a month before the September 1993 disciplinary actions and two years before the Family Proclamation (proclamation-1995). Compare packer-parentage-1984 for the same author performing the same operation on a different doctrine. Filed as an original with a citesId edge to fp-1909, cited in published footnote 2; footnote 37 relays the October 1942 First Presidency message at length, but that document has no entry here and no edge is drawn to it.

title: Dallin H. Oaks, “Apostasy and Restoration” — “Our theology begins with heavenly parents”
speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Those who have met the highest requirements for this kingdom, including faithfulness to covenants made in a temple of God and marriage for eternity, will be exalted to the godlike state referred to as the “fulness” of the Father or eternal life (D&C 76:56, 94; see also D&C 131; 132:19–20). (This destiny of eternal life or God’s life should be familiar to all who have studied the ancient Christian doctrine of and belief in deification or apotheosis.) For us, eternal life is not a mystical union with an incomprehensible spirit-god. Eternal life is family life with a loving Father in Heaven and with our progenitors and our posterity.
quotes.note: Deification named in the patristic vocabulary — “the ancient Christian doctrine of and belief in deification or apotheosis” — and then immediately domesticated into family life. The tag rests on the last sentence: eternal life as family life extending in both directions, “with our progenitors and our posterity,” which is the increase claim in kinship terms and nothing more explicit. D&C 132:19–20 is cited by reference in support and never quoted or glossed, which is the pattern the charter asks to be recorded: the verse that supplies “a continuation of the seeds forever and ever” is doing silent work behind a sentence about family. The parenthetical is the published text's, not an editorial insertion.

quotes.excerpt: This is a family-centered church in doctrine and practices. Our understanding of the nature and purpose of God the Eternal Father explains our destiny and our relationship in his eternal family. Our theology begins with heavenly parents. Our highest aspiration is to be like them.
quotes.note: The most quoted sentence pair on this subject in the modern corpus, and the reason to have the original in the dataset rather than only its later relays. Note three things about it in situ. First, it is a claim about foundations — not that we have heavenly parents but that the theology *begins* there, which makes plural parentage the first premise rather than a devotional extra. Second, the parents are plural and the Mother is never named, described, or defended anywhere in the address; the preceding sentence is about “God the Eternal Father” alone. Third, the second sentence is theosis with the plural pronoun — “to be like them” — which is as close as the address comes to making the Mother a term in the exaltation promise. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER and affirming on the same ground as renlund-divine-nature-2022-q1, which quotes exactly this pair twenty-seven years later.

quotes.excerpt: As earthly parents we participate in the gospel plan by providing mortal bodies for the spirit children of God. The fulness of eternal salvation is a family matter.
quotes.note: Untagged, and recorded for the semantics. “The spirit children of God” means us again — mortal parents supply bodies to spirits God already has — which is the closing sentence of the same paragraph as q2 and confirms that nothing in this address is a claim about begetting spirit children in the resurrection. The forward direction here is entirely a claim about kinship persisting, not about generation continuing.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1995/1995-04-oaks-apostasy-and-restoration.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; all four load-bearing sentences were independently re-fetched from that live page during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned verbatim, along with the byline “Elder Dallin H. Oaks, Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.” Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. This is the source of the sentence pair that renlund-divine-nature-2022-q1 quotes and that footnote 8 of that address cites as “Dallin H. Oaks, ‘Apostasy and Restoration,’ Ensign, May 1995, 87” — the dataset previously carried the relay without the original, and this entry closes that gap. Two dating facts belong on the record. First, this is five months before the Family Proclamation (proclamation-1995), which the address anticipates in its closing paragraph almost verbatim in theme but which contains no comparable statement about heavenly parents being where the theology begins. Second, the whole address is an apologetic against the creeds and the Nicene settlement, which is the setting in which the plural-parents claim is made: the doctrine surfaces here not as speculation but as the Restoration's answer to “without body, parts, or passions.” The apotheosis parenthetical in q1 is the earliest general-conference appearance in this dataset of the patristic-deification argument that essay-2014 would later build out at length. Filed as an original with a citesId edge to dc-132 for the D&C 132:19–20 reference in q1; no edge to D&C 76 or 131, neither of which has an entry here.

title: Robert D. Hales, “The Eternal Family” — eternal increase written into the definition of eternal life
speaker: Robert D. Hales
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, October 1996 (Ensign, Nov. 1996)

quotes.excerpt: The doctrine of the family begins with heavenly parents. Our highest aspiration is to be like them.
quotes.note: Plural heavenly parents named as the starting point of family doctrine, one year after the Proclamation. The formula Oaks repeats verbatim in October 2013 (“Our theology begins with heavenly parents”) — see oaks-no-other-gods-2013. Hales immediately glosses it with Hebrews 12:9, “God is the father of our spirits,” so the Mother is present only in the plural noun and is never returned to.

quotes.excerpt: Depending on our individual obedience to the laws, ordinances, and commandments of God, each mortal can have the blessing of attaining eternal life; that is, returning to live in the presence of their Heavenly Father and His Son, Jesus Christ, having eternal increase for all the eternities to come.
quotes.note: A definitional move rather than a promise listed alongside others: the “that is” makes eternal increase part of what eternal life *means*. What increases is never said, and the sentence is not developed anywhere else in the talk, so the register stays euphemism.

quotes.excerpt: “And again, verily I say unto you, if a man marry a wife by my word, which is my law, and by the new and everlasting covenant, and it is sealed unto them by the Holy Spirit of promise … they shall pass by the angels, and the gods, which are set there, to their exaltation and glory in all things, as hath been sealed upon their heads, which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever” (D&C 132:19).
quotes.note: Unglossed scripture. Hales reads D&C 132:19 in full as the answer to his own question — “What is the promise of these sealings which are performed in the temples?” — and adds no interpretation of “a continuation of the seeds”; the next paragraph turns to how we conduct ourselves in this life. Elision marks the omitted middle of the verse (the resurrection and Lamb's Book of Life clauses), which he also read.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the hosted talk on churchofjesuschrist.org; the Pulpit Vault transcript of the same address was previously diffed against that page at a 1.0000 match ratio. Filed as an original for the q2 gloss, which is Hales's own sentence, with citation edges to the two texts he reads aloud (the 1995 Proclamation and D&C 132:19).

title: Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Brigham Young, ch. 4, “Knowing and Honoring the Godhead”
speaker: Church Curriculum Department, quoting Brigham Young
office: Correlated priesthood/Relief Society manual
venue: Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Brigham Young (1997), 28–35

quotes.excerpt: The doctrine that God was once a man and has progressed to become a God is unique to this Church. How do you feel, knowing that God, through His own experience, “knows all that we know regarding the toils [and] sufferings” of mortality?
quotes.note: The manual's own editorial voice, in the “Suggestions for Study” section — not a Brigham Young quotation. Two things worth separating: it asserts God's past mortality (BACKWARD-MORTALITY under the taxonomy's first conflation trap — this is not a claim that God has a Father, and not a claim of ongoing progression), and it frames that doctrine as a distinctive the reader should feel good about, which is a register the later material abandons.

quotes.excerpt: Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause of all things; but it would be as easy for an ant to number the grains of sand on the earth. It is not for man, with his limited intelligence, to grasp eternity in his comprehension. … What then, should be the calling and duty of the children of men? Instead of inquiring after the origin of Gods—instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be, instead of endeavoring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess. Let them seek to know and thoroughly understand things within their reach, and to make themselves well acquainted with the object of their being here, by diligently seeking unto a super-power for information and by the careful study of the best books.
quotes.note: Excerpted in the manual and sourced there to DBY, 25 (Widtsoe's Discourses of Brigham Young compilation), not to the Journal of Discourses directly. The manual retains the “Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause” sentences that open the passage in the sermon, printing them in the same paragraph immediately before the quoted material; it was this entry's excerpt that dropped them, and they are restored above. Its wording differs slightly from the JoD text logged at young-origin-caution-1859 — “the origin of Gods” rather than “the origin of the Gods,” and a comma where the sermon has a dash — which is characteristic of the DBY compilation as intermediary.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live chapter; the manual does carry the origin-of-the-Gods caution, so this is filed as a citation of young-origin-caution-1859 as charter'd. The chapter is the pairing itself: within one lesson the manual proudly names God's past mortality as a doctrine unique to the Restoration, and hands the reader Brigham Young telling them not to inquire after where the Gods came from. That is the modern settlement in miniature, printed in 1997 — affirm the past-mortality datum, decline the genealogy — and it is worth noting that the decline is voiced by the same president who elsewhere pressed the chain hardest (see by-chain, delivered the day before the caution in the same 1859 conference). Hearsay A as a correlated manual; the Young material inside it is C-tier at origin (Watt shorthand) and passes through a second compiler before reaching this page.

title: L. Tom Perry reads Spencer W. Kimball into conference: godhood, worlds, and “a total knowledge of the sciences”
speaker: L. Tom Perry
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Peter and John had little secular learning, being termed ignorant. But they knew the vital things of life, that God lives and that the crucified, resurrected Lord is the Son of God. They knew the path to eternal life. This they learned in a few decades of their mortal life. Their righteous lives opened the door to godhood for them and creation of worlds with eternal increase.
quotes.note: Kimball's sentence, read aloud by an apostle in general conference. MANY-WORLDS on the same reading as kimball-create-worlds-1968, where the same speaker made world-making the unargued premise of an argument about study; here it is joined to increase in a single clause. FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than explicit because “eternal increase” is once again left to carry itself — worlds are named, godhood is named, offspring are not, and nothing states who or what populates the worlds. What is unusual is the referent: the promise is made of two named New Testament apostles, so the forward chain is attached to identifiable persons rather than to the generic faithful, which is closer to the nineteenth-century register than to anything else in the 1990s corpus. The excerpt sits inside Perry's block quotation of Kimball; the opening quotation mark of that block is trimmed rather than left unpaired.

quotes.excerpt: For this they would probably need, eventually, a total knowledge of the sciences. But whereas Peter and John had only decades to learn and do the spiritual, they have already had nineteen centuries in which to learn the secular or the geology of the earth, the zoology and physiology and psychology of the creatures of the earth.
quotes.note: Marked implied and flagged for review, because the sentence bears on the progression question without being about God. Kimball's subject is two men who are through the door to godhood and are, on his account, still nineteen centuries into acquiring the secular knowledge their work will require — an ongoing acquisition of knowledge by beings on the divine side of the transition. Read one way that affirms the proposition mcconkie-heresies-1980 called heresy one; read the other way it denies it, since total knowledge is presented as a prerequisite of the work rather than as something a god goes on lacking. The hedge is in Kimball's own adverbs — “probably,” “eventually” — and the entry does not resolve what he left unresolved. The datum is that a sitting apostle read it into general conference in 1997, sixteen years after the fireside.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1997/1997-10-perry-receive-truth.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the quotation was independently re-fetched from the live page during drafting and returned verbatim, including its source line. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Provenance of the inner quotation, which is the entry's whole substance: Perry is reading Spencer W. Kimball as printed in President Kimball Speaks Out (Deseret Book, 1981), 91 — a published Kimball text, so the relay does not degrade the grade, but the words are Kimball's and the act is Perry's. Filed as an original rather than a citation only because the underlying Kimball text has no entry in this dataset to point citesId at; if one is ever added, this should be retyped as a citation. The setting is worth recording because it is so mismatched to the content: the address is an appeal to teenagers to enrol in seminary and institute, and the godhood-and-worlds passage is the authority for why secular study matters. It is the twentieth century's most concrete statement of what exaltation involves, deployed as an argument for showing up at 6:30 a.m.

title: Joseph Fielding McConkie: God obtained his exalted status “by obedience to the laws of his own eternal Father”
speaker: Joseph Fielding McConkie
