One year after essay-2015 and hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991's fence had been standing for twenty-five years, a counselor in the First Presidency states the plural from the main Saturday-morning pulpit rather than the women's meeting, with an exclamation mark and no qualification — and still adds nothing about her. That combination, maximal confidence and zero content, is the modern settlement in one sentence.

title: Doctrine and Covenants Student Manual (2017), ch. 51 on D&C 131; 132:1–33
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Institute curriculum (correlated)
venue: Doctrine and Covenants Student Manual (2017), “Chapter 51: Doctrine and Covenants 131; 132:1–33”

quotes.excerpt: One of the blessings of becoming like God is the ability to have children in the eternities.
quotes.note: Under the commentary heading for Doctrine and Covenants 132:20, “Then shall they be gods, because they have no end.” The manual's own editorial voice, not a quotation of a leader. This is the sentence that closes the syllogism gospel-principles-2011 leaves open: becoming like God is stated to include having children.

quotes.excerpt: The phrase “continuation of the lives” means more than the promise of resurrection. It refers to the ability of those who obtain exaltation to create their own eternal families through bearing and rearing spirit children.
quotes.note: Under the commentary heading for Doctrine and Covenants 132:21–25, “This is eternal lives.” Also the manual's own editorial voice. Both nouns are present — “spirit children” — and the manual explicitly forecloses the deflationary reading it anticipates (“means more than the promise of resurrection”), which is the rare case of correlated print ruling a softer interpretation out rather than leaving room for it. No mechanism is described, so no viviparous tag: “bearing and rearing” is left unexplicated.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live chapter, both sentences and both section headings. The strongest forward-explicit statement in current institute curriculum, and the one that most complicates a simple taper narrative: it is editorial 21st-century prose, not a preserved 19th-century quotation, and it is hosted now. Read alongside seminary-2025 it sets the shape of the actual finding — the proposition survives in the manual an adult scripture student reads and disappears from the manual a sixteen-year-old's teacher reads. Note the citation direction: the explicitness is supplied by the curriculum, not by D&C 132, which this dataset rates as euphemism; same pattern as seminary-2014.

title: Dallin H. Oaks, “The Godhead and the Plan of Salvation” — the Father's nature, without His origin
speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, April 2017, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: It all begins with God the Father. While we know comparatively little about Him, what we know is decisive in understanding His supreme position, our relationship to Him, and His superintending role in the plan of salvation, the Creation, and all else that followed.
quotes.note: Marked implied and flagged for review, because the tag is a reading and the reading should be stated plainly rather than smuggled. Oaks does not raise the question of the Father's origin; he does not decline to answer it either. What he says is that little is known about the Father generally, in the opening sentence of the only section of the address devoted to Him, and the section that follows fills the gap entirely with what can be inferred from Christ. The agnostic tag records that posture; it must not be read as Oaks acknowledging and declining a regress question, which would be retrojection. Compare essay-2014-q1, where “little has been revealed” is said of the couplet's backward half specifically and the tag is earned outright.

quotes.excerpt: As Elder Bruce R. McConkie wrote just before his death: “In the ultimate and final sense of the word, there is only one true and living God. He is the Father, the Almighty Elohim, the Supreme Being, the Creator and Ruler of the universe.”
quotes.note: The maximal monotheizing formulation, endorsed from the general conference pulpit as the answer to what the Father is. Tagged reframe rather than for any position on the backward axis: “Supreme Being” and “Creator and Ruler of the universe” are the vocabulary of the tradition the nineteenth-century plurality teaching defined itself against, and adopting it does not deny a chain — it makes the chain unaskable, which is a different and more durable operation. Compare packer-parentage-1984, which performs the same defusing by redefining plurality as the arithmetic of the Godhead. The source is McConkie's A New Witness for the Articles of Faith (1985), 51, which has no entry here; mcconkie-mormon-doctrine is a different book.

quotes.excerpt: A great doctrinal statement by the First Presidency in 1909 declares Him to be “the firstborn among all the sons of God—the first begotten in the spirit, and the only begotten in the flesh.”
quotes.note: Untagged, and the omission is the point. Oaks reaches for the 1909 “Origin of Man” statement (see fp-1909) and takes from it only the two titles that distinguish Christ's spirit begetting from His mortal begetting — the document's actual argument, that man is the literal offspring of heavenly parents and that the Father was once as man now is, goes unmentioned. He cites the 1916 exposition the same way, for the “Father and the Son” title (see fp-1916). Both citesId edges are earned by these two references and by nothing further.

quotes.excerpt: God the Father is the Father of our spirits. We are His children. He loves us, and all that He does is for our eternal benefit. He is the author of the plan of salvation, and it is by His power that His plan achieves its purposes for the ultimate glory of His children.
quotes.note: Untagged context, and the whole of what the address says about divine parentage. Spirit fatherhood is asserted as a relation and left there — no Mother, no mechanism, no premortal begetting scene. Recorded to fix the boundary of the entry: whatever this talk is evidence for, it is not evidence for spirit birth in either direction.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned every excerpt verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2017/2017-04-oaks-the-godhead-and-the-plan-of-salvation.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. This is a negative datapoint and should be used as one. A full apostolic address on the nature of God the Father, in general conference, opening with the claim that His nature “is knowable and is the key to everything else in our doctrine” — and containing no King Follett, no Snow couplet, no Heavenly Mother, no divine progression, and no origin. What it does contain is the McConkie Supreme-Being formulation at q2 and two citations to the 1909 and 1916 statements stripped of everything those documents say about the subject of this dataset. Filed as an original because the argument and its selection of authorities are Oaks's own; the citesId edges are documentary rather than substantive. Referent recorded as father at entry level: the quotes concern the Father, even though none of them makes a backward claim about Him.

title: Dallin H. Oaks, “The Plan and the Proclamation” — exaltation defined as familial
speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session, October 2017, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: While there are various kingdoms and glories, our Heavenly Father’s ultimate desire for His children is what President Monson called “eternal life in the kingdom of God,” which is exaltation in families. This is more than salvation. President Russell M. Nelson has reminded us, “In God’s eternal plan, salvation is an individual matter; [but] exaltation is a family matter.”
quotes.note: Exaltation defined as intrinsically familial rather than individual, and defined that way by contrast — “this is more than salvation.” The generative content is structural: whatever exaltation is, it is not something a person has alone. What is never said is that the family in question grows. The bracketed “[but]” is the published text's.

quotes.excerpt: It also affirms that “gender is an essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity and purpose.”
quotes.note: Untagged, and worth the contrast it provides. The proclamation's eternal-gender clause is restated with no justification offered for why gender should be eternal. Renlund supplies one three years later — “because it provides the basis for the ultimate gift Heavenly Father can give, His kind of life” (renlund-2020-q3) — and that justification is what earns the euphemism tag there. Here the clause stands alone as a claim about identity, and reading the generative warrant into it would be retrojection.

quotes.excerpt: I testify of the truth and eternal importance of the family proclamation, revealed by the Lord Jesus Christ to His Apostles for the exaltation of the children of God (see Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4)
quotes.note: The closing sentence, with the increase passage attached as a bare parenthetical. D&C 131:1–4 is the new-and-everlasting-covenant-of-marriage passage that ends “he cannot have an increase” — the warrant is cited and never read. The same footnote-adjacency pattern as renlund-divine-nature-2022-q7 and ashton-the-father-2018-q2: the nineteenth-century argument is present in the citation apparatus and absent from the body.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned every excerpt verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2017/2017-10-oaks-the-plan-and-the-proclamation.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original despite quoting the proclamation at length, because the address's distinctive content is the insider account of the proclamation's drafting — subjects identified and discussed by the Twelve for nearly a year, language proposed and revised, a text presented to and further changed by the First Presidency — given by one of the seven signatories then living. That history is not excerpted here because it bears on the proclamation's provenance rather than on any category, but it is the reason a researcher would come to this talk, and it is at section IV of the hosted page. No edge to dc-132: the address cites D&C 131, not 132, and D&C 131 has no entry of its own (cfm-2025 is curriculum on that section, not the section).

title: Joy D. Jones re-reads Kimball's “your Mother in heaven” — and elides the spirit-form sentence
speaker: Joy D. Jones
office: Primary General President
venue: General Women's Session, general conference, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt:
President Spencer W. Kimball explained in these glorious words:

“God is your Father. He loves you. He and your Mother in heaven value you beyond any measure. … You are unique. One of a kind, made of the eternal intelligence which gives you claim upon eternal life.

“Let there be no question in your mind about your value as an individual. The whole intent of the gospel plan is to provide an opportunity for each of you to reach your fullest potential, which is eternal progression and the possibility of godhood.”
quotes.note: Both tags come from the same operation, and the operation is only visible against the original. The source is kimball-intelligence-spirit-form-1978, whose q1 runs: “God is your father. He loves you. He and your mother in heaven value you beyond any measure. They gave your eternal intelligence spirit form, just as your earthly mother and father have given you a mortal body. You are unique…” Jones's ellipsis falls exactly on the sentence that supplies the staging and the generative agency — the one place in Kimball's paragraph where heavenly parents *do* something. What survives is the Mother as a valuer, and “eternal intelligence” as a possession rather than as the first term of a sequence. HEAVENLY-MOTHER because she is named, from the pulpit, in 2017, in a general session for women. RETREAT-REFRAME because the cut removes an earlier teaching from a quotation offered as that teaching; the honest qualification is that a speaker trimming a quotation for length would cut the same sentence, and no intent is demonstrable from the text. Recorded because the dataset exists to make such cuts visible, not because it can establish why this one was made. The capitalization also shifts: Kimball's printed text has lowercase “mother in heaven,” the 2017 rendering has “Mother in heaven.” The second paragraph is theosis and nothing more — the A-framing trap — and is included only because it is inside the quotation Jones actually gives.

quotes.excerpt: President Thomas S. Monson said it perfectly when he quoted these words: “The worth of a soul is its capacity to become as God.”
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. Capacity to become as God is theosis, which by the taxonomy's first rule is not evidence for anything generative; kept because it is the address's own summary of human destiny and shows what the 2017 women's session says when it is saying the most — potential, not posterity. Monson is himself quoting, and the published footnote traces it to his April 2006 “Our Sacred Priesthood Trust,” which supplies no earlier source.

notes: Quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2017/2017-10-jones-value-beyond-measure.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline (“Joy D. Jones, Primary General President”), the Kimball quotation with its ellipsis and paragraph break exactly as given here, and footnote 2 in full (“Spencer W. Kimball, ‘Privileges and Responsibilities of Sisters,’ Ensign, Nov. 1978, 105”). Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as a citation rather than an original: the load-bearing sentences are Kimball's, Jones adds no gloss to them, and the footnote names the source precisely enough to draw the citesId edge with confidence — a rarity on this axis, where most Heavenly Mother quotations in conference are sourced to uncited devotional paperbacks (see komatsu-whitney-1987). Two things make the entry worth having. First, it is a 2017 datum on where the doctrine was permitted to appear: a general session for women, five years before renlund-divine-nature-2022 rebuilt the fence around it. Second, it is the only place in the corpus so far where a modern speaker's ellipsis can be laid directly against a dataset entry containing the elided sentence.

title: New Testament Student Manual, ch. 53 (Revelation 1–3)
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Institute curriculum (correlated)
venue: Institute of Religion student manual

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph Smith quoted Revelation 1:6 and focused on the phrase “hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father,” giving this explanation of its meaning: “God the Father of Jesus Christ had a Father. … Paul says that which is earthly is in the likeness of that which is heavenly. Hence if Jesus had a Father, can we not believe that He had a Father also?” (in History of the Church, 6:476).
quotes.note: A-tier as a manual, quoting a B-tier sermon.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph had earlier taught, “God Himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens!” (Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Joseph Smith [2007], 40; see Doctrinal New Testament Commentary, 3:436–37).
quotes.note: The very next sentence on the page. The manual does not stop at the regress: a King Follett past-mortality claim is carried in the same paragraph of current institute curriculum.

notes: The lone surviving explicit backward regress in current curriculum — and, under the citation model, not an independent one. Collapsing citations folds it into the 1844 sermon, which is the analytical payoff: no new backward-explicit original since 1844, and exactly one surviving citation.

title: Brian K. Ashton, “The Father” — born as spirits, and “what Heavenly Father has become”
speaker: Brian K. Ashton
office: Second Counselor in the Sunday School General Presidency
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, October 2018, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: In the premortal world, we were born as spirits to Heavenly Parents and lived with Them as a family. They knew us, taught us, and loved us. We wanted very much to be like our Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: Not marked implied, and the difference from proclamation-1995-q1 is the verb. The proclamation says each person is a spirit son or daughter of heavenly parents, which states a relation; this says we were born as spirits to them, which states an event. Birth rather than adoption, so the viviparous tag rather than the adoption one — but no physiology is described and none should be read in, and the published footnote for the sentence points to the family proclamation and to the “Mother in Heaven” Gospel Topics page rather than to any nineteenth-century account of the mechanism. Capitalized Heavenly Parents and Them as printed.

quotes.excerpt: However, to do so, we recognized that we would have to: Obtain glorified, immortal, physical bodies; Be married and form families by the sealing power of the priesthood; and Acquire all knowledge, power, and divine attributes.
quotes.note: The conditions of becoming like the Father, enumerated as three and only three, in the plainest list of requirements any recent conference address supplies. The generative content is entirely in the apparatus: the marriage condition's published footnote is “See Doctrine and Covenants 132:19–20,” the seeds verses, and the body never says what the sealing power is for beyond forming families. Rated euphemism for that reason; the second condition is what makes this more than a bare theosis statement. Rendered as a run-on because the three items are bullets in the published text; the wording and punctuation are exactly as printed.

quotes.excerpt: Given the distance between what we are as mortals and what Heavenly Father has become, it is not surprising that some feel that becoming like the Father is unattainable. Nevertheless, the scriptures are clear. If we will cleave in faith to Christ, repent, and seek God’s grace through obedience, eventually we will become like the Father.
quotes.note: Marked implied and flagged for review. “What Heavenly Father has become” is a present perfect, and on its face it presupposes divine becoming — which under the father-status precedent is attainment language without explicit mortality, and so FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone. But the claim is carried in a subordinate clause of a sentence about human discouragement, it is nowhere developed, and the same address lists “He does not change” among the Father's attributes four paragraphs earlier (see q4). The honest reading is that the older cosmology survives here as an idiom rather than as a teaching, and the tag records the idiom. No mortality claim of any kind appears in the address, so no FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE tag.

quotes.excerpt: Heavenly Father is love. … He keeps His covenants. He does not change. He cannot lie. … He knows all things—past, present, and future—from the beginning.
quotes.note: Untagged context for q3, and kept because the tension is the interesting thing about this address: a bulleted list of divine attributes that includes immutability, in a talk whose next section speaks of what the Father “has become.” Not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION in either direction — “He does not change” is footnoted to James 1:17 and stands in a catalogue of attributes, not in an intervention in the progression debate, and reading a denial into it would be retrojection of exactly the kind this dataset exists to prevent. Contrast roberts-progress-of-god-1911, which addresses the immutability argument head-on. Elisions mark bullet items omitted; each sentence is a separate bullet in the published text.

quotes.excerpt: There is much we do not understand about becoming like the Father. But I can testify with certainty that striving to become like the Father is worth every sacrifice.
quotes.note: The concession, and it is franker in the footnote than in the body. Published footnote 64 reads in full: “Why can't or won't God reveal more about the process of becoming like Him? I don't honestly know all the reasons. But there are at least two that I do understand. The first is that some things are simply incomprehensible in our mortal estate (see Doctrine and Covenants 78:17). It might be akin to trying to explain the internet to someone who lived in the Middle Ages. The context and perspective are just not there. And the second is that gifts of grace often come to us precisely because we must agonize and struggle through not knowing.” A general officer of the Church stating, in print, that the process of deification is unrevealed — in the same address that lists its three conditions and footnotes them to D&C 132. Tagged reframe for the same reason renlund-divine-nature-2022-q4 is: the reticence is relocated from the speaker to the state of revelation.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned every excerpt and footnote 64 verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2018/2018-10-ashton-the-father.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The most content-dense item in this batch after Packer, and the one whose components pull hardest against each other: literal premortal spirit birth to Heavenly Parents stated as an event; three enumerated conditions for becoming like the Father, one of them sealed marriage footnoted to the seeds verses; a present perfect that presupposes the Father became what He is; a bulleted attribute list containing “He does not change”; and a footnote conceding that the process is unrevealed. All five are in a fifteen-minute talk by a Sunday School general officer, and the address makes no attempt to reconcile any of them, which is itself the finding. Two citesId edges, both earned by published footnotes: footnote 3 to the family proclamation, footnote 6 to D&C 132:19–20. Referent father at entry level, on the strength of q3.

title: Henry B. Eyring: “men and women cannot be exalted alone”
speaker: Henry B. Eyring
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, general women's session, October 2018, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: The proclamation goes on: “Fathers and mothers are obligated to help one another as equal partners.” They are equal partners, equal in their potential for spiritual growth and for acquiring knowledge, and so are unified by helping each other. They are equal in their divine destiny to be exalted together. In fact, men and women cannot be exalted alone.
quotes.note: The coupled-exaltation doctrine in its flattest modern form, from a member of the First Presidency: exaltation is categorically unavailable to an individual. Rated euphemism because that is the whole of it — the doctrine that makes the couple necessary is not stated, and the sentence is doing pastoral work about equal partnership in gospel teaching rather than doctrinal work about what the couple will do. Compare renlund-divine-nature-2022-q7, where the same proposition (“Women and men cannot be exalted without each other”) appears in a footnote appended to D&C 132:19; here it is in the body and the scripture is absent.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned the excerpt verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2018/2018-10-eyring-women-and-gospel-learning-in-the-home.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. A lean entry by design: one sentence, quotable, and the rest of the address is about mothers as gospel educators in the home and bears on nothing this dataset tracks. The citesId edge to the family proclamation is earned by the quotation that opens the excerpt.

title: Dallin H. Oaks: “Children are our most precious gift from God—our eternal increase”
speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, general women's session, October 2018, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Children are our most precious gift from God—our eternal increase. Yet we live in a time when many women wish to have no part in the bearing and nurturing of children. … Each of these trends works against our Father’s divine plan of salvation.
quotes.note: The opening sentence of the address, and the technical term running the other way. Through the nineteenth century and well into the twentieth, “eternal increase” named the posterity of the exalted — see richards-eternal-increase-1915, slrichards-eternal-increase-1938, kimball-godhood-1952, morris-eternal-increase-1959, all of which locate it after this life. Here it is apposed directly to children born in mortality, in the first line of a talk whose argument is demographic. Two tags, and the second needs its caveat: nothing suggests Oaks is consciously performing an operation on the older usage, and the reading available on the plain text is simply that sealed children are eternal because the sealing is. The reframe tag records the semantic shift, not an intention. The euphemism tag is earned because the phrase still carries its eternal freight — mortal childbearing is being described in the vocabulary of exalted posterity, which is precisely how the claim survives without being made. Elision marks the demographic sentences between.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned the opening paragraph verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2018/2018-10-oaks-parents-and-children.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Delivered in the same session as eyring-exalted-together-2018, immediately after it, which is worth noting: within one hour the women of the Church heard that exaltation is unavailable alone and that children are our eternal increase, and neither statement was connected to the other or to what the exalted are said to receive. The citesId edge is earned by the address's own sentence that its teachings on motherhood “are all based on ‘The Family: A Proclamation to the World.’” No edge to dc-132 or to any increase text: the phrase is used without citation, which is part of what makes the shift legible.

title: Dallin H. Oaks, “Two Great Commandments”
speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General Conference women's session, October 2019, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: That highest destiny is possible only through marriage for eternity. Eternal life includes the creative powers inherent in the combination of male and female—what modern revelation describes as the “continuation of the seeds forever and ever.”
quotes.note: The final noun — spirit children — is left unstated; the scriptural code phrase carries the content. The clearest twenty-first-century conference instance of the euphemism register.

notes: Wording verified against the hosted talk (October 2019 general conference, Sunday morning session). Confirm the exact talk from the October 2019 sessions before publishing.

title: Dallin H. Oaks, “Trust in the Lord” — the standard of official doctrine applied to the next life
speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session, October 2019, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Many members of the Church have had visions or other inspirations to inform them about how things operate or are organized in the spirit world, but these personal spiritual experiences are not to be understood or taught as the official doctrine of the Church.
quotes.note: The first of three fences, and the narrowest: personal visions of postmortal conditions are disqualified as doctrine. Note the scope carefully — the subject throughout is the spirit world between death and resurrection, not the celestial kingdom and not exaltation.

quotes.excerpt: In the following conference, Elder Andersen taught this principle: “The doctrine is taught by all 15 members of the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve. It is not hidden in an obscure paragraph of one talk.” The family proclamation, signed by all 15 prophets, seers, and revelators, is a wonderful illustration of that principle.
quotes.note: The consequential one, and the reason this entry belongs in this dataset at all. Quoted approvingly from Neil L. Andersen (October 2012) and endorsed by a member of the First Presidency, the standard is that doctrine is what all fifteen teach — which, applied to the material this timeline collects, disqualifies most of it: an apostle's conference address, a general officer's enumeration, an institute manual paragraph. Oaks is not applying the rule to the generative teaching, and this entry does not claim he is. He is applying it to speculation about the spirit world. But the rule as stated is general, and the only example he offers of a teaching that meets it is the family proclamation.

quotes.excerpt: We can all wonder privately about circumstances in the spirit world or even discuss these or other unanswered questions in family or other intimate settings. But let us not teach or use as official doctrine what does not meet the standards of official doctrine.
quotes.note: The instruction, and the same relocation Renlund performs three years later: wondering is permitted, teaching is not (compare renlund-divine-nature-2022-q2, “Reason cannot replace revelation”). The permitted venue shrinks from the pulpit to the family circle.

quotes.excerpt: That same principle applies to unanswered questions about sealings in the next life or desired readjustments because of events or transgressions in mortality. There is so much we do not know that our only sure reliance is to trust in the Lord and His love for His children.
quotes.note: The one sentence that reaches past the spirit world. Sealings in the next life are named as an area of unanswered questions to which the do-not-teach rule applies — which touches the eternal-marriage axis directly, though not the generative one, and which is answering the plural-marriage question the address opens with (a widower's second wife asking whether she would have her own house). Recorded with that limit stated, because it is the passage most likely to be over-read.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned every excerpt verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2019/2019-10-oaks-trust-in-the-lord.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Distinct from oaks-2019, which is Oaks's other October 2019 address, “Two Great Commandments” (hosted at /study/general-conference/2019/10/35oaks) — different talk, different session, no overlap of content; the two entries should not be merged. Scope caution, and it should govern any use of this entry: the address is about the postmortal spirit world, and its explicit targets are near-death literature, members' private visions, and speculation about living arrangements after death. It says nothing about exaltation, spirit birth, divine progression, or the Father's origin. What it contributes is the boundary rule itself, stated by the First Presidency in conference and illustrated only by the family proclamation, which is the standard against which every other item in this dataset's twentieth-century material would have to be measured if the rule were applied backward.

title: Dale G. Renlund and Ruth Lybbert Renlund, “The Divine Purposes of Sexual Intimacy”
speaker: Dale G. Renlund and Ruth Lybbert Renlund
office: Quorum of the Twelve Apostles (Dale G. Renlund), writing with Ruth Lybbert Renlund
venue: Ensign, August 2020

quotes.excerpt: We were created by loving heavenly parents to grow up to become like them.
quotes.note: Lowercase “heavenly parents” as printed. Included as context for the quotes below: the article's frame is plural divine parenthood as the thing we grow into, which is what lets the later sexuality claims land without ever stating a mechanism.

quotes.excerpt: Our proper expression of sexuality makes it possible for God's plan to unfold on earth and in the eternities, qualifying us to become like our Heavenly Father.
quotes.note: “And in the eternities” is doing the load-bearing work — the sentence extends the relevance of sexuality past mortality without saying what it does there.

quotes.excerpt: That is why gender is not fluid in the eternities—because it provides the basis for the ultimate gift Heavenly Father can give, His kind of life.
quotes.note: The strongest encoding in the article: eternal sexed difference is justified by what it makes possible, and what it makes possible is named only as “His kind of life.” Compare gospel-principles-2011-q1, where “the kind of life God lives” is the term that gets defined as including spirit-parenthood. The two phrasings are near-identical; only the manual supplies the definition.

quotes.excerpt: After mortality, the faithful are promised that “they shall pass by the angels … to their exaltation and glory … which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever. Then shall they be gods, because they have no end” (Doctrine and Covenants 132:19–20).
quotes.note: The D&C 132 quotation arrives in an article explicitly about sexual intimacy, which is as close to an interpretive gloss on “seeds” as the article gets — adjacency rather than statement.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live article (byline as printed: “By Elder Dale G. Renlund of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Ruth Lybbert Renlund”). The most strongly encoded item in this batch. Every component of the generative claim is present and separately stated — heavenly parents we grow into, sexuality that matters “in the eternities,” eternal gender justified by the gift it enables, “continuation of the seeds” — and the article never assembles them. Tagged euphemism throughout on the v2 no-retrojection rule: the assembly is the reader's, not the authors'. Note also the counter-reading available on the plain text, that “His kind of life” means exaltation generally; the entry does not foreclose it.

title: The Eternal Family class preparation material (2022), Lesson 10
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Institute curriculum (correlated)
venue: The Eternal Family Class Preparation Material (2022), “Lesson 10 Class Preparation Material: The New and Everlasting Covenant of Marriage”

quotes.excerpt: Celestial marriage includes the blessing of “hav[ing] children in … celestial glory” (Joseph Smith, in History, 1838–1856 [Manuscript History of the Church], volume D-1, 1551 [josephsmithpapers.org]).
quotes.note: Under the heading “Why should I strive to have an eternal marriage?” Rated explicit because the children are located in celestial glory rather than in mortality — this is post-mortal childbearing named as a blessing, not “posterity” left ambiguous. But note what it does not say: “spirit” is absent, and the curriculum's bracket and ellipsis are both inside a four-word quotation, so the manual is transmitting Joseph Smith's phrase rather than authoring a claim of its own.

quotes.excerpt: We learn from the Bible Dictionary that “Abraham first received the gospel by baptism (which is the covenant of salvation). Then he had conferred upon him the higher priesthood, and he entered into celestial marriage (which is the covenant of exaltation), gaining assurance thereby that he would have eternal increase [an innumerable posterity]” (Bible Dictionary, “Abraham, covenant of”).
quotes.note: The page does gloss increase, in the manual's own bracket — the editorial hand ttf-2004 is faulted for withholding. Euphemism rather than explicit: the gloss stops at “posterity,” which does not discriminate spirit offspring from sealed mortal descendants.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page. Two corrections to the survey that flagged this item: the page contains no “creative powers” language and no male/female complementarity language at all — searches for “creative,” “procreative” and “male and female” return nothing on this page, though “exaltation” and “posterity” each appear twice — so any pairing of this lesson with the Oaks/Renlund creative-powers register is unsupported and would have to come from a different lesson in the course. What is here is the single bracketed Joseph Smith fragment above, together with the Bible Dictionary gloss of eternal increase carried at q2. Logged as an original because the quoted 1843 history statement has no entry in this dataset; if one is added, convert to a citation. Compare johnson-2025, which names post-mortal childbearing in a pastoral register and is rated the same way for the same reason.

title: Dale G. Renlund, “Your Divine Nature and Eternal Destiny” — revealed, and fenced
speaker: Dale G. Renlund
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, women's session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: The second truth is that we have heavenly parents, a father and a mother. The doctrine of a Heavenly Mother comes by revelation and is a distinctive belief among Latter-day Saints. President Dallin H. Oaks explained the importance of this truth: “Our theology begins with heavenly parents. Our highest aspiration is to be like them.”
quotes.note: The affirmation, and it is stronger than Hinckley's on the one axis that matters most. "The doctrine of a Heavenly Mother comes by revelation" is the direct contrary of hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q5, "her of whom we have no revealed knowledge," and it restores the epistemic claim that Hinckley's closing sentence had removed — thirty-one years later, to a comparable audience, from the same pulpit. It also restores what iverson-mother-in-heaven-1908 had asserted and 1991 had converted into an argument from silence. Note the ground shifts but the content does not: nothing further about her is stated here than in 1991.

quotes.excerpt: Very little has been revealed about Mother in Heaven, but what we do know is summarized in a gospel topic found in our Gospel Library application. Once you have read what is there, you will know everything that I know about the subject. I wish I knew more. You too may still have questions and want to find more answers. Seeking greater understanding is an important part of our spiritual development, but please be cautious. Reason cannot replace revelation.
quotes.note: The fence, and the pivot of the address. Three moves in six sentences: the content is capped ("very little"), the ceiling is set at a Gospel Library page rather than at an apostle's own knowledge ("you will know everything that I know"), and the traditional warrant for the doctrine is disqualified outright — "Reason cannot replace revelation." That last clause retires the argument that had carried the doctrine for 137 years: Erastus Snow's inference from nature (snow-heavenly-mother-1885), Rudger Clawson's "Who ever heard of a father where there was no mother?" (clawson-mother-there-1929), Orson F. Whitney's dare to prove it unphilosophic (whitney-father-and-mother-1907), and Hinckley's own "Logic and reason would certainly suggest" (hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q3). The 1991 affirmation and the 2022 prohibition rest on opposite epistemologies, and the 2022 one forbids the 1991 one. Carries both tags for the same reason the Hinckley entry does: the affirmation and the boundary are the same sentence-cluster.

quotes.excerpt: Speculation will not lead to greater spiritual knowledge, but it can lead us to deception or divert our focus from what has been revealed. For example, the Savior taught His disciples, “Always pray unto the Father in my name.” We follow this pattern and direct our worship to our Heavenly Father in the name of Jesus Christ and do not pray to Heavenly Mother.
quotes.note: The prohibition on prayer, restated for a new generation and — this is the point to record — restated without Hinckley. The published footnote for the sentence cites Russell M. Nelson's "Lessons from the Lord's Prayers" (Ensign or Liahona, May 2009), not the 1991 address that is the modern origin of the rule. The scriptural pattern argument survives from 1991 (hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991-q4); the argument from the absence of precedent among Church presidents does not reappear. Note also the framing: what was in 1991 the correction of a named practice by "some few women of the Church" is here a general caution against "speculation," with no group named and nothing to have been done wrong.

quotes.excerpt: Ever since God appointed prophets, they have been authorized to speak on His behalf. But they do not pronounce doctrines fabricated “of [their] own mind” or teach what has not been revealed. … Latter-day prophets are similarly constrained. Demanding revelation from God is both arrogant and unproductive. Instead, we wait on the Lord and His timetable to reveal His truths through the means that He has established.
quotes.note: The most consequential paragraph in the address and the one least often quoted. The reticence is relocated a third time. Spencer W. Kimball had relocated it to the Mother herself — "maternal modesty," "restrained, queenly elegance" (kimball-doctrinal-hymn-1978); Hinckley relocated it to the state of revelation; Renlund relocates it to the office, which is now described as constrained rather than reticent. Prophets do not decline to say more, they are unable to, and asking them to is "arrogant." The Balaam analogy is elided; the bracketed "[their]" is the published text's.

quotes.excerpt: The third truth in the opening paragraph of the Young Women theme is that we have “a divine nature.” This is intrinsic to who we are. It is spiritually “genetic,” inherited from our heavenly parents, and requires no effort on our part.
quotes.note: Inheritance language, scare-quoted. "Spiritually 'genetic'" is a heredity metaphor from a cardiologist and is as close as the address comes to any mechanism — but the quotation marks are doing the fencing, and the claim is about nature rather than about generation. HEAVENLY-MOTHER because the parents are plural and are the source; no SPIRIT-BIRTH tag, in either direction, because none is stated.

quotes.excerpt: Our Heavenly Father wants you to become His heir and receive all that He has. He cannot offer you more. He cannot promise you more.
quotes.note: The peroration, and the forward direction as it now sounds: maximal in scope, empty of content. "All that He has" is the D&C 84:38 formula, and the footnote points there. Compare renlund-2020-q3, where the same author encodes the same thing as "His kind of life" — the two together are the clearest available sample of how the generative claim is carried in current apostolic discourse, which is by inheritance vocabulary that never says what is inherited.

quotes.excerpt: Dallin H. Oaks, “Apostasy and Restoration,” Ensign, May 1995, 87; see also Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4; 132:19. Women and men cannot be exalted without each other.
quotes.note: Published footnote 8 in full, and the only place in the address where D&C 132 appears. The last sentence is Renlund's own gloss, not part of the Oaks citation: a bare statement that exaltation requires both sexes, appended to the "continuation of the seeds" verse (see dc-132) and to the new-and-everlasting-covenant-of-marriage verses, in a footnote to a talk about a Young Women theme. The whole nineteenth-century argument is present in that adjacency and is nowhere in the body text — which is precisely the pattern this dataset exists to make visible.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2022/2022-04-renlund-your-divine-nature-and-eternal-destiny.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline ("By Elder Dale G. Renlund of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles"), the opening of each excerpted paragraph, and footnote 8 in full, all verbatim. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. The direct sequel to hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991 and the entry that should be read immediately after it, but the relationship is not the one usually assumed, and three things should be checked against the text rather than repeated from summaries. First, Renlund does not quote or cite Hinckley anywhere in the address or its forty footnotes — the fence is rebuilt from scratch, citing Oaks (1995) for the affirmation and Nelson (2009) for the prayer restriction. Second, he does not cite "O My Father" or Eliza R. Snow, which is why this entry carries no citesId edge to o-my-father: the hymn that had licensed the doctrine from 1845 through Hinckley's own 1991 address has dropped out entirely, and the authority now runs to a Gospel Library page. That page and the Gospel Topics essay "Mother in Heaven" (essay-2015) are named in footnotes 7, 9 and 16 as the whole of what may be known; no edge is drawn to essay-2015 because it is itself a citation-type entry and the dataset draws citesId edges only to originals, but the delegation is the substantive fact and is recorded here. The only citesId is dc-132, earned by footnote 8. Third, the shape is the inverse of 1991 on the epistemic axis and identical on the practical one: Hinckley affirmed the doctrine on logic and then emptied it by denying revelation; Renlund affirms the revelation and then empties it by capping the content and disqualifying the logic. Both end in the same place — she is real, and there is nothing further to say — by opposite routes. What is genuinely new in 2022 is the handoff: the authority on the subject is no longer a hymn, an apostle, or an inference, but a page in an app, and the address says so twice.

title: Russell M. Nelson: procreation as “the one privilege of godhood”
speaker: Russell M. Nelson
office: President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, October 2023, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: Many of the adversary’s most relentless temptations involve violations of moral purity. The power to create life is the one privilege of godhood that Heavenly Father allows His mortal children to exercise. Thus, God set clear guidelines for the use of this living, divine power.
quotes.note: The President of the Church classifying procreation as an attribute of godhood — not as a stewardship, not as a sacred trust, but as one of the privileges of being a God, temporarily extended. Rated euphemism because the classification is all there is: it says the power mortals exercise is a divine one, and never says that the exalted exercise it. Structurally identical to packer-plan-of-happiness-2015-q1 eight years earlier, and delivered in the same setting, a chastity passage. Italics on one privilege are the published text's.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned the paragraph verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2023/2023-10-nelson-think-celestial.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. A lean entry: one sentence out of an address about eternal perspective, temple building, and twenty new temples. No citesId — the address quotes D&C 132:7 on covenants having an end when men are dead, which is a different passage from the D&C 132:19–20, 63 material recorded at dc-132, and drawing the edge on a shared section number would misrepresent what is being cited.

title: Matthew L. Carpenter, “Fruit That Remains”
speaker: Matthew L. Carpenter
office: Of the Seventy
venue: General Conference, April 2024, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: What are the blessings of exaltation? They include dwelling in God's presence for eternity together as husband and wife, inheriting “thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, … and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever,” receiving all that God the Father has.
quotes.note: The speaker poses the question directly — “What are the blessings of exaltation?” — which is exactly the moment a gloss would belong, and then answers it in the scripture's own vocabulary. The elision inside the quotation is the talk's own, not this dataset's.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live talk; the paragraph ends at “receiving all that God the Father has.” with nothing following. Structurally identical to oaks-2019 five years earlier: the D&C 132 code phrase is deployed in conference and the final noun is never supplied. Carpenter's case is the tighter one, because he is answering an enumerating question of his own asking and still declines the gloss — the omission is not an artifact of the talk drifting past the topic.

title: Brian K. Taylor brackets Whitney's “Father and Mother in heaven”
speaker: Brian K. Taylor
office: Of the Seventy
venue: General conference, April 2024, “Swallowed Up in the Joy of Christ”

quotes.excerpt: Helping us find further meaning in our trials, Elder Orson F. Whitney taught: “No pain that we suffer, no trial that we experience is wasted. It ministers to our education. … All … that we [patiently] endure … builds up our characters, purifies our hearts, expands our souls, and makes us more tender and charitable. … It is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our [heavenly parents].”
quotes.note: The published text prints the bracket: Whitney's original reads “more like our Father and Mother in heaven,” as quoted intact by Komatsu (April 1987, komatsu-whitney-1987) and Howard W. Hunter (October 1987, howard-hunter-whitney-1987). The substitution of “[heavenly parents]” for the named Mother is an editorial act inside a quotation — the same passage, thirty-seven years apart, with the Mother generalized away. HEAVENLY-MOTHER is hedges: the plural formula affirms her only implicitly, which is precisely what the edit accomplishes.

notes: Entered for the quotation's edit, not the sermon's argument — the talk is a pastoral address on affliction. Wording verified against the Pulpit vault text (1.0000 collation against the hosted page per vault frontmatter); the bracket is in the published text, not a transcription artifact. Pairs with jones-mother-in-heaven-2017, whose elision cuts the sentence where heavenly parents act: two independent instances of quotation-level softening around the Mother.

title: Rubén V. Alliaud: “God the Father ‘is an exalted man’” in general conference
speaker: Rubén V. Alliaud
office: Of the Seventy
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, October 2024, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: We believe that God the Father “is an exalted man” with a glorified “body of flesh and bones as tangible as man’s; [and] the Son also.” Thus, every time we talk about the nature of God, in some way, somehow, we are also talking about our own nature.
quotes.note: Attainment language without a mortality claim, which under the father-status precedent is FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone — the same reading given romney-exalted-man-1958-q1, where Joseph Smith's phrase is likewise quoted rather than argued. What Alliaud quotes is the first half of Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Joseph Smith, 40–41, and what he leaves out is the clause immediately around it in the source, “God Himself was once as we are now” (compare nt-manual-2018-q2, which quotes that clause in full). The symmetry sentence that follows is his own and is the strongest part of the passage: it makes talk about God's nature and talk about human nature the same conversation, which is the King Follett premise stated as a method. No mortality tag, because the address states none.

quotes.excerpt: Now, you might say, “But many people believe we are children of God.” Yes, that is true, but their understanding may be a little different from the implication of its deeper meaning that we affirm. For Latter-day Saints, this teaching is not metaphorical. Rather, we truly believe that we are all literally the children of God. He is “the Father of [our] spirits,” and because of that, we have the potential to become like Him, which seems to be inconceivable to some.
quotes.note: Marked implied. Literal divine sonship asserted against the metaphorical reading, and the literalness explicitly identified as what distinguishes the Latter-day Saint claim — but the mechanism is never stated and the spirit fatherhood is proof-texted to Hebrews 12:9 rather than to any account of begetting. Rated hedges on the same basis as proclamation-1995-q1. Note also the inference Alliaud draws from literal descent, which is theosis and not generation: “because of that, we have the potential to become like Him.” No Mother appears in the address.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page, which returned both excerpts verbatim; the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2024/2024-10-alliaud-sons-and-daughters-of-god.md carries a 1.0000 heavyweight diff against the same page. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as a citation, following the nt-manual-2018 logic: the backward-direction content is entirely inherited — an eight-word quotation from a correlated manual reprinting the King Follett material — and the collapse-to-originals view should fold it into kfd-1844. The reason to record it anyway is the date and the venue. This is the exalted-man formulation spoken from the general conference pulpit in October 2024, framed as “one of the most joyful, glorious, and powerful gospel truths that God has revealed” and offered as the explanation of why another Christian body would not recognize Latter-day Saint baptism. Ten years after essay-2014 declared that little has been revealed about the first half of the couplet and consequently little is taught, the second-hand version of the first half is still being taught.

title: Doctrine and Covenants Seminary Teacher Manual (2025), Lesson 140 on D&C 131
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Seminary curriculum (correlated)
venue: Doctrine and Covenants Seminary Teacher Manual (2025), “Lesson 140—Doctrine and Covenants 131: The New and Everlasting Covenant of Marriage”

quotes.excerpt: Read Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4, looking for what the Prophet taught about marriage.
quotes.note: The lesson does not reproduce the verses on the page; students are sent to them. So the word “increase” never appears in the manual's own text at all — the reading assignment carries it and the instruction narrows what to look for to “marriage.”

quotes.excerpt: To become like God and live with Him again in the celestial kingdom, we must enter the new and everlasting covenant of marriage.
quotes.note: The doctrinal statement students are told to write down — the lesson's takeaway, and the replacement for the 2014 manual's spirit-offspring material. Marriage is presented as the requirement; what marriage is a requirement *for* stops at “become like God.”

quotes.excerpt: Those who are exalted will live eternally with Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ and become like Them.
quotes.note: The lesson's only description of what exaltation consists of. Association and likeness, no generative content.

quotes.excerpt: How do you think marriage can prepare us to become more like God?
quotes.note: The discussion question. Opened and left open — the manual supplies teachers no answer that mentions children, posterity, or increase.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live lesson: I checked specifically for the word “increase” and for any gloss of it as spirit children, posterity, or offspring after the resurrection, and found none anywhere on the page. Lesson headings in order are Understanding marriage / Eternal marriage / The importance of marriage in God's plan / Explain the doctrine of marriage / Memorize / Additional Resources / Supplemental Learning Activities. The measurement is the contrast with seminary-2014, which taught the same scripture block to the same age group and gave teachers the First Presidency's “parents of spirit offspring,” McConkie's “spirit progeny,” and Parley Pratt's queen-mother passage; eleven years later the material is simply gone rather than replaced by a denial. Two cautions for the reader: (1) this is a softening in one lesson, not a repudiation — ftsoy-2025 printed “eternal spirit children of their own” the same year; (2) citesId points at dc-132 because that is the dataset's entry for the increase/seeds text, though the lesson itself is on D&C 131, which has no entry yet. Distinct from cfm-2025, which logs the Come, Follow Me treatment of the same block; the two are companion measurements, not duplicates.

title: David A. Edwards, “After This Life: Answers to Some Questions”
speaker: David A. Edwards
office: Church Magazines staff writer
venue: For the Strength of Youth (official magazine for teenagers), July 2025

quotes.excerpt: They participate in His work and glory. They were sealed in marriage for eternity and now live in eternal families, having eternal spirit children of their own.
quotes.note: Under the heading “What goes on in the celestial kingdom?” Both nouns are present and unhedged: “spirit children,” and “of their own” — the offspring belong to the exalted couple, not to God. No euphemism is doing any work here.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live page. The most explicit forward-generative statement in current correlated print, and the register is what makes it notable: not an institute manual for adult students of scripture but a staff-written FAQ placed before teenagers in 2025. The author is Church Magazines staff, not a General Authority — worth stating, because the explicitness of the sentence tempts a stronger attribution than the byline supports. Its value is as a correlation datum (an editorial decision to print the sentence), not as an authoritative pronouncement.

title: Camille N. Johnson, “Lessons Learned in Inviting Christ to Author My Story”
speaker: Camille N. Johnson
office: Relief Society General President
venue: Liahona (official magazine)

quotes.excerpt: ...whether we are sealed and bear children in this life or the next, our object is exaltation—which can be ours if we make and keep covenants.
quotes.note: Caveat in the v2 spirit of referent discipline: in context this comforts couples childless in mortality, and the plainest reading is posthumous fulfilment of sealing promises. It entails post-mortal childbearing but does not specify spirit children — the object of “bear children... in the next [life]” is left open, and a millennial or resurrected reading is available. Kept explicit because it does name post-mortal childbearing, which nothing else in current correlated print does.

notes: A rare recent explicit, arriving in a pastoral rather than doctrinal register — which may be precisely why it could be said at all.

title: Doctrine and Covenants curriculum (2025), D&C 131 material
speaker: Church Educational System
office: Come, Follow Me / seminary curriculum (correlated)
venue: 2025 Doctrine and Covenants curriculum

quotes.excerpt: There are many things we don’t know about exaltation or life in the highest degree of the celestial kingdom—the kind of life God lives. Much of it may be beyond our current ability to understand. But God has revealed a few precious clues, and many of them are found in Doctrine and Covenants 130–32.
quotes.note: The comparison to capture is narrow and concrete: same scripture block, eleven years apart, with the spirit-offspring sentence absent. Stronger than the entry anticipated: the week titled “Doctrine and Covenants 129–132” never cites section 131 at all (zero occurrences of “131” on the page) and never uses the word “increase” of exaltation — readers are routed to “Doctrine and Covenants 130–32” and then to D&C 132:13–21, 132:1–2, 29–40 and 132:19.

notes: Paired entry to the 2014 seminary manual. Both cite the same original, and the difference between what each adds to it is the measurement.

title: Ronald A. Rasband at the proclamation's thirtieth anniversary: “heavenly parents,” and a refusal to set the document aside
speaker: Ronald A. Rasband
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Saturday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: Everyone belongs to a family, whether you are a mother, father, daughter, son, grandchild, grandparent, aunt, uncle, brother, sister, or cousin. Most importantly, each of us is, as the proclamation states, “a beloved spirit son or daughter of heavenly parents … [with] a divine nature and destiny.”
quotes.note: The proclamation's second sentence, recited as the address's premise. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER because the parents are plural and are named as ours; no SPIRIT-BIRTH tag, because “spirit son or daughter” states the relation and not its origin, and the proclamation itself declines to say more. The ellipsis and the bracketed “[with]” are the published talk's own.

quotes.excerpt:
When presented, the proclamation did not align with the views of many in the world. Not then. Not now. There are those who take issue with the declaration on family, marriage, and gender. Some suggest the Church pull it back, revise, or even set the proclamation aside.

The proclamation on the family is, as President Hinckley stated, doctrine, my dear brothers and sisters. The principles are not out of step but perfectly in step with the ways of the Lord and His covenant path. The teachings of the proclamation were revealed by our Lord Jesus Christ to His Apostles then and now.
quotes.note: Untagged, and deliberately so: the taxonomy has RETREAT-REFRAME for a later text that softens an earlier teaching and nothing for the opposite move, which is what this is. Recorded because the opposite move is rarer and more informative. An Apostle names the revision proposals aloud from the pulpit, declines them, and reasserts the document's status in the strongest available word. Whatever else the thirtieth anniversary did, it did not loosen the “heavenly parents” clause — the clause is quoted twice in the address and defended once, and the defense is of the document rather than of the doctrine. Worth reading against renlund-divine-nature-2022, where the same axis is affirmed and then fenced; here it is affirmed and entrenched, with no fence and no caution about speculation anywhere in the text.

quotes.excerpt: President Nelson taught: “You are literally spirit children of God. … Make no mistake about it: Your potential is divine. With your diligent seeking, God will give you glimpses of who you may become.”
quotes.note: Relayed, not original: the published footnote gives Russell M. Nelson, “Choices for Eternity” (worldwide devotional for young adults, May 15, 2022). Tagged on the same ground as ballard-heavenly-parents-2013-q3 and fp-1916 — the word literally is the whole of the claim, and it excludes a figurative or adoptive reading without supplying a mechanism. Note the pairing it makes with q1: the proclamation clause gives plural parents without literality, the Nelson clause gives literality without a Mother, and the address never puts the two together.

quotes.excerpt: For those with concerns, know that you are a child of heavenly parents, part of your Heavenly Father’s family. No one knows you better or cares more deeply about you than He does.
quotes.note: The plural in Rasband's own voice, footnoted to the proclamation, addressed to members who feel excluded by the document. The second sentence is the pattern the whole corpus shows: the parents are plural in the premise and singular the moment anyone is asked to turn to them. Compare hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991 and renlund-divine-nature-2022, where the same asymmetry is stated as a rule rather than performed in passing.

notes: Quoted verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/2025/2025-10-rasband-the-family-proclamationwords-from-god.md, whose heavyweight pass diffed the vault body against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page paragraph by paragraph at a 1.0000 match; the live page was re-fetched during drafting on 2026-08-10 and returned the byline (“Elder Ronald A. Rasband, Quorum of the Twelve Apostles”) and the opening of each excerpted passage verbatim. Official published text, so A, and currently hosted, so current-correlated. Filed as an original with a citesId edge to proclamation-1995 rather than as a citation: the proclamation supplies the quoted clauses, but the address's own contribution — the refusal to revise, and the account of how the document came to be presented at a Relief Society meeting — is independent of it. Two contextual facts the entry should carry. First, the thirtieth-anniversary framing means this is the Church's own designated occasion for restating the document, which makes the absence of any softening a dateable fact rather than an impression. Second, the “heavenly parents” clause is doing pastoral work here, not cosmological work: it appears in the opening premise and again in the paragraph addressed to members who do not fit, and nothing in the address builds on it. Nothing in the text touches eternal increase, divine progression, or the Father's origin.

title: Neil L. Andersen: “thrones, powers, and dominions in the eternal world” — and “eternal posterity” in the footnote
speaker: Neil L. Andersen
office: Of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session

quotes.excerpt: At that moment, kneeling across the altar, we have a growing realization of the depth of our commitment to God and to each other. The sacred ordinance binds us together with our eternal companion and with God. We solemnly vow to keep the covenants, and the Lord promises us, as we are faithful, unspeakable blessings in mortality and beyond, including thrones, powers, and dominions in the eternal world.
quotes.note: The body-text version of the promise, and it is the D&C 132:19 list with the generative clause removed. The revelation reads “thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, dominions, all heights and depths … and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever”; what survives into the sentence a congregation hears in 2026 is the three nouns that name status and none of the words that name posterity. Hedges rather than affirms: nothing in the sentence commits to offspring, and the footnote that does is not read aloud.

quotes.excerpt: “A man and woman who are faithful to this covenant are joined together as husband and wife for all eternity. The couple has sealed upon them … all the blessings of God’s everlasting covenant, the highest of which is exaltation with eternal posterity (see Doctrine and Covenants 132:19–20; see also 66:2; 131:1–4; and 27.3 and 38.4 in this handbook).”
quotes.note: Published footnote 7, quoting “Temple Sealing” in the General Handbook, 3.5.3.5. This is where the content actually sits. “Exaltation with eternal posterity” gives increase an object, which the body text never does, and it is the current Church handbook — not a nineteenth-century sermon — saying it is the highest blessing of the everlasting covenant. Still hedges on the dataset's proposition, on the dew-2001 precedent: “posterity” does not distinguish new spirit offspring from mortal descendants sealed forward, and the handbook supplies no mechanism. The ellipsis inside the quotation is the published talk's own, not an editorial cut here. Recorded because the location is the finding: the strongest forward statement in a 2026 apostolic address is in a footnote, quoting an administrative handbook, citing D&C 132:19–20.

quotes.excerpt: President Russell M. Nelson said: “We need not be dismayed if our earnest efforts toward perfection now seem so arduous and endless. *Perfection is pending.* It can come in full only after the Resurrection and only through the Lord. It awaits all who love him and keep his commandments. It includes thrones, kingdoms, principalities, powers, and dominions. It is the end for which we are to endure. It is the eternal perfection that God has in store for each of us”
quotes.note: Published footnote 4, attached to the “thrones, powers, and dominions” sentence and quoting Nelson's “Perfection Pending” (Ensign, Nov. 1995, 88). The same operation performed twice in one talk: the D&C 132:19 list is recited — here at greater length, with kingdoms and principalities restored — and stopped one clause short of “a continuation of the seeds forever and ever.” The asterisks are the italics of the published text.
